en: The Introduction to the Pañcatantra. Om! Salutations to the illustrious Śāradā, Gaṇapati, and the Gurus.
Homage to the great poets!
Brahmā, Rudra, Kumāra, Hari, Varuṇa, Yama, Vahni, Indra, Kubera,
the Moon and Sun, Sarasvatī, the Ocean, the [four] Ages, the Mountains, Vāyu, the Earth, and the Serpents;
May the Siddhas, the rivers, the Aśvins, Śrī, Diti, the sons of Aditi, the Mothers beginning with Caṇḍikā,
the Vedas, the sacred fords, the Yakṣas, the Gaṇas, the Vasus, the Munis, and the Planets protect us eternally.
Salutations to Manu, Vācaspati, Śukra, Parāśara with his son,
and to the learned Cāṇakya— homage be to those authors of the treatises on polity.
Having surveyed the essence of all treatises on worldly affairs in this world, Viṣṇuśarman composed this most enchanting science by means of five chapters.
Thus it is heard:
there is a city named Mahilāropya in the southern country.

Therein lived a king named Amaraśakti, who was like a wish-fulfilling tree for the multitude of all supplicants; whose pair of feet were anointed by the mass of rays from the jewels in the crowns of preeminent kings; and who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.

He had three sons of extremely dull intellect, named Vasuśakti, Ugraśakti, and Anekaśakti. Then, observing that they were averse to the sciences and devoid of discernment, the king summoned his ministers and said: "Sirs, you are aware that these three sons of mine are indeed averse to the sciences and lacking in discrimination."
Therefore, for me who sees these things, even a vast kingdom does not bring happiness.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Between those unborn, those dead, and the foolish, it is better that sons be born or dead than that they be fools."
For those two, a fool might burn for as long as he lives, yet it would result in only slight suffering.
Better is miscarriage, better is not approaching one's wife during her fertile seasons,
better is a son born as a corpse, and better even is the birth of a daughter;
better is a barren wife, and better even is dwelling within the womb.
And even if a son is endowed with beauty, wealth, and virtue, he is not [dear] to those who lack discernment.
What is the use of that cow which neither gives birth nor yields milk?
What is the purpose of a son who is born but neither learned nor devoted?
Therefore, let some means be employed so that their intellects may be awakened. In this regard, there are five hundred scholars residing here who subsist on the stipend granted by me;
hence, let it be carried out in such a way that my desires reach fulfillment.
Thereupon, one said: "Your Majesty, grammar is studied for twelve years;
after that come the treatises on Dharma such as those of Manu and others, the treatises on Artha such as those of Cāṇakya and others, and the treatises on Kāma such as those of Vātsyāyana and others.
In this way, the treatises on Dharma, Artha, and Kāma are mastered."
Then, an awakening occurred.
Then, from among them, a minister named Sumati said: "This realm of life is impermanent;
the treatises on grammar require a vast amount of time to master."
Therefore, let some brief treatise be composed for the sake of awakening them;
for it has been said:
"The science of grammar is indeed infinite and boundless."
Likewise, life is very short and obstacles are many;
therefore, one should extract the essence, discarding what is worthless, just as swans take milk from the waters of the ocean.
"There is here a Brahmin named Viṣṇuśarman, who has mastered all the sciences and has attained renown in the assembly of students. Entrust these boys to him;
he will surely awaken them quickly."

Having heard that, the king summoned Viṣṇuśarman and said: "O venerable one, for the sake of showing me favor, act in such a way that you may quickly make these boys peerless in the science of polity (artha-śāstra);
then I shall endow you with a hundred land grants."
Then Viṣṇuśarman said to the king: "Your Majesty, hear my truthful words:
I will not sell my knowledge even for a hundred royal edicts.
Furthermore, if I do not make these sons of yours masters of the science of polity within six months, then I shall abandon my own name."

Then that king, having heard that impossible promise of the Brahmin, was filled with joy and wonder along with his ministers; he respectfully entrusted those princes to him and attained supreme satisfaction. Viṣṇuśarman, for his part, took them and composed the five treatises known as *Mitrabheda*, *Mitraprāpti*, *Kākolūkīya*, *Labdhapraṇāśa*, and *Aparīkṣitakāraka*—the so-called *Pañcatantra*—and taught them to the princes.

Those princes, having studied them, became as described within six months. From that time forth, this treatise on ethics known as the *Pañcatantra* has circulated upon the earth for the purpose of instructing the young. What need is there to say more?
He who constantly studies this treatise on ethics and listens to it shall never suffer defeat, even at the hands of Śakra.
Thus ends the introduction to the story. [Now begins] "The Separation of Friends," the narrative of Vardhamāna.
Now, therefore, begins the first treatise, named "The Breach of Friendship," the first verse of which is as follows:
"A great affection grew between a lion and a bull in the forest."
He was destroyed by a jackal who was both malicious and excessively greedy.
Thus it is heard:
In a country of the south, there was a city named Mahilāropya.
There lived a merchant’s son named Vardhamānaka, who possessed vast wealth acquired through righteous means.
Once, while he was lying in bed at night, a thought arose in him:
"Even though my wealth is abundant, I must consider and devise means for further acquisition.
For it has been said:
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished through purposeful means;
therefore, a wise person should strive with effort to achieve a single goal.
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
That is no knowledge, no charity, no craft, no art,
and no steadfastness on the part of the wealthy which is not sung about by beggars.
In this world, even a stranger becomes like a kinsman to the wealthy; yet even a kinsman always behaves like a wicked person toward the poor.
For indeed, all activities proceed from objects that have grown and accumulated here and there, just as rivers flow from mountains.
That even one unworthy of worship is worshipped, that even one who should not be approached is approached,
and that even one unworthy of salutation is saluted— this is the power of wealth.
Just as all the sense organs depend upon food, so too do all effects depend upon it;
for this reason, wealth is said to be the means for accomplishing everything.
This world of living beings, seeking only wealth, frequents even the cremation ground;
abandoning its own progenitor, it casts him far away once he has become destitute.
Even for men whose youth has passed, those who possess wealth remain young;
but those who are destitute of wealth are old, even in their prime.
And that wealth for men is acquired through six means: by begging, by service to a king, by agricultural labor, by the acquisition of knowledge, by trade, or by the business of commerce.
Of all these, the gain of wealth through commerce is unsurpassed.
And as it has been said:
Alas! Alms have been prepared by many, yet the king bestows what is not fitting; agriculture is laborious, and learning is exceedingly difficult due to the conduct of discipline toward a teacher;
from laziness comes poverty, while from the loosening of the knots held in the hands of others [comes wealth].
I do not consider there to be any livelihood in this world superior to trade.
Among all means, O King, the accumulation of merchandise as a means for the sake of wealth is praised as the one; any other is fraught with uncertainty. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.12)
And that commerce is of seven kinds for the acquisition of wealth,
namely: trade in perfumes,
and the depositing of funds.
The business of the cow-pen, the arrival of a familiar buyer, and the false statement regarding the purchase price.
Using false scales and measures, and importing goods from other regions. And it has been said:
"Among all commodities, the commodity of perfumes is the best; what need is there for others, such as gold and the like?"
Where that which was purchased for one is given away for a hundred.
When the deposited object fell from the mansion, the merchant praised his own deity:
"The depositor will die; I shall fulfill my vow by offering it to you. (Pancaka 1.14)
Appointed to the task of managing the cattle-pen, the guild-president thought with a joyful heart:
"Today I have obtained the earth filled with wealth; what need is there for anything else? (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.15)
As he approaches, having accumulated [merit], she gazes at the seeker with longing;
she rejoices just as one does upon obtaining wealth, or when a son is born. (Pañcagatidīpanā 1.16)
Furthermore:

"Constantly deceiving acquaintances during the measuring of full or incomplete [quantities], as well as speaking falsely regarding the purchase price—this would be the natural disposition of the Kirātas. (Pañca 1.17)
Those who are skilled in the buying and selling of goods obtain wealth two or three times greater than their capital through enterprise, having traveled to distant foreign lands. (Pancadashi 1.18)
Having thus reflected, he took his goods bound for Mathurā and, on an auspicious lunar day, permitted by his elders, set out mounted upon a noble chariot.
With him were two auspicious oxen born in his own home, named Saṃjīvaka and Nandaka, who were capable of bearing the yoke.
Of these two, the one called Saṃjīvaka, having descended to the bank of the Yamunā and encountered a place filled with thick mud, became stuck in his feet; breaking the yoke, he fell into despair.
Then, beholding him in that state, Vardhamāna fell into profound despondency;
and for his sake, with a heart moistened by affection, he halted his journey for three nights.
Then, seeing him dejected, the merchants said to him: "O Merchant!"
"Why have you placed the entire caravan at risk in this forest, which is so full of dangers and teeming with lions and tigers, for the sake of a single bull? As it is said:
'A wise man should not destroy a great deal for the sake of a small thing. This alone is wisdom in this matter: that one protects the great by means of the small. (Pañcatantra 1.19)
Then, having understood that, he appointed guards for Saṃjīvaka and set out, leading the entire caravan.
Now, the guards, perceiving that forest to be full of many dangers, abandoned Saṃjīvaka and went back; on the following day, they said falsely to the caravan leader: "Master, this Saṃjīvaka is dead."
"But we, thinking it was the caravan leader's wish, have cremated him with fire.
Upon hearing this, the caravan leader, his heart moistened with affection out of gratitude, performed all the funeral rites for him, including the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).

Saṃjīvaka, however, because some life remained in him, had his body revived by extremely cold breezes mingled with the waters of the Yamunā; somehow managing to rise, he reached the bank of the Yamunā.
There, eating the tips of young grasses that resembled emeralds, within a few days he became fat, humped, and strong like the bull of Hara;
every day, he remained bellowing as he tore apart the tops of anthill peaks with his two horns.
And this is well said:
That which is unprotected remains, protected by the gods;
that which is well-protected perishes when struck down by the gods.
Even one abandoned in the forest without a protector may live.
Even one who has exerted effort perishes at home.

Then once, a lion named Piṅgalaka, surrounded by all kinds of animals, descended to the bank of the Yamunā to drink water while distressed by thirst; from afar he heard the exceedingly deep roar of Sañjīvaka.
Upon hearing that, his heart became extremely agitated; concealing his appearance with trepidation, he stationed himself beneath a banyan tree in the fourfold formation.
The arrangement of the four circles is as follows: the lion, those who follow the lion, the crows, and those of indifferent conduct.
Now, that king had two jackals named Karaṭaka and Damanaka, sons of ministers who had been dismissed from their offices, who were his constant companions.
These two were deliberating with one another.
Thereupon Damanaka said: "My dear Karaṭaka, our master Piṅgalaka has descended to the bank of the Yamunā to fetch water and remains there.
For what reason has he turned back even though he was distressed by thirst, and now stands here at the foot of this banyan tree, overwhelmed by dejection after having arranged his battle formation?"
Karaṭaka said: "My good friend, what is the use of this business for us? For it has been said:
The man who desires to engage in an activity that does not concern him meets his own destruction, just like the monkey who pulled out the wedge. (Pañcatantra 1.21)
Story 1: The Story of the Monkey Who Pulled Out the Wedge.
In the vicinity of a certain city, a merchant’s son began to construct a temple in the midst of a grove of trees.
And there, those laborers such as the sthapatis and others would go into the middle of the city at midday for the sake of food.
Now, once upon a time, a troop of monkeys arrived, wandering here and there in that vicinity.
In that place, there was a pillar made of *añjana* wood, half-split by a certain craftsman, which stood held together by a stake of *khadira* wood inserted through its center.

In the meantime, those monkeys began to play as they pleased upon the tops of trees, the terraces of palaces, mountain peaks, and the edges of timber. One among them, whose death was near, out of restlessness sat down upon that half-split pillar.

Having grasped the wedge with both hands, as he began to pull it out, what happened to his testicles—which were caught in the middle of the pillar as the wedge shifted from its place—has already been related.
Therefore, I say: "In matters that are not one's concern... etc.
"There is indeed food remaining from what we have eaten;
so why this exertion?
Damanaka said, "Is it then that you desire food alone?"
That is not tenable; and it has been said:
"The wise seek the patronage of kings for the sake of assisting friends and even for the sake of harming enemies; who does not merely sustain their belly? (Pañca 1.22).
Furthermore: "He by whose living many live—let him live here;
do not the birds fill their own bellies with their beaks? (Pañcatantra 1.23)
And thus:
that life which is lived even for a moment by men who are renowned and endowed with wisdom, heroism, power, and noble virtues—
Those who know the truth declare that such a thing is not life at all;
even a crow lives for a long time and eats the offerings of others.
What indeed is the fruit of life for that man in the world of mortals who feels no compassion for his own kin when they are distressed, nor for the class of fellow men?
Even a crow lives for a long time and partakes of offerings.
A small stream may be easily filled, and the hollow of a mouse's paws may be easily filled;
likewise, a base person is easily satisfied, for he finds contentment even with very little.
Furthermore:
What is the use of that birth which merely robs the mother of her youth, yet does not rise like a banner to the pinnacle of its own lineage? (Pancaka 1.27)
In this revolving cycle of saṃsāra, who indeed does not die and who is not born?
But among those born, he alone is counted here as truly born who vibrates with preeminent glory.
Moreover:
Even for that blade of grass born upon the riverbank, its birth is fruitful, in that it becomes a handhold for people distressed by sinking in the water. (Pancatantaka 1.29)
And so it is said:
"Steady yet rising in their movement, removing the distress of people, virtuous persons like rain-clouds are born only rarely in this world. (Pañca. 1.30)
Therefore, the wise remember that the mother possesses unsurpassed greatness,
since she carries within her an indescribable being.
He who becomes the teacher even of the great.
Even a capable person who has not manifested their power meets with contempt;
fire dwelling within wood may be stepped over, but not when it is blazing.
Karaṭaka said: "We two are, after all, not the primary ministers; so why should we involve ourselves in this matter?
And it has been said:
'That foolish man who, being unasked and not a principal official, speaks before the king [is punished].'"
Not only does he receive disrespect, but also derision.
And thus:
Speech should be employed where what is spoken obtains its fruit, and attachment becomes absolutely enduring, like [dye] on a white cloth. (1.34)
Damaka said: "Do not speak thus!
One who is unimportant may become important if he serves a king;
even one who is important may become unimportant if he is devoid of service. (Pañca 1.35)
As it has been said:
"A king favors only that person who is close at hand, even if they are devoid of learning, of low birth, or unrefined."
Generally, lords of the earth, women, and creepers alike tend to entwine around whatever is situated at their side. (Pancatantra 1.36)
And so it is said:
"Those servants who discern the objects of a king's anger and favor gradually ascend even to the heights of one who shakes them off. (Pañcatantra 1.37)

For those possessed of learning, those with great aspirations, those distinguished by their artistic skill and valor, and those who know the profession of service, there is no refuge other than a king. (Pancatanttra 1.38)
And for those who do not approach kings who possess great enthusiasm for [their] birth and so forth, begging for alms until death is prescribed as their penance. (Panc_1.39)
And those wicked-souled ones who say that kings are difficult to propitiate have merely revealed their own negligence, laziness, and dull-wittedness. (Pancatantra 1.40)
Having seen serpents, tigers, elephants, and lions brought under control by skillful means,
what small measure of "kingship" is there for the wise who are free from heedlessness?
Only by relying upon a king does the wise man attain the supreme goal;
without the Malaya mountain, sandalwood does not grow elsewhere.
When the king is pleased, there are white parasols, delightful horses, and elephants that are always in rut.
Karaṭaka said, "Then what do you intend to do?
He replied, "Today our master Piṅgalaka is terrified, as is his entire retinue.
Therefore, having gone there and ascertained the cause of his fear, I shall arrange for one of the six political measures—peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, seeking refuge, or duplicity."
Karaṭaka said, "How do you know that this master is overcome by fear?
He replied, "What is there to be known here?
For it has been said:"
A meaning expressed even by a beast is understood;
horses and elephants carry their loads when urged;
but a wise person infers even that which has not been spoken.
For the intellects of others are indeed like fish that perceive the movements [of their prey]. //Panc_1.44//
And so Manu says (8.26): "By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by activity, and by speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is perceived. (Panc 1.45)

"Therefore, having approached him today while he is overwhelmed by fear, I shall, by the power of my own intellect, render him fearless, bring him under my control, and secure for myself the position of his minister.
Karataka said, "You are ignorant of the principles of service;
how then will you bring him under your control?"
He said: "How am I unacquainted with service?
For while playing on my father's lap, I heard the essence of the duty of service from visiting holy men as they were reciting the treatises on ethics (nīti-śāstra); that has been fixed in my heart.
Listen to it: [The verses follow...]"]
Three kinds of men gather the earth that is in bloom with gold:
the hero, the learned man, and he who knows how to serve.
That service which benefits the master should be accepted especially through his words; a wise man should approach the king only by means of that [minister], and not otherwise. (Pancatantra 1.47)
A wise person should not serve one who does not recognize another's virtues;
for no fruit whatsoever comes from such a person, just as from a well-tilled saline wasteland.
Even one who lacks wealth and ritual action should be served if he is endowed with the qualities of one worthy of service;
for from him there arises a livelihood, and even after a lapse of time, a fruit [of that service].
Even if he sits like a withered stump, wasting away and overcome by hunger,
a wise man does not seek his livelihood from one who is devoid of self-knowledge.
The servant hates his master with harsh words and stinginess;
does he not hate himself, he who knows not what is worthy of service and what is not? (5.51)
That king upon whom his servants, afflicted by hunger, must depend for rest should always be abandoned, even though he is like a tree that is always laden with flowers and fruit.
One should always behave toward the king’s mother, the queen, the prince, the chief minister, the domestic priest, and the chamberlain as one would toward the king himself. (Pancaka 1.53)
He who, when addressed as "Live!", being skilled in discerning what ought and ought not to be done,
acts without hesitation— he shall become the king’s favorite.
He who offers up wealth obtained through the favor of the Lord, and who wears upon his body garments and other such gifts, shall become a favorite of the king. (Pañcāstikāya 1.55)
He who does not hold secret counsel with those who frequent the inner apartments,
nor with the king's wives, shall be the favorite of the monarch.
He who perceives gambling as resembling the messengers of Yama, liquor as being like the halāhala poison,
and his wife as having a false appearance, shall become a favorite of the king.
He who is a leader at the time of battle, yet always follows behind in the city,
and remains by the door of his master’s palace, shall be the king’s favorite.

Thinking, "I am always authorized by the Lord," one might transgress even in times of distress; such a person would be a favorite of the king, yet he would not be established in the bounds of propriety.
The man who is constantly intent on hating those who hate, and who performs desired deeds for those who are dear,
shall become a favorite of the lord of men.
He who does not give a contradictory reply when questioned by his lord,
and who does not laugh loudly in his presence, shall become the king’s favorite.
Free from fear, he regards the battlefield as a refuge and his own city as a place of exile; such a person shall become a favorite of the king.
One should not form an association with the women of the lord of men, nor engage in criticism or dispute; thus one shall become a favorite of the king.
Karaṭaka said: "Then, having gone there, what will you say first? Let that be told.
Damanaka said:
"As those who speak proceed from one answer to another, a further response arises."
Like another seed produced from a seed endowed with the quality of a good rain.
The wise, employing the qualities of political ethics, [perceive] misfortune arising from the observation of wrong means and success arising from the observation of right means.
They describe her as if she were shimmering right before one's eyes.

In some, eloquent sayings leap forth beautifully from the mouth like parrots; in others, they remain silent within the heart like mute ones; while in yet others, they leap forth beautifully both from the heart and the mouth.
And I shall not speak when the time has not yet arrived;
for while formerly sitting upon my father’s lap, I heard the essence of political ethics:
even Bṛhaspati, were he to utter speech at an inappropriate time, would be censured.
One receives much contempt and abundant dishonor.
Karaṭaka said:
"For kings are indeed difficult to propitiate, like mountains;
they are always infested with wild beasts, extremely rugged, harsh, and frequented by the wicked. (Pañcatantra 1.68)
And so it is said:
"Kings are like serpents: they possess enjoyments, are encased in armor, are crooked, act with cruelty, are extremely wicked, and must be subdued by mantras. (Pañcatantra 1.69)
Tongue-tied, cruel in their deeds, ungrateful, and seeking out vulnerabilities—
kings see such people from afar, just like serpents.
O Lord of the Earth, those of evil mind who do even the slightest harm to one who is dear to the king are consumed like moths in a fire.
The station of kings, which is difficult to ascend and honored by all the world,
becomes defiled even by a slight offense, just like the status of a Brahmin.
The fortunes of kings are difficult to propitiate, difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain;
they remain for a long time only so long as they are firmly established within oneself, like water held in a vessel.
Damanaka said: "This is indeed true; however— For whatever the disposition of each person may be, one should act in accordance with that very disposition.
Having gained their confidence, a wise man should quickly bring them under his own control. (Pañcatantra 1.74)
Following the will of one's master and conducting oneself with good character are the hallmarks of dependents;
even Rākṣasas are captured by those who constantly comply with their desires.

When the king is angry, offering words of praise; when he is pleased, showing affection; when he is hostile, showing hatred; and praising his acts of generosity—this is subjugation without mantras or ritual procedures. (Pancatantaka 1.76)
Karaṭaka said, "If this is what you desire, then may your paths be auspicious;
let it be carried out according to your wish.
He too, having bowed, set out toward Piṅgalaka.
Then, seeing Damanaka approaching, Piṅgalaka said to the doorkeeper: "Let the cane-staff be removed;
this is our long-standing minister’s son, Damanaka, whose entrance is unrestricted.
Therefore, let him enter as a participant in the second circle."
He said, "It is exactly as you have spoken.
Then Damanaka approached, was directed to a seat, bowed to Piṅgalaka, and sat down once he had received permission.
Placing his right hand, adorned with a claw-like thunderbolt, upon [Damanaka's] head, he spoke with great courtesy: "Is all well with you?"
"Why have you been seen after such a long time?

Damanaka replied: "Your Majesty, there is nothing that we have that is of use to Your Highness; however, something must be said by us as the time for it has arrived, since kings have need of all—whether they be superior, middling, or inferior. And it is said:
Even for lords, a blade of grass serves their purpose, whether as a toothpick or as a tool for scratching an itch.
What need is there for a man to praise the speech of others?

"Likewise, O Lord, we are hereditary servants of Your Majesty; even in times of calamity, we remain at your side. Although we do not receive our full emoluments, nevertheless, this [act] is not fitting for Your Majesty.
And it has been said:
'Servants and ornaments should both be employed in their proper places.'"
For a crest-jewel is not bound upon the foot on the grounds that it possesses the power [to illuminate].
For it is said:
A king who is ignorant of virtues is not followed by his servants, even if he is wealthy, of noble birth, and has ascended the throne through hereditary succession. (Pancatantra 1.79)
And it is said:
"Being compared with those who are unequal, and having his honor diminished by those who are equal,"
A servant who, though not yoked to the burden, abandons his master for three reasons [is to be shunned].

And when a king, through lack of discernment, appoints servants who are worthy of the highest rank to a low and inferior position, it is not the fault of those [servants] alone, but rather the fault of the monarch. And it has been said: "One who is fit for the wearing of golden ornaments..."
If a jewel is fastened onto lead, it neither rings out nor does it shine; rather, there is only blame for the one who joined them. (5.81)
And as for what the master says— that he is seen after a long time— let that also be heard:
where there is no distinction between the left and right hands, [how could one say he is seen only now?]
What noble person, possessing a means of going, would remain there for even a single moment?
In the presence of those whose intellects waver, mistaking glass for a gem and a gem for glass,
not even one who is a servant in name alone will remain.
In a land where there are no connoisseurs,
jewels born of the ocean have no value; it is said that in the land of the Ābhīras, even the moonstone is not prized.
The cowherds sell it for three cowries.
Where there is no distinction between the gem called *lohita* and the ruby (*padmarāga*), how can there be a sale of jewels in such a place? (5.85)
When a master behaves without distinction and treats his servants equally,
the enthusiasm of those capable of exertion declines.
There is no king without servants, nor are there servants without a king;
their mutual relationship is one of reciprocal dependence.
Even though he is radiant with splendor like the sun, a king does not shine by himself without servants who act for the benefit of the world, just as the sun does not shine without its rays.
The hub is held together by the spokes, and the spokes are established upon the hub;
in this same way, the wheel of activity between master and servant revolves.
Even hair, though constantly borne upon the head and nurtured with affection, becomes discolored when deprived of oil; how much more so, then, servants who are devoid of affection?
A king who is pleased indeed bestows mere wealth upon his servants;
they, however, through mere honor, assist him even with their lives. (Pañcatantra 1.91)
Knowing this, a ruler of men should employ servants who are discerning,
of noble birth, endowed with valor, capable, devoted, and hereditary.
He who, having performed for the king a most difficult and supreme service,
says nothing out of shame— by him the king has a true companion.
He upon whom one may entrust one's duties and dwell with an unhesitating mind— that servant should be regarded as yet another wife.
He who comes unbidden, who always stands at the door, and who, when questioned,
speaks the truth and measuredly— he is a servant worthy of kings.
Even without being commanded by the king, he who strives for the destruction of anything seen to be harmful is a servant worthy of monarchs. (Pancatantra 1.96)
Even when beaten, reviled, or punished by the king,
he who does not harbor malice is a servant worthy of kings.
He who does not harbor pride when honored, nor suffers distress when insulted,
and who preserves his own character— he alone is worthy to be a servant of kings.
He who is not oppressed by hunger, nor ever by sleep,
nor by cold, heat, and the like— that servant is worthy of kings.
That servant who, upon hearing news concerning his master regarding an impending battle, maintains a cheerful countenance, is worthy of kings.
The king's dominion increases like the moon in the bright fortnight;
he is a servant worthy of kings in whom the administration of justice is firmly established.
The kingdom shrinks like a piece of leather placed over a fire;
therefore, a servant who remains [unrestrained] must be abandoned by one who desires the state.
Furthermore, it is improper for my master to show me contempt by thinking, "This is merely a jackal.
For it has been said:
"Silk is born from worms, gold from stone, and even durva grass from the hair of a cow."
The lotus from the mud, the moon from the ocean, the blue water-lily from cow dung,
fire from wood, the jewel from the hood of a serpent, and the yellow pigment (rocanā) from a cow’s bile—
do those possessed of virtues attain their renown through their birth, or rather through the manifestation of their own qualities? (Pañcatantra 1.103)
Even a mouse born in one's own house must be killed if it causes sleep;
yet people obtain a lover who acts for their benefit by providing them with food.
Just as there is no use for woodwork even when castor, bhiṇḍa, arka, and reeds are gathered in great abundance, so too is there no purpose served by those who lack wisdom.
"What is the use of devotion if one is incapable, and what is the use of capability if one does no harm?
O King, you ought not to despise me, for I am both devoted and capable."
Piṅgalaka said: "Let it be so for now. Whether you are capable or incapable, you are our long-standing minister's son;
therefore, speak with confidence whatever you wish to say."
Damanaka said, "Your Majesty, there is something I wish to report. Piṅgalaka said, "Then state what you intend.
He replied:
"Even the most trivial matter that pertains to a lord of the earth must not be spoken in the midst of an assembly," so said Bṛhaspati. (Pañcatantra 1.107)
Therefore, may Your Majesty listen to my confidential report. For it is said:
"A counsel with six ears is leaked; a counsel with four ears remains secure.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid a six-eared counsel by every possible effort. (Pancatantra 1.108)
Then, having heard those words, all the others—the tiger, the leopard, the wolf, and the rest—who understood Piṅgalaka’s intention, immediately withdrew from the assembly.
Thereupon Damanaka said, "Why has our master, who set out for the purpose of fetching water, returned and stayed here?
Piṅgalaka replied with an embarrassed smile, "Nothing at all."

He said: "Your Majesty, if it is something that should not be told, then let it rest. And it has been said: 'Something should be hidden from servants, something from one's own kin, something from friends, and something from one's sons.'"
"Having reflected on whether this is appropriate or inappropriate, a wise man should speak out of great consideration for others.
Hearing this, Piṅgalaka thought: "This one appears to be worthy."

Therefore, I shall declare my intention before him; for it is said: "When one has disclosed one's suffering to a master who recognizes other virtues, to a virtuous servant who is obedient, to a counselor who is discerning, and to a friend whose heart is constant, one becomes happy. (Pañcatantra 1.101)
"O Damanaka, do you hear that great sound from afar?
He replied, "Master, I hear it. "What is it?
Pingalaka said, "My good friend, I wish to depart from this forest."
Damanaka said, "Why?
Piṅgalaka replied, "Because today some unprecedented creature has entered our forest, of whom this great sound is heard;
and his prowess must surely be commensurate with that sound."
Damanaka said: "That Your Majesty has become afraid even at the mere sound of a word is also improper. And it is said:
A dike is breached by water, and likewise a secret counsel is ruined if not guarded;
affection is destroyed by backbiting, and one who is afflicted is broken by harsh words. (Pañcatantra 1.111)
Therefore, it is not right for the master to abandon the forest acquired by his ancestors;

for sounds are of many kinds, distinguished as the drum (*bherī*), flute (*veṇu*), lute (*vīṇā*), clay drum (*mṛdaṅga*), cymbals (*tāla*), kettle-drum (*paṭaha*), conch (*śaṅkha*), and trumpet (*kāhalā*).
Thus, one should not be afraid of mere sound alone. And it has been said:
When an exceedingly fierce and terrible enemy has arrived, he whose fortitude does not falter—
that lord of the earth does not suffer defeat.
Even when the Creator displays his power, the steadfastness of the wise shall not be destroyed;
for even when all lakes are dried up by the summer heat, the ocean becomes only more surging.
And so it is said:
"The mother who gives birth to that rare son who feels no despondency in adversity, no joy in prosperity, and no cowardice in battle—he is the ornament of the three worlds. (Pañcatantra 1.114)
And so it is said:

"The destiny of one who is bowed down by a deficiency of power, who is devoid of essence, and who is exceedingly light due to being stripped of pride, is the same as that of a blade of grass. (Pañcagatidīpana 1.115)
Moreover:
What is the use even of the physical form of one who, upon encountering the prowess of another, fails to attain firmness—like that of an ornament made of lac? (Panc_1.116)
Therefore, knowing this, the master should maintain steadfastness;
one should not be afraid of mere sound. Moreover:
"I already knew that this [body] was entirely filled with fat."
Having entered within, he discerned everything, down to the hide and the wood.
Piṅgalaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 2.
The Story of the Jackal and the Drum:
A certain jackal named Gomāyu, his throat parched with hunger, was wandering here and there in the forest when he saw a battlefield where two armies had fought.
There, he heard the sound of a fallen drum being struck by the tips of creepers and tree branches driven by the wind.
Then, with an agitated heart, he thought: "Alas, I am ruined!
Therefore, before I come within the range of his vision while this sound is still being uttered, I shall depart elsewhere.
Or rather, it is not proper to act so precipitately."
Whether in fear or in joy, he who reflects when such states arise and does not act out of impulsive force will not experience remorse.
First, I shall find out whose voice this is.
Resolving to remain patient, he began to investigate as he walked very slowly; then he saw a drum.
Recognizing it, he approached and struck it himself out of curiosity.
Furthermore, out of joy he thought: "Aha! After a long time, this great feast has come to us.
It must surely be filled with flesh, fat, and blood.
Then, having somehow torn through that covering of coarse hide and made an opening in one place, he entered into its midst with a heart full of delight.
However, beyond tearing the hide, his fangs were broken.
Then, having become hopeless and looking at what remained of that wood, he recited this verse: "I already knew this before.
Therefore, one should not be afraid based on mere words.
Piṅgalaka said: "O friend, behold! All my subjects have their minds agitated by fear and wish to flee;
how then can I maintain my composure?
He replied: "Master, this is not their fault."
For servants become exactly like their master. And it has been said:
A horse, a weapon, a treatise, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—having encountered a particular kind of person, they become either unworthy or worthy. (Pañcatantra 1.119)
"Having taken possession of that man's prowess, you must wait right here until I return after learning the true nature of this sound;
thereafter, we shall act as is appropriate.
Piṅgalaka said, "Are you able to go there?"
He said: "Is there anything that a good servant ought to do or not do by the command of his master? And it has been said:
'By the command of his master, O sir, nothing whatsoever is impossible for a good servant;
he might even enter the mouth of a serpent or the great ocean so difficult to cross. (Pañcatantra 1.120)
And so it is said:
"A servant who, though commanded by his master, considers equal what is unequal, should not be retained by a king desiring prosperity. (Pañcatantra 1.121)
Piṅgalaka said, "My good friend,
if that is so, then go;
may your paths be auspicious."

Damanaka also, having bowed to him, set out following the sound of Sañjīvaka. Then, after Damanaka had gone, Piṅgalaka, his mind agitated by fear, reflected: "Alas, I have not acted wisely, in that I placed my trust in him and revealed my own intention."
"Perhaps this Damanaka, having become a double-agent, might harbor evil intentions toward me now that his office has been stripped from him. And it is said:
'Even those of noble birth, once honored and then insulted by a king, always strive for his destruction. (Pañcatantra 1.122)
Therefore, I shall go to another place and wait there to discover what he intends to do;
perhaps Damanaka wishes to take him and kill me. And it is said:
"Even the weak are not bound by the strong if they remain distrustful."
For it is those who trust who are bound, even the powerful by the weak.
Even toward Bṛhaspati, a wise man should not place his trust if he desires his own prosperity, long life, and happiness. (Pañcatantra 1.124)
One should not place trust in an enemy, even if bound by oaths;
Vṛtra, intent on seizing the kingdom, was slain by Śakra through those very oaths.
Without trust, even an enemy cannot be overcome, even by the gods;
through trust, the embryo of Diti was destroyed by the Lord of the Thirty-three.

Having reflected thus, he went to another place and stood alone, watching the path of Damanaka. Damanaka, for his part, went to Sañjīvaka; recognizing him as a bull, he was delighted at heart and thought: "Aha! A splendid opportunity has arisen. Through this means—by way of alliance or conflict with him—Piṅgalaka will come under my control. And it is said:
A king does not act upon the advice of his ministers out of considerations of noble lineage or personal affection,
as long as he encounters misfortune or even sorrow.
A king who is perpetually beset by calamity becomes the prey of his ministers;
for this very reason, ministers desire a monarch who is in distress. (Pañcatantra 1.128)
Just as one who is free from disease never desires a skilled physician,
so too a king who is devoid of calamity does not seek a minister.
Reflecting thus, he set out toward Piṅgalaka.
Piṅgalaka, seeing him approaching, remained as he was before, concealing his true form. Damana, too, having gone into the presence of Piṅgalaka, bowed and sat down.
Piṅgalaka said, "Was that creature seen by you?"
Damanaka said, "It was seen by the grace of my lord.
Piṅgalaka said, "Is it true? Damanaka said, "How could anything untrue be reported in the presence of my lord’s feet? And it has been said:"
Even one who speaks even a very small falsehood in the presence of kings or gods perishes swiftly, however great he may be.
And so it is said:
"The king is proclaimed by Manu to be composed of all the gods;
therefore, one should regard him as a god and never with ill-will. (Pancatantra 1.131)
Even though he embodies all the gods, this is the distinction of the king:
the fruit of good and evil arises from the king immediately, whereas from a god it arises in another life.

Piṅgalaka said: "It will indeed be seen by you that the great do not become angry with the lowly; therefore, you were not struck down by him. For—as the saying goes—'The wind does not uproot blades of grass.'"
Gentle and bowed low on all sides—this is the very nature of those with lofty minds: they display their prowess only against the great. (Pañcatantra 1.133)
Moreover—
though struck by the soles of the feet of intoxicated bees wandering about, their passion fixed upon the ichor on his temples;
Even a serpent of extreme strength does not become angry; however, one who is strong becomes provoked when faced with an equal in strength. (1.134)
Damanaka said: "Let it be so; he is indeed a great soul, while we are wretched.
Nevertheless, if my master commands it, then I shall appoint him to the service."
Piṅgalaka said with a sigh of relief, "Are you truly able to do this?
Damanaka replied, "What is impossible for the intellect? And it is said:
'That which cannot be achieved by weapons, nor by great elephants, nor by horses, nor by foot-soldiers...'"
An undertaking reaches successful completion when it is accomplished through right understanding.
Piṅgalaka said, "If it is so, then you are appointed to the office of minister;
from this day forward, it is my firm resolve that the matters of favor and punishment shall be carried out by you alone.
Then Damanaka went quickly and, addressing him with reproach, said, "Come, come here, you wicked bull!"
"Lord Piṅgalaka summons you.
Why do you cry out in vain again and again without any apprehension?
Upon hearing this, Sañjīvaka said, "My good friend, who is this Piṅgalaka?"
Damanaka said: "Do you not even know our master Piṅgalaka?
Wait for that moment;
you shall know by the result itself."
"Indeed, here at the foot of the banyan tree stands our lord, the lion named Piṅgalaka, surrounded by all manner of wild beasts.
Upon hearing this, Sañjīvaka, considering himself as good as dead, fell into extreme despondency and said:
"My good friend, you appear to be of virtuous conduct and eloquent in speech."
"Therefore, if you must take me there, you should obtain a favor from my master by granting him a pledge of safety.
Damanaka said, "O friend, what you have said is true;
for this is the way of policy:"
The limits of the earth, the ocean, and even the mountains can be found; but the end of a king's mind can never be reached by anyone, anywhere.
"Stay right here until I have seen him at the appointed time, and after that, I shall bring you [to him].
When this had been carried out, Damanaka went into the presence of Piṅgalaka and said: "Master, that is no ordinary creature;
for he is the bull who serves as the vehicle of the Blessed Lord Maheśvara."
When questioned by me, he said this:
"I was commanded by the gratified Maheśvara to graze on the tips of young grass on the banks of the Kālindī. In short, this forest has been granted to me by the Blessed One for my sport."
Piṅgalaka said with fear: "Truly, I have now understood.
Without the favor of the gods, those who feed on grass would not wander so fearlessly and joyfully in a forest infested with beasts of prey as this one.
Therefore, what did you say?"
Damanaka said: "Master, I have already stated this: that this forest has become the domain of Piṅgalaka, who serves as the mount for Caṇḍikā.
Therefore, since you have arrived as a dear guest, you should go into his presence and spend your time in one place, sharing food, drink, and recreation with him out of brotherly affection."
Then he also agreed to all of this and said joyfully, "The master should be requested to grant the gift of safety. Therefore,
in this matter, the master is the authority.
Having heard that, Piṅgalaka said: "Excellent, Sumati! Excellent!
O minister, O learned Brahmin, excellent!
Having consulted with my own heart, you have spoken this."
"Therefore, I have granted him the gift of safety.
However, let him also be brought back even more quickly after he has requested the gift of safety for my sake.
Now, this is well said:
A kingdom is sustained by ministers who possess inner integrity, who are straightforward, free from flaws, and thoroughly tested, just as a mansion is supported by sturdy pillars. (Pañcatantra 1.137)
And so it is said:

"The wisdom of ministers is revealed in the reconciliation of those who are divided, and that of physicians in the treatment of complex disorders (*sānnipātika*); for who is not wise when dealing with one who is healthy? (Pañcāstikāya 1.138)
Damanaka, having bowed to him, set out toward Sañjīvaka and thought joyfully: "Aha! Our master has become favorable toward us and has come under the influence of our words;
therefore, there is no one more fortunate than I. And it is said:
"Nectar is cool fire; nectar is the sight of a beloved."
Honor from kings is nectar; a meal of milk is nectar.
Then, having approached Saṃjīvaka, he spoke with humility: "O friend, I have requested from my master on your behalf that he grant you an assurance of safety;
therefore, go there with confidence.
However, once you have obtained the king's favor, you must conduct yourself toward me according to the laws of friendship."
"You must not act out of pride, relying on your own power.
I too, by your agreement, shall undertake the entire burden of the kingdom and the office of minister.
When this is done, the fortune of royal sovereignty will belong to both of us. For it is said:"
Through the practice of hunting, wealth comes under the control of men;
one person impels the human subjects, while another slays them like deer. (Pancavimshati 1.140)
And so it is said:
"He who, out of pride, does not honor those who are superior, inferior, or middling—even if he himself is honorable—he falls from his position, just like Dantila. (Pañca 1.141)
Saṃjīvaka asked, "How was that? He replied:
Story 3: The Story of Dantila and Gorambha.
On this earth there is a city named Vardhamāna. There lived a merchant of various wares named Dantila, who was the leader of the entire city.
By performing his duties toward both the city and the king, he brought satisfaction to the inhabitants of that city as well as to the monarch.
What more need be said? No one has ever seen or heard of anyone so clever.
Or rather, this which has been said is true:
"He who acts for the benefit of the king becomes an object of hatred in the world."
"One who acts for the welfare of the realm is abandoned by the lords of kings.
Thus, when such a great conflict exists between the king and his subjects, it is difficult to find anyone capable of accomplishing what must be done. (Pancatanttra 1.142)
Now, as time passed in this manner, once a wedding took place for Danitla.
There, he invited all the city-dwellers and those present at the royal court with due honor, fed them, and honored them with garments and other gifts.
Then, after the wedding, the king, along with his harem, was brought to his own home and received with worshipful hospitality.

Now, a royal servant named Gorambha, who was the sweeper of that king’s palace, arrived at the house; however, because he sat in an improper place, the king, showing him contempt, gave him the "half-moon" (a slap with the palm) and sent him away.
From that time forward, sighing due to his humiliation, he did not even sleep at night.
He remained there thinking, "How can I cause the loss of the king's favor for that merchant?"
Or rather, what is the use of this futile emaciation of the body?
Nothing at all can be done by me to harm him.
Or rather, it is well said:
For what man here is truly shameless who becomes angry when he is unable to retaliate?
Even a chickpea, once it has sprouted, is indeed capable [of growing].
Why would you break the frying pan?

Then once, at dawn, while the king was immersed in the sleep of yoga, a certain man performing a cleaning near the king’s bed said this: "Oh, how great is Dantila’s arrogance, that he embraces the queen!
Hearing this, the king rose up in alarm and said to him: "O Goramabha!
Is what you have spoken true?"
"Why was she embraced by Dantila?
Gorambha replied, "Your Majesty,
while I was awake through the night due to my addiction to gambling, sleep came upon me involuntarily."
Therefore, I do not know what I have said. The king, with jealousy, said to himself: "This Dantila has indeed moved about our house with unimpeded access;
perhaps he has seen the queen being embraced by him."
Therefore, this was stated; and it has been said:
"Whatever a mortal desires by day, or looks upon, or performs—that he speaks or performs even in a dream due to the habituation to that. (Pañcāstikāya 1.144)
And so it is said:
"Whatever merit or sin resides in the hearts of men, even if it be well-concealed, that may be known from dreams, from speech, and likewise from intoxication. (Pañc 1.145)

Or rather, what doubt can there be regarding women? They chatter with one man, they look toward another with flirtatious gestures, and they think of someone else entirely within their hearts; who indeed can truly be called a lover to women? (Pañca 1.146)
Moreover:
With one [man], they speak many words with their lips pale-red from a smile; with another, they gaze from here with eyes throbbing like blossoming night-lotuses;

and with yet another, whose noble conduct and wondrous wealth they contemplate in their minds from afar—by what means could such love of the fair-browed women be considered truly meaningful in the ultimate sense? (Pancika 1.147)
And so it is said:
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman ever satiated with men. (Pañcāstikāya 1.148)
"There is no privacy, there is no opportune moment, and there is no man who does not desire them;
therefore, O Nārada, the virtue of chastity arises in women."
That fool who, out of delusion, thinks, "This amorous woman belongs to me," will remain perpetually under her control, like a bird in a cage.
He carries out their words and tasks, whether they be very few or very weighty; yet by performing them, he attains insignificance in every respect throughout the world.
Women desire precisely that man who seeks them out, approaches them closely, and performs even a slight service for them.
Because men do not desire them and out of fear of their attendants,
women— who are themselves beyond all restraint— always remain within the bounds of propriety.
There is no man inaccessible to them, nor do they abide by age;
whether he be ugly or handsome, a man is enjoyed simply because he is a man.
For one who is passionate becomes an object of enjoyment for women, like a garment that is rubbed against the hips when it is tucked there by its hem. (Panc_1.155)
Just as a man who has been squeezed for lac becomes red with it,
so too is one who is forcibly made impassioned by women cast down at their feet.
Thus, having lamented in many ways, from that time forth the king became averse to showing favor toward Dantila. To say more, even his entry into the royal palace was forbidden.
Dantila, too, observing that the monarch had suddenly turned away from showing him favor, reflected: "Ah, it is well said:"
Who, having acquired wealth, has not become arrogant? To which sensualist have calamities not come to an end?
By whom on earth has the mind not been shattered by women? Who indeed is beloved by kings? Who has not fallen within the range of Time? And what suppliant has ever attained dignity?
Or what man, having fallen into the snares of the wicked, has ever escaped in safety?
And so it is said:

"Purity in a crow, truthfulness in gamblers, forbearance in a serpent, the quelling of desire in women, fortitude in a eunuch, and contemplation of reality in a drunkard—by whom has a king as a friend ever been seen or heard of? (Pañcatantra 1.158)
"Furthermore, I have never done anything harmful to this king, nor to anyone else related to the royal family, even in my dreams.
So why is the king turning his face away from me?
Thus, once seeing Dantila blocked at the palace gate, the sweeper Gorambha laughed and said this to the doorkeepers: "O, O doorkeepers!"
"This Dantila is empowered by the king's favor and is himself the one who exercises both punishment and grace.
Therefore, if he is restrained, you too will receive a half-moon [punishment], just as I have.
Hearing this, Dantila thought to himself, "This must surely be the doing of this Gorambha."
Or rather, it is well said:
"Even if he is of low birth, even if he is a fool, and even if he is devoid of honor—if he serves a king here, he is honored everywhere. (Pañcatantra 1.159)
Even if a man serving a king should be a coward or a base person, nevertheless,
that individual does not suffer defeat at the hands of others.

Having lamented in this way at great length, his mind filled with shame, agitated, and his power diminished, he summoned Gorambha at the onset of night, honored him with a pair of garments, and said: "My good man, I did not dismiss you at that time out of passion;
rather, you were dismissed because you were seen sitting in an improper place in front of the brahmins, and thus you were insulted."
Therefore, please forgive me.
Having obtained that pair of garments, which was like the kingdom of heaven, he too attained supreme satisfaction and said to him: "O merchant!
I have forgiven you for that."
"Therefore, behold my intellectual power and royal favor for the sake of this honor.
Having spoken thus, he departed with satisfaction.
And it is well said:
With a slight [weight] it rises, and with a slight [weight] it goes downward;
oh, how similar is the behavior of a wicked person to that of a balance beam!

Then, on the following day, that Gorambha went to the royal palace and, while performing the task of sweeping for the king who was in yogic sleep, said this: "Oh, how lacking in discernment is our king, that while performing the voiding of excrement, he eats the *carbhaṭī*!
Hearing that, the king spoke to him with astonishment: "Hey there, Gorambha!
"Why do you prattle on about irrelevant matters? Thinking of you as a mere domestic servant, I have not yet killed you. Have you ever seen me performing such an action?"
He said: "While I was occupied with gambling and sweeping during the night, sleep came over me by force;
possessed by it, I spoke something, but I do not know what."
"Therefore, may my lord show favor to me who am overcome by sleep.
Hearing this, the king thought: "In no other birth have I ever eaten a *cirbhaṭikā* while voiding excrement;
thus, this improbable occurrence has been recounted to me by this fool."
Such is the certainty regarding Dantila as well.
Therefore, it was not right that I acted in such a way as to deprive that poor man of his honor;
such conduct is not to be expected from men of his caliber.
In his absence, none of the royal duties nor the civic affairs would fall into neglect.
Having reflected thus in many ways, he summoned Dantila, endowed him with garments, ornaments, and other personal regalia from his own body, and appointed him to his office.
Therefore I say: "He who, out of pride, does not honor... etc.
Saṃjīvaka said, "My good friend, it is exactly so;
whatever you have spoken must indeed be done by me.
When this had been said, Damanaka took him and went into the presence of Piṅgalaka.
And he said: "O King, this Saṃjīvaka has been brought by me; now Your Majesty is the authority. Saṃjīvaka, too, having bowed respectfully to him, stood before him with humility.
Piṅgalaka also, placing his right hand—adorned with claws like thunderbolts and possessing a full, broad hump—upon him, spoke with great respect: "Is it well with you?
From where have you come to this desolate forest? He, in turn, related his own story.
He reported everything exactly as his separation from Vardhamāna had occurred.
Having heard this, Piṅgalaka spoke to him with great respect: "Friend, you need not fear;
protected by the cage of my own arms, you may now conduct yourself as you wish."
Furthermore, you must always remain by my side;
for this reason, the forest— full of many dangers and inhabited by fierce creatures— is unfit to be frequented even by powerful beings,
let alone by those who feed on grass.
Having spoken thus, surrounded by all his deer, he descended to the bank of the Yamunā, took up water, and entered that very forest at his own will.
Thereafter, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to Karakaṭa and Damanaka, he remained there with Saṃjīvika, enjoying conversations on wise sayings.
Or rather, it is well said:
Even a single encounter with a virtuous person, when it occurs by chance, becomes ageless and eternal; it does not depend on the process of repeated practice.

Through Sañjīvaka’s immersion in numerous treatises, which had produced a boldness of intellect, the dull-witted Piṅgalaka was made wise in just a few days; he was so transformed that, having been separated from the ways of the forest, he was established in the ways of the village. To put it briefly, day after day, Piṅgalaka and Sañjīvaka consulted with one another in private alone.
All the rest of the animal folk remained at a distance;
even Karaṭaka and Damanaka could not gain entrance.
Furthermore, due to the absence of the lion’s prowess, all the animals and those two jackals, afflicted by the disease of hunger, took refuge in one direction and stayed there.
And it has been said:
"Servants abandon even a high-born king who is elevated yet destitute of wealth;
they depart from him here as birds leave a withered tree. (Pañcatantra 1.163)
And so it is said:
"Even those of noble birth who are endowed with honor and devoted to their service will surely abandon the protector of the earth if their livelihood is destroyed. (Pañcatantra 1.164)
Furthermore:
Servants who do not allow their master to exceed the proper time for their livelihood will never abandon him, even when they have been rebuked. (Pancatantra 1.165)
And thus, not only are servants of such a nature, but even this entire world exists for the sake of devouring one another through means such as conciliation and the like. For example:
Kings over countries, physicians over the sick, Merchants over buyers, and scholars over fools. (Pañcatantra 1.166)
Likewise, thieves are for the heedless; beggars are for householders;
courtesans are for those possessed by lust; and artisans are for the entire world.
Armed with snares such as conciliation and the like, they await their prey day and night;
for by their power, they indeed subsist upon others, just as aquatic creatures live off the clouds.
Or rather, it is well said:
"The intentions of serpents, of the wicked, and of those who seize the property of others do not succeed; by this, the world continues to exist. (Pañcāstikāya 1.169)

The serpent, afflicted by hunger, desires to eat the rat of Gaṇapati; the peacock of the enemy of Krauñca [Kārttikeya] desires that serpent; and even the lion of the Mountain’s Daughter [Pārvatī] desires the eater of serpents.
Thus, in whose house even Śambhu’s own dependents find such a state of mutual predation!
In that case as well, how could it not belong to the world, since that is indeed its own nature?
Then, deprived of their master’s favor and with throats parched by hunger, Karaṭaka and Damanaka consulted with one another.
Thereupon, Damanaka said: "Noble Karaṭaka, we have both fallen into a state of insignificance."
This Piṅgalaka has become so enamored with Saṃjīvaka that he has turned his back on his own duties;
all his attendants have departed as well.
So, what is to be done?
Karaṭaka said: "Even if he does not act upon your words, nevertheless the master must be spoken to for the sake of destroying his own faults. And it has been said:

'Even if he does not listen, the lord of the earth must be made to understand by his ministers, just as the son of Ambikā was [advised] by Vidura for the destruction of his own faults. (Pañcatantra 1.171)
And so it is said:
"When a king or an elephant, intoxicated with pride, goes astray, those standing nearby—the high ministers or the mahouts—become objects of reproach. (Pañcatantra 1.172)
Therefore, you brought this grass-eater into the presence of his master;
thus, coals were drawn out by your own hand.
Damanaka said, "This is true."
"This fault is mine, not my master's. And it has been said:
"The jackal by the fight over a ram, and we by Āṣāḍhabhūti."
The female messenger, by acting on behalf of another, has herself committed three faults.
Karaṭaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 4.
The Story of the Wandering Mendicant Devaśarman:
In a certain secluded region, there was a monastery.
Therein dwelt a wandering mendicant named Devaśarman.
Through the sale of fine garments given to him by many virtuous people, a great amount of wealth gradually accumulated for him.
Consequently, he trusted no one;
day and night, he would not let that wealth out of his armpit.
Or rather, it is well said:
"There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure—fie on wealth, which is a refuge of misery! (Pañcatantra 1.174).

Then a rogue named Āṣāḍhabhūti, a thief of others' wealth, having noticed that amount of money tucked inside his [the monk's] armpit, thought: "How can I steal this amount of wealth from him? He considered:
"In this monastery, for the time being, there is no way to break through the wall because of its solid accumulation of stone."
Furthermore, because of its great height, there would be no way to enter through the gate.
Therefore, having gained his confidence with deceptive words, I shall assume the role of a student, so that he, being trusting, may eventually place his trust in me. And it is said:
"One who is free from desire cannot hold office; one who lacks ambition does not delight in adornment."
One who is not clever should not speak what is pleasing; one who speaks clearly is not a deceiver.
Having thus resolved, he approached him, uttered "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," prostrated with all eight limbs, and spoke with humility: "O Blessed One, this saṃsāra is essence-less;
youth is like the rush of a mountain river;
life is like a fire in grass."
Enjoyments are like the shadow of autumn clouds; the connection with the circle of friends, sons, wife, and servants is like a dream.
Thus have I correctly understood.
Therefore, by doing what will my crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra come to pass?

Having heard that, Devaśarman said respectfully: "My son, you are blessed that such a state of detachment has arisen in you even at this first stage of life. And it is said: 'He who is peaceful in his early years—he, in my opinion, is truly peaceful.'"
When the elements are wasting away, in whom does tranquility not arise?
For the virtuous, aging first arises in the mind and then in the body;
for the wicked, however, it arises in the body but never in the mind.
And as for that which you ask me— the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra—
let that be heard:
whether he be a śūdra, or even another, or even a caṇḍāla wearing matted locks;
Initiated by means of the Śiva-mantra, he whose limbs are smeared with ashes shall become Śiva himself.
Whoever personally offers even a single flower upon the crown of the Liṅga with the six-syllable mantra is not born again.
Having heard that, Āṣāḍhabhūti took hold of his feet and said with humility: "Venerable sir, in that case, please favor me by granting me initiation.
Devaśarman said: "Child, I shall grant you favor."
However, you must not enter the interior of the monastery at night, because detachment is praised for ascetics, both for you and for me. And it is said:
"A king perishes through bad counsel, an ascetic through attachment, and a son through excessive indulgence."
A Brahmin’s [status] perishes from neglecting Vedic study; a family perishes from a bad son; character from attending upon the wicked;
friendship from a lack of affection; prosperity from misconduct; affection from living abroad;
a wife from pride and neglect; agriculture from abandonment; and wealth from heedlessness. (Pañcatantra 1.180)
"Therefore, after you have taken the vow, you must sleep in a small grass hut at the door of the monastery.
He replied, "Venerable sir,
your command is authoritative."
"For I have need of him in the future.
Then, having subdued Devaśarman at the appointed time for his rest, he brought him under discipleship according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
He, too, gratified him with service such as massaging his hands and feet.
Nevertheless, the sage still did not release even a single measure from his armpit.
As time passed in this manner, Āṣāḍhabhūti thought:
"Alas! He does not place any trust in me whatsoever."
"Should I therefore kill him even by day with a weapon?
Or should I administer poison?
Or should I slay him according to the custom of wild beasts?"
While Devaśarman was reflecting thus, a certain disciple’s son arrived from the village to invite him and said, "Venerable sir,
please come to my house for the sake of the Pavitrāropaṇa ceremony."
Having heard that, Devaśarman set out with Āṣāḍhabhūti with a joyful heart.
Now, as he was traveling in this manner, a certain river appeared before him.

Seeing it, he took his mother down from his armpit, placed her very securely within the folds of his patched garment (*kaṇṭhā*), bathed, performed the worship of the gods, and immediately thereafter said this to Āṣāḍhabhūti: "O Āṣāḍhabhūti!"
"Until I return after having relieved myself, you must protect this rag-robe with your own vigilance, O Lord of Yoga.
Having said this, he departed.
When he had vanished from sight, Āṣāḍhabhūti also took his portion and set out in haste.
Devaśarman, his mind delighted by the qualities of his pupil, remained seated with full confidence; meanwhile, in the midst of a herd of golden-haired goats, he saw a fight between two rams.
Then, out of rage, the pair of rams retreated a great distance, only to come together again and strike each other with their foreheads until much blood flowed.
And the jackal, out of greed for the tongue, entered the arena and began to taste it.
Devaśarman, seeing this, thought: "Alas, this jackal is dull-witted!
If by some chance he falls into the clash of these two, I think he will surely meet his death."

A moment later, in the very same way, as he entered between them out of greed for the taste of blood, the jackal fell and died from the collision of their heads. Devaśarman, lamenting him while thinking of his mother, set out slowly; when he did not see Āṣāḍhabhūti, he performed his purification out of anxiety and, upon looking at his patched garment, did not see his mother there either.
Then, crying out, "Alas! Alas! I have been robbed!", he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Having regained consciousness after a moment, he rose once more and began to wail: "O Āṣāḍhabhūti!
Where have you gone, having deceived me?"
"Give me an answer to that!
Having lamented thus at great length, he set out slowly, following the track of his footsteps. As he was proceeding in this manner, at the time of evening, he reached a certain village.
Now, from that village, a certain weaver set out for a nearby city with his wife to drink wine.
Seeing him, Devaśarman said, "O good sir, we are travelers who have arrived at your place;
we do not know anyone here in this village."
Therefore, let the duty toward a guest be observed. And it has been said:
"When a guest arrives in the evening as the sun sets, those householders who honor him attain the status of deities. (Pañca 1.181)
And so it is said:
"Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these are never lacking in the dwellings of the virtuous. (Pañcatantra 1.182)
The sacrificial fires were satisfied by his welcome; Indra, lord of a hundred sacrifices, by his seat;
the ancestors by the washing of his feet; and Śambhu by the guest-offering (argha) for the visitor.
The Kaulika, having heard this, said to his wife:
"My dear, go now with the guest toward our home; after honoring him with water for washing the feet, food, a place to lie down, and so forth, remain right there.
For your sake, I shall bring back plenty of wine."
Having spoken thus, he set out.
His wife, that unchaste woman, taking him with her, set off toward home with a smiling face, while in her mind she meditated upon Devadatta.
Or rather, as this well-said proverb goes:

On a dark day, when dense darkness prevails and the city streets are difficult to traverse, there is supreme pleasure for the woman of loose character when her husband departs for a foreign land. (Pañcatantra 1.184)
And so it is said:
"Lusting after secret love-making, passionate women regard a bedspread on a couch, a husband who is compliant and charming, and even a bed itself as light as a blade of grass. (Pañca 1.185)
And so it is said:
"Amorous play burns away modesty; love-making leaves only bones; endearments are bitter;
and satisfaction comes from the three types of bonds. When the husband is present, nothing at all is desirable. (Pañcatantra 1.186)
The unchaste woman, constantly attached to another man, accepts the ruin of her family, the censure of people, imprisonment, and even the risk to her life. (Panc 1.187)

Then the Kaulika’s wife went home and, having handed over the broken bed and the worn-out mattress to Devaśarman, said this: "O venerable sir, until I return quickly after paying my respects to a female friend who has come from the village, you must remain vigilant in my house. Having spoken thus and prepared herself for amorous dalliance, as she was setting out toward Devadatta, her husband met her, his limbs reeling with intoxication, his hair disheveled, stumbling at every step.
Carrying a vessel of wine, he approached.

Upon seeing him, she turned back very quickly and entered her own house, where she resumed her former state, having cast off her elaborate ornaments and finery. The weaver, too, seeing her fleeing while still adorned with that extraordinary finery—his heart already agitated by the scandal he had heard of her through the succession of rumors—concealed his true feelings.
She remained there constantly.
Then, having observed such behavior and being convinced by what he saw, he fell under the sway of anger; entering the house, he said to her: "Ah, you sinful harlot!
Where have you gone?"
She said: "I have come from your presence and have not gone anywhere else;
so how is it that, under the influence of drinking liquor, you speak what is irrelevant?
Or rather, it is well said:"
Impairment, falling to the ground, and speaking inappropriately—liquor displays all these symptoms of a deranged humoral imbalance (*saṃnipāta*). (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.188)
Trembling hands, casting off one's garment, loss of luster,
and a state of flushed redness— these conditions arising from contact with wine are experienced even by the Sun.
Having heard those hostile words and observing her change of dress, he said to her: "O harlot!
For a long time I have heard reports of your misconduct;
therefore, having now gained personal conviction myself, I shall today inflict upon you the punishment you deserve."

Having spoken thus, and having reduced her body to a state of ruin with blows from a club, he bound her with a firm tethering to a pillar; then Devadatta, intoxicated by pride, went there and said, "He is waiting for you in that place;
therefore, come quickly."
She said: "Behold my condition!
So how can I go? Therefore, having gone there, tell that lover that there will be no union with you this night."
The barber’s wife said: "Friend, do not speak thus! This is not the way of an unchaste woman. And it has been said:"
I consider the birth of those whose resolve is fixed on the effort to grasp sweet fruit while standing in a precarious place to be as praiseworthy as that of camels. (Pancatanttra 1.190)
And so it is said:
"In a world where the next life is uncertain and public scandal is manifold, those who enjoy the fruit of youth while possessing their own beloveds are truly blessed. (Pañcāstikāya 1.191)
Furthermore:
Even if, by the power of fate, a man who is ugly and a seducer should meet her in secret, she would surely not abandon her own beloved husband, even at great hardship. (Pancatantra 1.192)
She said, "If that is so, then tell me how I may go there while bound by firm fetters,
for this wicked husband of mine is close at hand.
Nāpitī replied, "Friend," and continued:
"This man, overwhelmed by intoxication, will regain consciousness when touched by the rays of the sun;
therefore, I shall release you.
Bind me in his place and return as quickly as possible after having seen Devadatta."
She replied, "So be it.

Thereupon, the barber's wife released her friend from her bonds and bound herself in her place as before; she then sent her to the rendezvous with Devadatta. When this had been done, the weaver rose at a certain moment, his anger somewhat subsided and his intoxication gone, and said to her: "O you who speak so harshly!"
If from this day forward you do not go out of the house and do not speak harshly,
then I shall release you.
Fearing a change in his voice, he did not say anything at all;
meanwhile, he continued to say that very same thing to her again and again. Then, as she gave no answer whatsoever, he spoke further.
Then, becoming enraged, he took a sharp weapon and cut off her nose, saying: "O harlot!
Stay right there now!"
"I shall please you yet more," he said,
and once again fell under the power of sleep. Devaśarman, too, his throat parched with hunger due to the loss of his wealth and deprived of sleep, witnessed all that conduct of the woman.

That wife of the weaver, too, having enjoyed the pleasure of sexual union with Devadatta according to her desire, returned to her own home at a certain moment and said this to the barber woman: "O lady, may it be well with you!
This wicked soul did not rise while I was away."
He said further: "Without the nose, the rest of the body is not auspicious.
Therefore, quickly release her from her bonds before he sees me, so that I may go to my own home."
When this had been carried out, the weaver rose once more and said to her: "Whore!
Why do you still not speak?
Shall I inflict upon you an even more severe punishment than this by cutting off your ears?"
Then, with indignation and reproach, she said this: "Fie upon you, great fool! Who is capable of assailing or defiling me, a woman of great virtue?
Let all the world-protectors hear this!"
The sun, the moon, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and the other gods are not able to conquer those sense faculties which cause extreme suffering; they are powerful and exceedingly difficult to subdue.
Those who conquer in this world are but a few among the powerful.
Therefore, if my chastity is true—
if not even in thought have I desired another man—
then may the gods restore my nose once more to its former, uninjured state.
"Or rather, if even the slightest delusion regarding another man should arise in my mind, let them reduce me to ashes!
Having said this, she spoke to him once more: "O wicked soul!"
"Behold, by the power of my chastity, my nose has become exactly as it was before.
Then, taking a firebrand, he looked; and at that moment, he saw her nose restored to its original form upon the ground, along with a great torrent of blood.
Then, with a mind filled with wonder, he released her from her bonds, placed her upon his bed, and gratified her with hundreds of endearing words.
Devaśarman, too, having observed the entire sequence of events, said this with a mind struck by amazement:
"Whatever magic belongs to Śambara, and whatever magic belongs even to Namuci..."
They know all those women to belong to Bali and Kumbhīnasa.
These women laugh at one who laughs and weep even when he weeps;
they win over an enemy with pleasant words through the power of time.
Whatever treatise Uśanas knows and whatever Bṛhaspati knows, they are not superior to the intellect of women; how then can they be guarded by men?
"They say that falsehood is truth, and likewise that truth is falsehood;
O hero, how are those [conventions] to be guarded by men in this world? (Pancadaśī 1.197)
It is also said elsewhere:
"One should not allow excessive attachment toward women,
nor should one desire that one's power increase over women."
For those women sport with men who are excessively attached to them, like crows whose wings have been clipped.
They speak with a pleasant face, yet they strike with a sharp mind;
honey resides in the speech of women, but in their hearts is the great poison, *hālāhala*. (Pañcatantra 1.199)

For this very reason, their lips are sipped and their hearts are struck with fists by men who, like bees greedy for honey, are deprived of even a fragment of happiness—just as one might do to a lotus. (Pañca 1.200)
Moreover:
A whirlpool of doubts, an abode of immodesty, a port for rash acts, a repository of faults, a field consisting of a hundred deceits, a soil of mistrust;

an obstacle to the gate of heaven, the mouth of the city of hell, a casket of all illusions—a machine of woman by whom was it created? It is poison made of nectar, a snare for the world of living beings. (Pañcāstikāya 1.201)
