Roughness in their breasts, tremulousness in their eyes, falsehood in their speech, praise-worthy crookedness in their tresses, dullness in their words, stoutness in their hips, constant timidity in their hearts, and the employment of deceit toward their lovers—those fawn-eyed women for whom such a multitude of faults is considered a collection of virtues shall become beloved by men. (Pancatantra 1.202)
These women laugh and weep for the sake of their own ends;
they inspire confidence in others while remaining untrustworthy themselves.
Therefore, a man endowed with noble birth and good character should avoid women as one avoids the funeral urns at a cremation ground. (Pañcatantra 1.203)
Therefore, a man of noble birth and virtuous conduct should always avoid women as one would avoid the thickets of a cremation ground;
for they are like lions with gaping mouths and disheveled manes.
And the nāgas shone forth, resplendent with abundant ichor.
They perform pleasing acts first,
so long as they do not know that the man is attached; but once they know him bound by the noose of passion, [they abandon him].
They pull them out like a fish that has swallowed bait.
By nature as fickle as the waves of the ocean,
possessing passion for only a moment like a streak of twilight clouds,
women abandon a man once their purpose is achieved, leaving him destitute.
They cast them off like lac-dye squeezed out from its base. //Panc_1.206//
Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, folly, excessive greed,
impurity, and mercilessness are the faults of women born of their very nature.
Deluding, intoxicating, mocking, crushing, delighting, and disheartening—
having entered these, they [afflict] the simple hearts of men.
Or what, indeed, do those with lovely eyes not practice?
For these women are filled with poison within, yet they are charming on the outside; by whom were they fashioned, resembling the seeds of the *guñjā* plant? (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.209)
As that wandering mendicant was reflecting thus, the night passed with great difficulty.
And that female messenger, her nose having been cut off, went to her own home and thought: "What should be done now?
How is this great breach to be concealed?"

Now, while she was reflecting thus, her husband, detained at the royal palace on account of some business, returned to his own home at dawn; standing at the doorway and eager for various civic duties, he said to her: "My dear lady, let the barber's kit be brought quickly, so that I may go to have my hair and beard shaved."
She too, though her nose was cut off, while still standing in the middle of the house, drew a single razor from the barber's kit for the sake of performing her task and hurled it at him.

The barber, seeing that single razor with impatience, became possessed by anger and likewise hurled his razor right back at her. In the meantime, that wicked woman, raising her arms and intending to hiss, stepped out from the house.
"Alas! Behold, this wicked man has cut off the nose of me who walks the path of virtuous conduct!
Therefore, save me, save me!
In the meantime, the king's men arrived, and having reduced that barber to a pulp with blows from clubs, they bound him with firm fetters.

Having bound her together with that woman whose nose had been cut off, they led them to the seat of the court of justice and said to the members of the assembly: "Listen, honorable members of the court!
Without any offense, this barber has disfigured this jewel of a woman."
When he was told, "Therefore, let that which is appropriate for him be done," the members of the assembly said, "O barber!
For what reason have you disfigured your wife?"
Has she desired another man?
Or has she committed an act of violence against living beings? Or perhaps has she practiced the deed of theft?
"Then let her offense be told!
But even the barber, his body tormented by the blows, was unable to speak.
Then, seeing him silent, they spoke again: "Alas!"
This speech of the king’s men is true; this man is evil-minded.
By him, this poor, innocent woman has been defiled. And it is said:

With a faltering voice and altered facial complexion, his gaze filled with apprehension and his vital energy suddenly flaring up, a man who has committed an evil deed indeed becomes terrified by his own karma. (Pañca 1.210)
And so it is said:
"He approaches with faltering steps, accompanied by a change of facial color;
his forehead is covered in sweat, and he speaks words in a great, stammering voice. (Pañcavastuka 1.211)
A man who has committed a sin will speak with downcast eyes when he enters the assembly;
therefore, they should be carefully identified by these signs by those who are discerning.
Furthermore:
A pure man is seen with a serene countenance and clear speech; yet in the assembly, he speaks with indignation and self-assurance, his eyes full of wrath. (Pancatantre 1.213)
Thus, this man is seen to possess the characteristics of wicked conduct; because he has violated a woman, he is to be put to death.
Therefore, let him be mounted upon the stake.
Then, seeing him being led to the place of execution, Devaśarman went to those officials of justice and said: "O sirs, this wretched barber is not to be executed by you;
he is a man of virtuous conduct."
"Listen then to my words: 'The jackal by means of the fight between two rams.
Then those members of the assembly said: 'O Venerable One, how was that?'"
Then Devaśarman related the entire account of those three in detail.
Upon hearing this, their minds filled with great wonder, they released the barber and said to one another: "Aha!
Brahmins, cows, women, children, and kinsmen are not to be slain."
And those whose food one might eat, and those who have come for refuge.

Thus, the cutting off of her nose was indeed brought about by her own karma; however, the king's punishment shall be the cutting off of her ears. When this had been carried out, Devaśarman, freed from the grief arising from the loss of his wealth, returned once more to his own monastery.
Therefore I say: "The jackal by means of a fight with a ram" (1.174).
Karaṭaka said: "In such a situation, what should we do?
Damanaka replied: "Even in such a time, my wit will find a way."
By which means I shall separate Sañjīvaka from his master.
And it is said:
"An arrow discharged by an archer may kill one person or may not kill anyone at all."
But an intellect cast off by wisdom would destroy even those within the womb.
"Therefore, by resorting to a concealment through the artifice of illusion, I shall break it open.
Karaṭaka said, "My good friend,
if by any chance Piṅgalaka should discover your entry through this illusion,"
"Or rather, Sañjīvaka will surely meet his end.
He replied, "Father, do not speak thus."
Those of hidden intelligence should employ their intellect even during times of calamity when fate is adverse;
effort must not be abandoned.
For sometimes, by the maxim of the "worm's letter," the sovereignty of intelligence prevails. And it has been said:
One must not abandon fortitude even when fate is adverse;
for through fortitude, one may sometimes attain stability,
just as when a ship is wrecked at sea, it may still reach the shore.
The merchant seafarer desires only action.
And so it is said:
"Prosperity ever attends the industrious man here;
those who are cowards say, 'It is fate, indeed, it is fate.'"
Overcoming destiny, exercise human effort through your own power; if success is not achieved despite the exertion, what fault is there in that?
Therefore, having understood this, I shall separate these two from one another by means of my power of highly concealed intellect, so that neither of them will discover it. And it is said:
"Even Brahmā cannot reach the end of a well-applied deception."
A member of the Kaula sect, in the form of Viṣṇu, serves the king's daughter.
Karaṭaka said, "How was that?
He replied—
Story 5.
The Story of the Weaver and the Carpenters: In a certain town there lived two friends, a weaver and a carpenter.
From their childhood, they had been companions who were exceedingly devoted to one another; they spent their time always staying together in the same place.
Then, once upon a time, a great festival procession took place at a certain temple in that city;

and there, as they were wandering through the crowd of actors, dancers, and minstrels, surrounded by people gathered from various lands, those two companions beheld a certain princess mounted upon a female elephant, endowed with all auspicious marks and attended by chamberlains and eunuchs.
They saw her arrive for the purpose of visiting the deity.
Then, upon seeing her, that artisan fell suddenly to the ground like one afflicted by poison, as if seized by an evil spirit, being struck by the arrows of love.
Observing him in such a state, the chariot-maker, pained by his suffering, had him lifted up by trusted men and brought to his own home. There—
And while being treated by physicians with various cooling remedies prescribed by them and by practitioners of mantras, he somehow regained consciousness after a long time.
Then the carpenter asked him: "O friend, why have you suddenly become unconscious like this?"
"Therefore, let the nature of the self be told.
He said: "Friend, if it is so, then hear my secret, by which I shall declare to you the entire knowledge of the self."
"If you consider me a friend, then please show me this favor by providing the wood;
and may you forgive whatever improper thing I have done toward you out of excessive affection.
Having heard this, he, with eyes clouded by tears, spoke with a faltering voice: "Friend," he said.
Tell me whatever cause of suffering there may be, so that a remedy may be applied, if it is possible to do so. And it has been said:
"Of medicines, effective mantras, and the wisdom of great-souled ones..."
There is nothing within this world, even that which lies in the midst of the cosmic egg, which is impossible to accomplish.
"Therefore, if that goal of these four can be accomplished, then I shall accomplish it.
The Kaulika said, "Friend,
even by thousands of other means besides these, that sorrow of mine remains unaccomplished."
"Therefore, do not delay my death.
The chariot-maker said, "O friend,
even if it is impossible, nevertheless, inform me so that I too, considering it impossible, may enter the fire along with you."
"I shall not endure separation from you even for a moment;
this is my firm resolve.
The weaver said, "Friend,"
That princess who was seen there at the festival mounted upon a female elephant—
immediately after seeing her, this state has been brought upon me by the god whose banner bears the sea-monster.
Therefore, I am unable to endure that agony.
And so it has been said:
"Exhausted by the fatigue of love-making upon her pair of breasts, which are as expansive as the frontal globes of a rutting elephant and moist with saffron..."
When, having obtained a moment of union with her, shall I sleep for a while, resting my chest within the cage of her arms?
And so it is said:
"He has lips red as a bimba fruit; his pair of jar-like breasts possess the pride of full youth;
his navel is deep; his hair is naturally curly; and even his waist is slender."
Let these things indeed forcibly produce weariness here in my mind as soon as they are thought of;
yet, that it repeatedly burns my two clear cheeks—that is not right.
The chariot-maker, having heard those words with pleasure, said this with a smile: "Friend, if that is so, then by good fortune our purpose is accomplished;
therefore, let a meeting with her be arranged this very day."
The Kaulika said: "Friend, how can there be a union for me with her in that maiden's inner apartments, where no one may enter except for the wind, and which is presided over by guards?
Why then do you mock me with such false words?"
The chariot-maker said, "Friend,

behold the power of my intellect! Having spoken thus, he instantly fashioned from the wood of the *vāyuja* tree a pair of arms like those of Garuḍa, capable of moving a stake, and endowed with a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, along with a crown and the *kaustubha* gem.
Then, having placed the weaver upon that [platform], marked him with the signs of Viṣṇu, and demonstrated the knowledge of moving the pegs, he said:
"Friend, go at night in this form of Viṣṇu to the princess's inner apartments; there, you will find the royal maiden alone on the uppermost floor of the seven-storied palace.
She is of a simple nature, and thinking you to be Vāsudeva, you must delight her with your own clever and artful words."
"Enjoy her according to the method taught by Vātsyāyana. Having heard this, the Kaulika went there in that manner and said to her, "O Princess,
are you asleep or are you awake?"

for that reason, I did not come."
Nevertheless, observing the destruction of the king’s purpose, his heart burning with distress, he has come here of his own accord out of agitation to speak. And it is said:
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, auspicious or inauspicious, one should speak what is beneficial—even if unasked—to one whom one does not wish to see defeated. (Pañcatantra 1.262)
Then, having heard his intentional words, Piṅgalaka said, "What is it that you wish to say?
Let that which is to be told be spoken.
He replied, "Your Majesty, Sañjīvaka harbors a malicious intent toward your Highness."
When I had gained his confidence, he said this to me in that secluded place: "O Damanaka!
I have perceived the true worth and worthlessness of this Piṅgalaka.
Therefore, having slain him, I shall make you the possessor of the entire sovereignty over the deer, endowed with the rank of minister."
Piṅgalaka, having heard those harsh words which were like a blow from the essence of a thunderbolt, fell into a state of stupor and said nothing at all.
Damanaka, observing his condition, thought: "This king is indeed bound by passion for Sañjīvaka; therefore, this minister will surely bring about the king's destruction. And it is said:
When a lord of the earth appoints a single minister as the sole authority in the kingdom, pride takes hold of him through delusion; and from that pride, he becomes weary of servitude.
In the heart of one who is weary, there arises a longing for independence; and through that longing for autonomy, he then seeks to destroy the life of the king. (Pañcatantra 1.263)
"What, then, is appropriate here?
Piṅgalaka, having regained his composure, said to him with some difficulty: "Sañjīvaka is a servant as dear to me as my own life;
how could he harbor a treacherous intent toward me?"
Damanaka said: "O King, the distinction between a servant and a non-servant is not absolute. And it has been said:
'There is no man among kings who does not desire sovereignty.'"
Being indeed powerless in every respect, they wait upon the lord of men.
Piṅgalaka said: "My good friend, nevertheless, my mental state toward him does not undergo any change.
Or rather, it is well said:"
To whom is this body, corrupted by manifold defects, not dear?
Even while committing offenses, he who is beloved remains truly beloved.
Damanaka said: "For this very reason, this is a fault. And it has been said:
'Whomever a king fixes his gaze upon excessively, whether he be of low birth or of noble birth, that man becomes a vessel for prosperity.'"
Furthermore, by what special quality does my lord keep Sañjīvaka near him, even though he is devoid of merit?
Or rather, O King, if you think thus: "He is large-bodied;
I shall use him to destroy my enemies."
Therefore, this will not succeed for us, because he is a consumer of young grass,
whereas the enemies of Your Majesty, on the other hand, are eaters of flesh.
"The means to overcome that enemy cannot be achieved with his assistance;
therefore, let him be corrupted and then slain.
Piṅgalaka said:
One who fears the violation of his own promise should not speak of the faults of that person who was previously declared virtuous in the assembly. (Pancatantira 1.267)
Moreover, I have granted him the gift of safety according to your word;
how then could I kill him myself? In every respect, this Sañjīvaka is our friend.
"One should harbor no resentment toward him. And it has been said:
"That Daitya, having attained prosperity from this [source], does not deserve destruction from this very same source;
for even a poison-tree, having nurtured it oneself, is unfit to be cut down by one's own hand. (Pañca 1.268)
At first, one should either not grant a request to those who seek it,
or once granted, it must be nurtured daily;
for to cast away what has been raised up brings shame upon oneself.
For one who stands upon the ground, there is no fear at all of falling.
What merit is there in the goodness of one who is good toward those who help him?
He who is good toward those who do him harm is called "good" by the virtuous.
"Even toward one who harbors malice toward me, I must not act in opposition.
Damanaka said, "My Lord, this is not the duty of a king, that even malice should be forgiven. And it is said:"
He who does not slay a servant who possesses equal wealth, equal capability, knows his vital secrets, is industrious,
and seizes half the kingdom, will himself be slain.
Furthermore, because of your friendship with him, you have abandoned all the duties of a king; and due to the absence of royal duty, your entire retinue has become disaffected.
Sañjīvaka is one who feeds on grass, while you are a meat-eater.
Moreover, since your subjects are excluded from the effort to kill you, how could they eat your flesh?
Deprived of that [flesh], they will abandon you and depart;
consequently, you too are utterly ruined.
Through association with him, your mind will never again turn toward hunting. And it is said:
"By whatever kind of servants one is served, and by whatever kind of people one serves, a person becomes like them; of this there is never any doubt. (Pañcatantra 1.272)
And so it is said:
"The very name of water is not known when it rests upon heated iron;
yet that same water, when placed upon a lotus leaf, shines forth as pearls."
When it falls into the belly of a sea oyster during the asterism Svāti, it generally becomes a pearl;
its qualities—whether inferior, middling, or superior—arise from its dwelling there.
And so it is said:
"Through the fault of associating with the wicked, even a virtuous mind falls into delusion;
by staying abroad for a single night, a piece of wood hanging from a reed becomes entangled. (Pañcatantra 1.274)
For this very reason, the virtuous avoid association with the base. And it has been said:
"One should not grant shelter to one whose character is unknown; by the fault of a bedbug, the slow-spreading [leprosy] was destroyed. (Pañcatantra 1.275)
Piṅgalaka said, "How was that?
He replied—
Story 9.
The Story of the Louse named Manda-visarpiṇī:
A certain king had a delightful bedchamber;
there, a louse named Manda-visarpiṇī lived, situated between a pair of very white cotton sheets.
And she remained there, savoring the king's blood and passing her time in pleasure.
One day, while wandering somewhere upon that bed, a bug named Agnimukha arrived.
Upon seeing him, she, with a dejected countenance, said:
"O Agnimukha, from where have you come here to this improper place?
Therefore, depart quickly before anyone finds out.
He replied, "Venerable lady, it is not fitting to speak thus even to one who is not virtuous when he has come to one's home. And it is said:"
"Come, come! Sit down upon this seat. Why have you been seen after such a long time? What is the news? You are very weak; is all well? I am delighted by the sight of you.
Those who thus address their dear friends who have arrived with such respect—it is proper for them to always go to their mansions with an untroubled mind. (Pancatantra 1.276)

Furthermore, due to a defect in my diet, I have tasted the various kinds of blood of many humans—blood possessing bitter, pungent, astringent, and sour flavors—but never once have I tasted sweet blood. Therefore, if you grant me your favor, I shall bring about pleasure for my tongue by tasting that sweet blood which has been produced in this king’s body through his consumption of various side dishes, foods, drinks, things to be sucked, and things to be licked. And it is said:
The pleasure of the tongue is considered equal for both a pauper and a king;
that alone is remembered as the essence, and for its sake people strive. (Pañcaskandhaka 1.277)
If there were no such thing as action in this world that brings satisfaction to the tongue,
then no one would ever become a servant or remain under the control of another.
Whatever untruth a mortal may speak, whatever is unfit to be pursued that he pursues, and whatever foreign land he travels to—all that is solely for the sake of his belly. (Pañcatantra 1.279)
"Therefore, even though I am afflicted by hunger, having come to your home, I must request food from you.
Thus, it is not proper for you, being alone, to provide this king with a meal of blood.
Having heard that, Mandavisarpiṇī said, "O bug!"
"I shall drink the blood of this king who has fallen under the power of sleep.
Furthermore, you are fire-mouthed and fickle; therefore, if you will drink blood with me, then stay and taste this most desired blood."
He said, "O Blessed One, I shall do exactly as you say.
As long as you have not tasted the king's blood first, let there be a curse upon me, even one imposed by my deity or guru, if I should taste it.
While the two were thus conversing with one another, the king reached that bed and fell fast asleep.
Then that bug, out of an excessive longing born from the greed of its tongue, bit that lord of the earth even though he was awake.
Or rather, it is well said:
"One's own nature cannot be changed by instruction."
Even water that has been thoroughly heated returns once again to a state of coolness.
If fire were cold or the moon were of the nature of heat,
then the inherent nature of mortals could not be made otherwise.
Then that lord of the earth, as if pierced by the point of a needle, abandoned that bed and rose up at that very moment, saying, "Aha!
Let it be known whether a bug or a louse surely dwells here upon this covering cloth, for by it I have been bitten!
Then the chamberlains who were standing there quickly took the covering cloth and examined it with keen vision.
In the meantime, that bug, out of restlessness, crawled to the edge of the bed; she, though moving slowly, was seen by them as she entered between the seams of the garment and was killed.
Therefore I say: "Indeed, one should not trust the character of an unknown person.
Having understood this, you deserve to be put to death.
"Otherwise, he will cause you to perish. And it has been said:
"He by whom his own people have been abandoned and outsiders have been made his own, he alone meets with death, just like King Kakudruma. (Pañca 1.282)
Piṅgalaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 10.
The Story of the Jackal Named Caṇḍarava:
In a certain region of the forest there lived a jackal named Caṇḍarava.
Once, overcome by hunger and driven by the greed of his tongue, he entered the middle of a city.
Then the dogs living in that city, seeing him, began barking from all sides and running around, and with the tips of their sharp fangs, they began to devour him.
While being devoured by them, out of fear for his life, he entered the nearby house of a washerman.
There, a large vessel filled with indigo dye had been prepared.
There, attacked by dogs, he fell into the midst of some goods;
then, as soon as he emerged, he turned the color of indigo.
Thereupon, the other dogs, not recognizing him as a jackal, went off in whatever direction they pleased.
Caṇḍarava also, having reached a much more distant region, set out toward the forest;
for the blue color never abandons its own hue. And it is said:
"The diamond-stain, the fool, women, and the crab—[these do not change their nature]."
But for fish, there is only one perception, just as there is for those intoxicated by indigo dye or liquor.

Then, beholding that unprecedented being whose luster was like the tamāla tree of the poison in Śiva’s throat, all the forest-dwellers—lions, tigers, leopards, wolves, and the rest—their minds agitated by fear, fled in every direction.
And they said: "It is not known what kind of behavior or prowess this one possesses."
Therefore, let us go even further away. And it is said:
"A wise person who desires his own prosperity should not place trust in one whose conduct, lineage, or prowess he does not know. (Pañcatantra 1.284)
Caṇḍarava, perceiving that they were agitated by fear, said this: "O beasts of prey! Why do you flee in terror upon merely seeing me?
You need not be afraid."
"Today, having created me myself, Brahmā commanded me: 'Since there is no king over the beasts of prey, you shall today be consecrated by me as their sovereign, named Kakudruma;
go then to the surface of the earth and protect them all.'"
Therefore, I have come here.
All wild beasts must dwell within the shade of my umbrella;
for I am the king named Kakuddruma, born even throughout the three worlds.
Having heard that, the beasts of prey, led by the lion and the tiger, surrounded him, saying, "O Master, O Lord, give us your command!
Then he granted the position of minister to the lion and the office of bed-guardian to the tiger.
The leopard holds the office of betel-bearer;
the wolf serves as doorkeeper;
and he does not even engage in mere conversation with his own jackals.
All the jackals were expelled after being given the "unrighteous moon.
Thus, while he was engaged in the administration of the kingdom, those lions and others would kill deer and cast them before him;
he too, according to the duty of a lord, would divide them all and distribute them.
As time passed in this manner, once while he was traveling through a distant region, he heard the clamor of a pack of jackals howling.
Upon hearing that sound, his body bristling with joy and his eyes filled with tears of bliss, he rose up and began to cry out in a piercing voice.
Then those lions and others, hearing that piercing cry and thinking, "This is a jackal," stood for a moment with their heads cast down in shame and said: "O sir!"
"We have been driven away by this wretched jackal;
therefore, let him be killed!
Having heard this, he too, wishing to flee, was torn to pieces and killed right where he stood by the lion and the others.
Therefore I say: "By whom even his own kin have been abandoned.
Upon hearing this, Piṅgalaka said: "O Damanaka, what proof is there in this matter that he harbors evil intent toward me?"
He said, "That which he resolved before me today— that he would slay Piṅgalaka at dawn—
is the proof right here.

At dawn, at the hour of opportunity, with his face and eyes blood-red, his lower lip quivering, and looking toward the quarters while seated in an improper place, he will gaze upon you with a cruel look."
"Having understood this, one should do what is appropriate.
Having said this, he went into the presence of Sañjīvaka, bowed to him, and sat down.
Sañjīvaka, seeing him approaching with a look of agitation and moving slowly, spoke to him with even greater respect: "O friend!"
Welcome! It has been a long time since we last saw you. Is all well with you?
Therefore, tell me what it is that I may give to you, even if it is not rightfully yours, since you have come to my home. And it is said:
“Blessed are they, wise in discernment, and truly civilized on this earth, in whose homes friends come for the sake of their business. (Pañcatantra 1.285)
Damanaka said:
"O sir, how can there be well-being for a servant?
Prosperities are always dependent on others, and the mind is never at peace."
Those who serve the king have no confidence even in their own lives.
And so it is said:
Behold what has been done by those foolish servants who, desiring wealth through service, have lost even that independence which belongs to their own bodies. (Pañcatantra 1.287)
First there is birth, which leads to extreme suffering, and from that, constant wretchedness;
even there, one's livelihood depends on service—alas, what a succession of miseries! (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.288)
It is said that even while living, five types of people are as good as dead in Bhārata:
the poor, the diseased, the ignorant, the exile, and the perpetual servant.
He does not eat out of pure eagerness, he does not wake up sleepless, and he does not speak words without hesitation; even as a servant, he lives here [in this state]. (Panc 1.290)
Those who have declared that service is the livelihood of a dog have spoken falsely;
for here, the master acts according to his own will, while the servant acts under the command of another. (Pañcāstikāya 1.291)
Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, emaciation, and eating light food—
these are like the specific characteristics of a servant or an ascetic, born of sinful tendencies.
The hardships such as cold and heat that a servant endures for the sake of wealth are minor, provided he does not abandon his virtue.
Of what use is that sweetmeat, however soft, well-rounded, perfectly smooth, and attractive, if its consumption results in no digestion? (Panc 1.294)
Sañjīvaka said, "Then what is it that you intend to say? He replied, "Friend, it is not proper to disclose the counsel of ministers. And it has been said:"
He who, having been appointed to the office of minister, should betray his master’s counsel, destroys the king’s business and shall himself go to hell. (Pañcatantra 1.295)
"Nārada said: 'Whosoever has caused a rift between a king and his minister, by him has the king been slain without the use of weapons.'"
Nevertheless, bound by the fetters of affection for you, I have betrayed the secret counsel;
for at my word, you entered this royal palace with full confidence. And it is said:
"When someone meets death through the confidence placed in another..."
The sin arising from that [killing] was described by Manu as follows: "The killing of that [person]... (Pañca 1.297).

Therefore, this wicked-minded Piṅgalaka is plotting against you; today he spoke before me in private, saying that at dawn he would kill Sañjīvaka and, with his entire retinue of deer, finally bring himself satisfaction.
Then I said to him: "My Lord!"
It is not right that one should live by betraying a friend. And it has been said:

"Even after committing the murder of a Brahmin, one is purified through penance; but for one who betrays a friend, there is no purification whatsoever, even by performing such [penances]. (Pañcatantra 1.298)
Then, filled with indignation, he said to me: "O evil-minded one, Sañjīvaka is a consumer of grass,
whereas we are eaters of flesh."
Since this is our natural enmity, how can an enemy be ignored?
Therefore, he must be destroyed by means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest.
And there would be no fault in his being slain. As it has been said:
Even after giving away his daughter, a wise man must destroy an enemy who cannot be overcome by other means; no fault is found in killing such a person.
A Kṣatriya engaged in battle should not consider what ought or ought not to be done;
formerly, Dhṛṣṭadyumna was slain while asleep by the son of Droṇa.
Having understood his resolve, I have come here to your presence;
now I am free from the fault of betraying confidence.
I have disclosed to you the well-guarded mantra.
"Now, do whatever seems best to you.
Then Sañjīvaka, having heard those words of his which were as harsh as the falling of a thunderbolt, fell into a state of stupor.
Having then regained consciousness, he spoke this with a sense of detachment: "O, it is well said:"
Women are generally accessible to the wicked; a king is usually devoid of affection; wealth follows the miserly; and a cloud rains upon mountain fastnesses. (Pancatantra 1.301)
For he who, being esteemed by the king, thinks in such a way,
should be known as a foolish ox devoid of horns.
Better is the forest, better is alms, better is living by begging,
and better for men even disease than prosperity attained through authority.

Therefore, what I have done is appropriate; I have established friendship with him. And it is said: "Only between those whose wealth is equal and whose lineage is equal should there be friendship and marriage, not between the prosperous and the destitute. (Pañca 1.304)
And so it is said:
Deer follow their association with deer;
cows with cows; and horses with horses.
Fools form friendships with fools, and the wise with the wise, through a commonality of character and inclination.
Therefore, even if I go and try to appease him, he will still not be appeased. And it has been said:
"For he who becomes angry for a specific reason..."
Surely he becomes pacified upon their departure;
for how can a man satisfy one who is intent on causeless hatred? (Pañcaviṃśatikā 1.306)
Ah, well said is this:
"Even for those who are devoted, who have rendered assistance, whose souls are intent on the welfare of others, who know the true nature of service and social conduct, and who are free from malice."
Failure is certain amidst one's lapses, while success may or may not occur;
therefore, service to a lord of the earth is always fraught with apprehension, like that of the lord of the waters.
And so it is said:
In this world, even a benefit rendered by those who are naturally affectionate leads to aversion, whereas even a direct injury inflicted by others results in affection.
Because the minds of kings, which rely on many shifting dispositions, are difficult to grasp, the duty of service is extremely profound and inaccessible even to yogins. (Panc 1.308)
"That was understood by me; however, his attendants, unable to endure my favor, incited this Piṅgalaka.
Therefore, he speaks thus to me even though I am innocent. And it is said:
'In this world, servants cannot endure the favor shown by their master to another.'"
Like rival co-wives enraged even by the good deeds of their rivals.
And it is thus: when those possessed of virtues are present nearby, those devoid of virtue do not find favor. As it has been said:
"The virtues of the virtuous are eclipsed by one who is even more virtuous;
the brilliance of a lamp’s flame at night does not shine when the sun has risen. (Pañca 1.310)
Damanaka said: "O friend, if it is so, then you have no cause for fear;
even if he has been provoked by wicked men, he will become gracious through the artful composition of your words."
He said: "O sir, what you have said is not right.
It is impossible to dwell even among small wicked people;
having employed some other means, they will surely kill one. And it is said:"
Many petty scholars, all of whom subsist on illusion,
might perform what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, just as crows and other birds do upon a camel.
Damaka asked: "How was that?
He replied:
Story 11.
The Story of the Lion Madotkaṭa:
In a certain region of the forest there lived a lion named Madotkaṭa.
He had other followers: a leopard, a crow, and a jackal.
Then, on one occasion, while they were wandering here and there, they saw a camel named Krathanaka who had strayed from his caravan.
Thereupon the lion said, "Aha! This is an extraordinary creature.
Let it be determined whether it is a wild animal or a domestic one."
Having heard that, the crow said:
"O Master, this creature named a camel is a common beast and your food;
therefore, let him be slain."
The lion said, "I do not kill one who has come to my home. And it is said:
'If one should kill even an enemy who has reached his home, trusting and free from fear, that person's sin shall be equal to the slaughter of a hundred Brahmins. (Pañca 1.312)
"Having granted him that gift of safety, let him be brought into my presence so that I may ask the reason for his arrival.
Then, having been inspired with confidence by everyone, he was granted the gift of safety and brought into the presence of Madotkaṭa; he bowed and sat down.
Thereupon, when questioned by him, he related his own story, beginning with the loss of his caravan.
Then the lion said: "O Krathanaka!
Do not go back to the village and again become a partaker of the hardship of carrying burdens.
Therefore, stay here in this very forest with me at all times, eating the tips of the young grass that resemble emeralds, free from fear."
He too, having said "So be it," wandered among them and lived happily, free from fear of anything whatsoever.
Then one day, a battle took place between him and a great forest-dwelling elephant, fierce with rut;
consequently, he was afflicted by the blows of the elephant's pestle-like tusks.
Distressed, he somehow did not lose his life;
yet, due to the incapacity of his body, he was unable to move even a single step anywhere.
All those crows and others as well, being powerless and overcome by hunger, experienced supreme suffering.
Then the lion said to them, "Sirs! Search somewhere for some creature; having killed it, I shall provide food for you, even though I myself have reached this state.
Thereupon, all four began to wander about, and while they saw no creature whatsoever, the crow and the jackal consulted with one another.
The jackal said: "O crow, what is the use of wandering about so much?
Here is our master Krathanaka, sitting in full confidence."
"Therefore, let us kill him and sustain ourselves.
The crow said, "What you have said is reasonable; however, my master has granted him a promise of safety, saying, 'He is not to be killed.'"
The jackal said: "O crow, I shall inform my master and act in such a way that the master will carry out the execution.
Therefore, may you all remain right here."
"I shall go home, receive my master's command, and return.
Having spoken thus, he set out quickly toward the lion. Then, having reached the lion, he said: "Master!"
Having wandered through the entire forest, we have returned; not a single living being has been found. So, what shall we do?

At present, we are so overcome by hunger that we cannot move even a single step. Your Majesty also observes a dietary regimen; therefore, if it be your command, let the prescribed diet be prepared today with the flesh of Krathanaka.
Then the lion, having heard those harsh words of his, spoke this with indignation: "Fie upon you, lowest of sinners!
If you speak thus again, I shall kill you at that very moment."
Therefore, I have granted him safety;
how then could I kill him? And it has been said:
"Neither the gift of cows nor the gift of land [is as great as the gift of fearlessness]."
Indeed, the gift of food is not as preeminent as the wise here proclaim the gift of fearlessness to be the foremost among all gifts. (Pañca 1.313)
Having heard that, the jackal said: "Master, if a killing is carried out after granting a promise of safety, then that is a fault.
However, if he offers his own life out of devotion to your Majesty’s feet, then there is no fault.

Therefore, if he himself appoints himself for execution, then he is to be killed; otherwise, one of us must be killed. For your Majesty, being a consumer of wholesome food, [will suffer] from the suppression of hunger..."
"They will reach their final stage [of death].
Therefore, what is the use of these lives of ours if they do not go for the sake of our master?
Furthermore, even later on, we must enter the fire if anything unfortunate should happen to our lord’s feet. And it is said:
In whatever family a man is the principal one,
he must be protected with every effort;
when he is destroyed, one's own family is destroyed.
For indeed, when the hub is broken, the spokes do not remain in place.
Hearing that, Madotkaṭa said, "If it is so, then do whatever pleases you.
Having heard this, he went quickly and said to them, "Sirs! My master is in a very critical condition."
"What is the use of wandering about?

Without him, who here will protect us? Therefore, let us go and offer our own bodies to him as he departs for the next world due to a disease of hunger, so that we may become free from our debt to our master's favor. And it is said:"
If a master should fall into calamity while his servant looks on, and that servant does not intervene while his own life still remains, that servant shall go to hell. (Pañcatantra 1.315)
Immediately thereafter, they all sat down after bowing to Madotkaṭa with eyes filled with tears.
Seeing them, Madotkaṭa said:
"O friends, have you encountered or seen any creature?"
Then, from among them, a crow said: "Master, we have indeed wandered everywhere, yet we have neither found nor seen any living creature.
Therefore, let the Master sustain his life today by eating me."
"By this, there shall be consolation for Your Majesty, and for me, moreover, the attainment of heaven. And it is said:
"The servant who, endowed with devotion, would sacrifice his life for the sake of his master, attains the supreme state, free from old age and death. (Pañca 1.316)
Having heard that, the jackal said: "Sir, you are small of body;
from eating you, your master will not even have enough for his sustenance."
Furthermore, another fault arises; and it has been said:
"Even the flesh of a crow is thus left over, meager, and even that is of poor quality. What is the use of eating that by which no satisfaction is produced? (Pañca 1.317)
Thus you have demonstrated devotion to your master, discharged your debt to the food provided by your lord, and attained the praise of the virtuous in both worlds.
Therefore, move aside;
I shall inform the master.
When this had been done, the jackal bowed respectfully and sat down, saying: "Master! By devouring me today, provide for my sustenance and ensure my attainment of both worlds. For it is said:
'The lives of servants, acquired through their earnings, always depend upon their master.'"
Therefore, there is no fault in the possibility of their being apprehended.

Then, having heard that, the leopard said: "O sir, you have spoken well; however, you too are small-bodied and of your own kind, and because you have claws as weapons, you are simply not to be eaten. And it is said:

'A wise man should not eat what is forbidden to eat, even if his life-breaths have reached his throat; especially so that which is both small in quantity and destructive to both worlds. (Pañcatantra 1.319)
Thus you have demonstrated your own noble lineage;
or rather, it is well said:
"It is for this purpose that kings gather together those of noble birth."
In the beginning, middle, and end, they do not undergo any transformation.
"Therefore, move aside from my front so that I may inform my master.
When this was done, the leopard bowed and said to Madotkaṭa, "Master!"
Let my sustenance of life be maintained today by means of my own life-breaths; let an imperishable dwelling be granted to me in heaven;
and let abundant fame be spread for me upon the surface of the earth.
Therefore, one should not feel astonishment in this regard; and it has been said:
"For servants who follow their master in his service even unto death, there shall be an imperishable residence in heaven and fame upon the surface of the earth. (Pañca 1.321)
Having heard that, Krathanaka reflected: "All of these have indeed spoken flattering words, yet not even one of them has been destroyed by the master.
Therefore, I too shall say what is appropriate for the occasion, so that these three may corroborate my speech.
Having thus resolved, he said: "Sirs, what you have said is true; however, you too are armed with claws."
How then can my master devour you? And it is said:
"Whoever contemplates harm even in his mind toward those of his own kind, for him those very things come to pass in this world and in the next. (Pañca 1.322)
"Therefore, move aside from my front so that I may inform my master.
When this was done, Krathanaka stood before him, bowed, and said, "Master!"
"These are not to be eaten by you; therefore, let my life-sustenance be provided by means of my own life, so that I may attain both worlds. And it is said:
"Neither those who perform sacrifices nor even yogis go to that destination which the best of servants reach when they have surrendered their lives for the sake of their master. (Pañcatantra 1.323)
When this had been said, Krathanaka, his flanks torn open by the jackal and the leopard, gave up his life-breaths;
thereupon, he was devoured by all those petty "wise" ones.
Therefore I say: "Many are the petty wise men."
Therefore, my good man, I have correctly perceived that this king of yours has a base retinue and is unfit to be served by the virtuous. And it is said:
"When a king is of impure nature, the people do not feel affection for him."
Just as a swan might behave when in close proximity to vultures.
And so it is said:
"Even one who has the appearance of a vulture should be served by courtiers who have the appearance of swans;
yet even one who has the appearance of a swan must be abandoned by those courtiers who have the appearance of vultures. (Pancatantaka 1.325)
Surely this has been incited against me by some wicked person, and for that reason he speaks thus;
or rather, it may be so. And it has been said:
Even the plateaus of mountains do not yield when being excavated by soft water,
nor do they succumb to the whispered incitements of those skilled in sowing discord.
How much more so, then, the tender hearts of human beings?
Bereft of sense by the poison of flattery, what will a foolish person not do?
He even assumes the guise of a mendicant and drinks liquor from the cup of hell. (Pañcāstikāya 1.327)
Or rather, it is well said:
even if struck by a foot or even struck by a firm staff, the serpent kills indeed that which it touches with its fangs.
This very same nature of a malicious and cruel man touches another only by the ear, yet destroys that other person along with their very roots.
And so it is said:
"Alas! How perverse is the method of slaying employed by this serpent-like rogue:
the arrow strikes one ear, yet another is deprived of life. (Pañca 1.329)
"Since things have come to this pass, I ask you out of friendship: what should be done?
Damanaka replied, "In such a case, it is proper to go to another country; one should not continue to serve such a wicked master. And it is said:"
Even a guru, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what should and should not be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, is ordained to be abandoned.

Sañjīvaka said: "When our master is angry with us, it is impossible to go away; nor does peace come even to those who have gone elsewhere. And it has been said: 'One who has offended the great should not feel secure, thinking, "I am far away. "
The arms of the wise man are long; with them, he strikes back at the assailant.
"Other than that battle, nothing else has appeared to me as more conducive to my welfare. And it is said:
"Those worlds sought by those desiring heaven cannot be attained through sacred fords, nor through austerity, nor through hundreds of gifts, nor through virtuous conduct."
For those wise ones of excellent conduct who, in battles, abandon their very lives in an instant—
By the dead, heaven is attained; by the living, supreme fame.
Thus, both of these virtues belong to the brave, and they are very difficult to obtain.
If blood flowing from the forehead of a hero should enter his mouth,
that shall be equal to the drinking of the Soma juice.
It was duly ordained for the sacrifice of battle.
And so it is said:

"That fruit which is attained through sacrifices properly performed with oblations, according to the rules of ritual offering, and through the worship of assemblies of virtuous brahmins accompanied by abundant and well-bestowed sacrificial fees;"

The fruit that men obtain through dwelling at sacred fords and hermitages, performing fire-sacrifices and observances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, is attained instantly when those same acts are dedicated in battle.
Having heard that, Damanaka reflected: "This wicked soul appears determined for battle.
Therefore, if he should ever strike our master with those two sharp-witted jackals, a great calamity will ensue.
Thus, I shall once again awaken him through my own wit and act accordingly."
Just as he travels to another country,
he said: "O friend,
you have spoken correctly."
But what kind of conflict can there be between a master and a servant? And it has been said:
"Upon seeing a powerful enemy, one should indeed protect oneself;
yet even against those who are powerful, one should maintain a radiance like that of the autumn moon. (Pañcatantra 1.336)
Furthermore:
He who initiates enmity without knowing the prowess of his enemy meets with defeat, just as the ocean did because of the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. (Pancatantra 1.337)
Sañjīvaka said: "How was that?
He replied:
Story 12.
The Story of the Couple of *ṭiṭṭibha* Birds:
In a certain part of the ocean lived a couple of *ṭiṭṭibha* birds. As time passed, when the proper season arrived, the female *ṭiṭṭibha* conceived a young.
Being near her time to give birth, she said to the *ṭiṭṭibha*: "O beloved, my time for delivery has arrived;
therefore, consider some place free from danger where I may lay my eggs."
The *ṭiṭṭibha* said, "My dear, this region of the ocean is delightful;
therefore, you should lay your eggs right here.
She replied, "On the day of the full moon, the tide of the ocean comes in here."
"She can even drag away intoxicated lordly elephants;
therefore, let some other place far away be sought.
Hearing this, the ṭiṭṭibha laughed and said, "My dear, what you have said is not proper."
What portion of the ocean could possibly defile my offspring?
Have you not heard how it constantly fills the path of the sky-faring gods, free from smoke, yet always inspiring great fear?
What man of dull intellect would enter the fire of his own free will?
Who indeed would wake a sleeping lion— who has exerted himself in splitting the temples of rutting elephants and resembles Death itself— merely out of a desire to see the realm of Yama?
Who, having gone to the abode of Yama, commands Death himself without fear:
"Take my life from me, if you have any power at all"? (Pañca 1.340)
When the morning breeze blows, chilled and mixed with particles of frost, what man who discerns virtues and faults can dispel that cold with water? (Pañca 1.341)
Therefore, release your fetus right here with confidence. And it is said:
"If a man who is terrified of defeat abandons his own place, and yet he has a mother who possesses a son, by whom can she be called barren? (Pañcatantra 1.342)
Having heard that, the ocean reflected: "Oh, what arrogance this insect-bird possesses!
Or rather, it is well said:
'The *ṭiṭṭibha* bird stands with its feet lifted up out of fear of falling from the sky.'"
Whose pride, imagined by one's own mind, does not exist even here?
"Therefore, I must see for myself its size, even out of curiosity;
what can he possibly do to me now that I have carried off his egg?
Having thought this, he remained there.
Then, shortly after the laying of eggs, while the female *ṭiṭṭibha* had gone out for the sake of her livelihood, the ocean carried off her eggs under the pretext of its tide.
Upon returning, the *ṭiṭṭibhī*, seeing the place of laying empty, spoke to the *ṭiṭṭibha* while lamenting: "O fool!
I told you that there would be destruction of the eggs by the ocean's tide; therefore, let us go to a much more distant place. But out of folly, relying on your own pride, you did not heed my words."
Or rather, it is well said:
"He who does not follow the advice here of friends who desire his welfare, that fool, like the tortoise, perishes after falling from the wood. (Pañcatantra 1.344)
The *ṭiṭṭibha* asked, "How was that?
She replied:
Story 13.
The Story of the Tortoise Named Kambu-grīva:
In a certain body of water there was a tortoise named Kambu-grīva.
He had two friends of the swan species, named Saṅkaṭa and Vikaṭa, upon whom he relied with the utmost affection at all times.
Having thus reached the shore of the lake, they engaged in conversation with many celestial and great seers, and at the time of sunset,
they both took refuge in their own nests.
Then, as time passed, due to a lack of rain, the lake gradually began to dry up.
Then, pained by that sorrow, the two of them said: "O friend!
This lake has become nothing but mud. Therefore, how will you fare? Such anxiety dwells within our hearts."
Having heard that, Kambugrīva said: "Sirs, at present we have no means of survival due to the lack of water; nevertheless, let some remedy be devised. And it is said:
One must not abandon fortitude even in times of adversity;
through fortitude, one may sometimes find a way out,
just as when a ship is wrecked even upon the ocean.
The merchant seafarer desires only to cross over.
Furthermore:
"A wise person always exerts effort for the sake of friends and kinsmen; when calamities have arisen, Manu spoke these words with diligence: [Pañcatantra 1.346].
Therefore, let some strong rope or a light piece of wood be brought;
and let a lake abounding in water be sought out,
so that when I have seized it by the middle with my tusks, you two may grasp that wood along with me at its two ends and carry it to that lake.
The two of them said, "O friend,
we shall do so;
however, you must remain under a vow of silence."
"If not, you will fall from the wood.
When he had acted accordingly, Kambugrīva, as he was going along, saw a certain city situated below him.
Seeing him being carried away in that manner, the citizens there spoke with wonder: "Aha! Some kind of wheel-shaped object is being carried by two birds!"
"Look, look!
Now, having heard their clamor, Kambugrīva said:
'O sirs, what is this clamor?'"
Intending to speak thus, he fell while his words were half-uttered and was cut into pieces by the citizens.
Therefore I say: "Of friends who desire one's welfare... And likewise: "One who provides for the future, as well as one with presence of mind,"
These two prosper in happiness: he who is destined for the future and he whose destruction has occurred.
The *ṭiṭṭibha* asked, "How was that?
She replied:
Story 14.
The Story of the Three Fish: Anāgatavidhātṛ, Pratyutpannamati, and Yadbhaviṣya.
In a certain body of water there lived three fish: Anāgatavidhātṛ, Pratyutpannamati, and Yadbhaviṣya.
Once, some fishermen passing by saw that pond and said, "Oh, this lake contains many fish!"
We have never sought him at any time;
today, however, the need for food has arisen and the hour of twilight has arrived.

"Therefore, it is decided that you must come here at dawn. Having heard those words of theirs, which were like the falling of a thunderbolt, the fish who had not foreseen the future summoned all the fish and said this: "O, have you heard what has been said by the fishermen?"
Therefore, even at night, you should go to some nearby lake. And it is said:
"Those who are powerless against a strong enemy should either flee or take refuge in a fortress; there can be no other recourse for them. (Pañcatantra 1.348)
Therefore, it is certain that at the time of dawn, the fishermen will gather here and cause the destruction of the fish;
this is what dwells in my mind. Thus, it is not proper to remain here even for a moment. And it has been said:
Those wise ones for whom there exists a path that brings happiness even elsewhere do not perceive the destruction of the body or the ruin of their lineage.
Having heard that, Pratyutpannamati said: "Aho! What you have said is true;
this is also my own desire.
Therefore, let us go elsewhere. And it is said:
Fearing the dangers of foreign lands, full of deceit and impotent, crows, base men, and deer meet their end in their own country. (Pancatantra 1.350)
Why should he who has access everywhere come to ruin through attachment to his own country,
saying, "This is my father’s well"?
Base men drink alkaline water.
Then, having heard that, Yad-bhaviṣya laughed loudly and said: "Aha!
What you two have counseled is not correct;
for how could it even be proper for them to abandon this lake, inherited from their fathers and grandfathers, by mere words?"
If there is an exhaustion of the life-span, then death will certainly occur even for those who have gone elsewhere. And it has been said:
"That which is unprotected remains protected by fate;
that which is well-protected perishes when struck down by fate."
Even one who is abandoned in the forest lives on as a protectorless person,
whereas one who exerts effort at home does not live.
"Therefore, I will not go; you two must do whatever seems best to you.
Then, having understood his resolve, Anāgata-vidhātā and Pratyutpanna-mati departed together with their followers.
Then at dawn, those fishermen, having stirred up that body of water with their nets, deprived that lake of its fish along with Yad-bhaviṣya.
Therefore I say: "One who provides for the future.
Having heard that, the *ṭiṭṭibha* said: "My dear, why do you regard me as being like a fatalist (*yadbhaviṣya*)?"
"Therefore, behold the power of my intellect, by which I shall dry up this wicked ocean with my own beak!
The female *ṭiṭṭibha* said: "Aho! What conflict do you have with the ocean?
It is not proper to direct anger toward it. And it is said:"
The anger of men who lack self-control leads to their own ruin;
a cauldron that burns excessively blazes most fiercely against its own sides.
And so it is said:
"One who, not knowing his own strength and that of his enemy, rushes headlong toward fire out of eagerness, meets his destruction like a moth. (Pañcatantra 1.354)
The *ṭiṭṭibha* said: "My dear, do not speak thus!
Even those who possess the power of resolve overcome their superiors, however slight they may be. And it is said:"
Out of particular resentment, an intolerant enemy advances against one who is fully perfected,
just as even today the Rāhu-demon advances toward the moon.
And so it is said:
Even though he is superior in size, the lion places his paw upon the head of a rutting elephant that has shed ichor from its temples. (Pañca 1.356)
And so it is said:
"Even the rays of the young sun fall upon the mountains;
for those born with innate brilliance, what use is age? (Pañca 1.357)
The two hands are very large, yet they are under the control of the goad; is the goad merely the size of a hand?
When a lamp is lit, does darkness perish; is the darkness merely the size of the lamp? Even mountains struck by a thunderbolt fall; is the mountain merely the size of the thunderbolt?
He whose splendor shines forth is powerful; what proof is there for [the existence of] gross things?
"Therefore, with this beak of mine, I shall lead all its water to dry land.
The female ṭiṭṭibha said: "O beloved, where the Ganges itself constantly enters, carrying hundreds of new rivers?"
Likewise with the Indus.
How then will you dry up that [ocean], which is being filled by eighteen hundred rivers, with a beak that carries but a single drop? Why do you speak what you yourself do not believe?
The *ṭiṭṭibha* said: "O beloved, perseverance is the root of prosperity; my beak is like iron;
days and nights are long; why then does the ocean not dry up? (Pañca 1.359)
The supreme state is difficult to attain as long as a person has not exerted human effort;
even the radiant sun triumphs over the masses of clouds once it has ascended its zenith.
The *ṭiṭṭibha* said: "If you must indeed carry out hostilities with the ocean, then summon other birds as well and act thus together with your circle of friends. For it is said:
'A coalition, even of many who are individually weak, is indeed difficult to conquer.'"
Just as a rope is wound from blades of grass, so too is even a great elephant bound.
And so it is said:
"By means of a sparrow, a wooden trap, and a wasp, as well as by means of frogs and public opposition, the elephant met his destruction. (Pañcatantra 1.362)
The *ṭiṭṭibha* asked, "How was that?
She replied—
Story 15.
The Story of the Elephant and the Sparrow Couple.
In a certain region of the forest, a sparrow couple lived in a nest they had built in a *tamāla* tree.
Then, as time passed, offspring were born to them.
On another day, a certain wild elephant, intoxicated and distressed by the heat, sought out that very *tāla* tree for shade and took refuge beneath it.
Then, out of excessive rut, he pulled at the branch where the sparrows were perched with the tip of his trunk and broke it;
by its breaking, all the sparrow's eggs were shattered.
Because their life-span was not yet exhausted, the two sparrows somehow did not part with their lives;
however, that female sparrow, overcome by the breaking of her egg, found no happiness as she uttered lamentations.
In the meantime, having heard those lamentations of hers, a bird named Kāṣṭhakūṭa, her dearest friend, approached—distressed by her sorrow—and said to her: "O Blessed One!"
What is the use of idle lamentation? For it has been said:
"The wise do not grieve for what is lost, dead, or past;
for this is remembered as the distinction between the wise and the foolish. (Pañca 1.363)
And so it is said:
"The fool who grieves for beings here who are not to be grieved for, obtains further suffering from that sorrow; he thus pursues two misfortunes. (Pañca 1.364)
Furthermore:

Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should certainly not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability. (Pancatanttra 1.365)
The sparrow said: "Let this be so;
however, by that wicked elephant, through his rutting, my lineage has been destroyed.
Therefore, if you are a true friend to me, devise some means for the slaughter of this wretched elephant."
By the performance of which my suffering from the destruction of my lineage shall depart. And it is said:
"I consider that man to be born all over again who, having been helped by one in times of distress and laughed at by another in adverse circumstances, returns the favor to both of them. (Pañca 1.366)
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said: "O Blessed One, what you have said is true; and it has been said:
'He who stands by one in the time of misfortune is a friend, even if he is born of another caste.'"
In times of prosperity, everyone becomes a friend to all embodied beings.
He is a friend who stands by you in times of misfortune; he is a son who is devoted;
he is a servant who knows how to obey; she is a wife in whom there is true happiness.
Behold the power of my intellect!
I have a fly named Vīṇāravā who is even a friend to me;
therefore, I shall summon her and return.
By means of which that wicked-natured, evil elephant is bound.
Then, having encountered a fly together with the sparrow, he said: "My dear lady, this sparrow of mine has been tormented by a certain wicked elephant through the crushing of her eggs."
"Therefore, you ought to assist me as I carry out the means for his destruction.
The fly replied, "My good friend, what more need be said in this matter? And it is said:"
Furthermore, a favor is done for friends in order to repay them;
but as for the service that should be done for a friend's friend, has it not already been performed by those friends? (Pancatantaka 1.369)
This is true;
however, I too have a friend named Meghanāda the frog who stays nearby.
Let us summon him as well and do what is appropriate. And it is said:
The principles reflected upon by wise men— who are beneficial, of virtuous conduct, learned in the scriptures, and possessed of keen intelligence— are not subject to doubt in any way.
Then those three also went and, having reported the entire account in the presence of Meghanāda, stood there.
He then said: "How insignificant is that wretched elephant before an enraged multitude!
Therefore, my counsel must be followed."
"O fly, go at the time of midday and make a sound like the resonance of a lute in the ear of that elephant intoxicated with pride, so that,
longing for the pleasure of hearing it, he closes his eyes.

Then, when his eyes are burst open by the beak of Kāṣṭhakūṭa and he has become blind, tormented by thirst, and having heard the sound of me and my attendants situated on the bank of the pit, he will approach, thinking it to be a body of water."
"Then, having reached the pit, he will fall and meet his death.
Thus a conspiracy should be formed so that it results in the execution of the enmity.
Then, when it was carried out accordingly, that intoxicated elephant—his eyes closed in the pleasure of the songs sung by the flies, his vision stolen by the heap of wood—[fell].
"Wandering at midday and following the sound of frogs, he went along and, having reached a large pit, fell into it and died.
Therefore I say: 'The sparrow by the wooden trap.
The ṭiṭṭibha said, "My dear,"
"So be it;
together with the assembly of my circle of friends, I shall dry up the ocean.
Having thus resolved, he summoned the cranes, saras-cranes, peacocks, and others, and said: "O friends, I have been defeated by the ocean, which has stolen my eggs."
"Therefore, let a means for its drying up be devised.
Having consulted together, they said, "We are powerless to dry up the ocean;
so what is the use of this futile exertion? And it is said:
The weak man who, deluded by pride, goes forth against a powerful enemy for the sake of battle, will turn back like an elephant with broken tusks. (Pancatantra 1.371)
Therefore, let our master Vainateya be informed of all this cause for humiliation,
so that, incensed by the insult to his own kind, he may discharge his debt of enmity.
Or even if he should act with arrogance here, there will still be no suffering for you. And it has been said:
"When one's suffering is reported to a friend who is ever-present, to a virtuous servant who is obedient, and to a master who is endowed with power, one becomes happy. (Pañcatantra 1.372)
"Therefore, let us go to the presence of Vainateya, for he is our master.
When they had done so, all those birds, with dejected faces and eyes filled with tears, approached Vainateya and began to wail in a piteous voice: "Alas!
An outrage! An outrage!"
Now that the ocean, the lord of the well-behaved *ṭiṭṭibha*, has seized his eggs, that bird family is now perished;
others too shall be destroyed by the ocean according to its own will. And it is said:
"Having observed whose action is it that another person performs even a censurable deed?"
The world follows what has come before; it is not the ultimate reality.
The subjects must be protected from those who use flattery, thieves, the wicked, as well as those who act with recklessness, and from those who employ harshness, deceit, and the like.
A sixth part of the merit of the subjects accrues to the king who protects them;
likewise, a sixth part of their demerit arises from the failure of one who does not protect them. (Pancaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 1.375)
The fire born from the suffering and oppression of the subjects does not turn back until it has consumed the king’s fortune, his lineage, and his very life.
The king is the kinsman of those who have no kin; the king is the eye of the sightless;
the king is both father and mother to all who walk the path of justice.
A king seeking the fruits [of his rule] should protect the worlds with diligent effort, like a gardener nourishing sprouts with water consisting of gifts, honors, and the like. (Panc_1.378)
Just as a subtle sprout from a seed, when protected with care over time,
will yield fruit in its due season, so too does the world, when well-protected.
Gold, grain, jewels, various vehicles, and whatever else belongs to the subjects—that all belongs to the king. (5.380)
Then, having heard this, Garuḍa, pained by their sorrow and overcome with anger, reflected: "Aha!
What these birds have said is true.
Therefore, let us go today and dry up that ocean."
As he was thinking thus, a messenger of Viṣṇu approached and said: "O Garuḍa!
I have been sent to your side by the Blessed Nārāyaṇa;
the Blessed One will go to Amarāvatī for the sake of the gods' business."
"Therefore, come quickly.
Having heard that, Garuḍa spoke with pride: "O messenger!
What will the Blessed One do with me, his unworthy servant?"
Therefore, go and say to him: "Let another servant be appointed to the position of driver;
let my salutations be conveyed to the Blessed One. And it has been said:
"A wise man should not serve one who does not recognize his virtues."
For from that [mind], no fruit whatsoever arises, just as from a well-tilled saline wasteland.
The messenger said: "O Vainateya, never before has such a thing been spoken by you regarding the Blessed One. Therefore, tell me."
"What offense has been committed by you against the Blessed One?
Garuḍa said, "The ocean, which serves as the Blessed One's abode, has stolen our *ṭiṭṭibha* eggs.
Therefore, if he does not inflict punishment, you must say with certainty: 'I am no longer a servant of the Blessed One.'"
Therefore, you must go very quickly and speak to the Blessed One.
Then, having learned through the mouth of a messenger that Vainateya is offended by my affection, I shall bring him here with due honor. As it is said:
"One should not treat with contempt a servant who is devoted, capable, and of noble birth."
One who desires prosperity for oneself should always cherish [the mind] as one would a son.
Moreover: Even when pleased, a king bestows only material wealth upon his servants;
yet they, being duly honored, serve him even at the cost of their own lives. (Pancatantra 1.383)
Having reflected thus, he went quickly to the presence of Vainateya in Rukmapura.

Vainateya, too, beholding the Blessed One arrived at his home, bowed with his face cast down in shame and said: "O Blessed One, the ocean, intoxicated by its reliance upon you, has seized the eggs of my servant and thereby committed an insult against me."
"But it was only out of shame before the Blessed One that I delayed.
Otherwise, I would have taken him to another place this very day;
for even Śravaṇa does not strike out of fear of his master. And it is said:"
A servant of noble family should not perform any action that might cause even the slightest disrespect or distress in the mind of his master, even at the cost of his own life. (Pancadashi 1.384)
Having heard that, the Blessed One said: "O Vainateya, you have spoken the truth. And it has been said:
'Since the punishment arising from the fault of a servant falls upon the master...'"
Therefore, shame does not arise in him as it does in a servant.
Therefore, come, so that we may take the eggs from the ocean and show our respect to the *ṭiṭṭibha*, and let us go to Amarāvatī.
When this had been carried out, the Blessed One, having rebuked the ocean, aimed the fire-weapon (*āgneya-śara*) at it and said: "O wicked soul!"
"Let the eggs of the *ṭiṭṭibha* birds be given;
otherwise, I shall carry you to dry land.
Thereupon, the ocean, being filled with fear, surrendered those eggs of the *ṭiṭṭibhas*.
The *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, too, entrusted [the eggs] to his wife;
therefore I say: "Without knowing the strength of the enemy... For this reason, a man must not abandon his effort.
Having heard that, Sañjīvaka asked him once more: "O friend, how am I to recognize that he is of evil intent?
Until now, I have been regarded by him with ever-increasing affection and favor."
"Never has any change in him been observed.
Therefore, tell me how I may make an effort to kill him for the sake of my own protection.
Damanaka said, "My good friend,"
What is to be known here?
This is your proof:
if, upon seeing you, he—with bloodshot eyes, wearing a three-pronged frown, and repeatedly licking the corners of his mouth—becomes [agitated], [then know him to be a demon].
Therefore, [one may have] a wicked mind,
or otherwise, a very clear and serene one;
so, command me.
I am going to my own abode.
You must act in such a way that this breach of the secret counsel does not occur.
If you are able to depart upon reaching the onset of night, then you should leave that place; for:
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of one's own self.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.

For one who has been overcome by a powerful foe, the policy is either to go to a foreign land or to enter into his service; otherwise, that country must be abandoned. Alternatively, one's own self must be protected by means such as conciliation (*sāman*). And it has been said:
A wise person should protect their life even at the cost of children or a wife;
for as long as these exist, all things can be obtained again by embodied beings.
And so it is said:
"By whatever means possible, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one should rescue one's own distressed self; once capable, one should practice the Dharma. (Pañca 1.389)
The fool who practices deceit regarding wealth and other things at the cost of his life—his very life-breaths perish;
and with those breaths lost, that [wealth] is truly lost as well. (5.390)
Having spoken thus, Damanaka went into the presence of Karaṭaka.
Seeing him approaching, Karaṭaka said: "My good friend, what has been accomplished by your honor?"
Damanaka said: "I have, for my part, sown the seeds of policy; what follows depends upon the decrees of fate. And it is said:
Even when fate is adverse, a wise man must perform his duty."
For the destruction of one's own faults and for the stabilization of one's own mind.
And so it is said:
Fortune approaches the industrious lion among men; "it is to be given by fate," say the cowards.
Overcoming destiny, perform manly effort through your own power; if success is not achieved despite the exertion, what fault is there in this?
Karaṭaka said, "Tell me then, what kind of seed of policy did you sow?
He replied, "I have created such a rift between them through mutual false accusations that you shall never again see them consulting together while staying in one place.
Karaṭaka said, "Aho!"
What you have done is not right, in that those two, whose hearts were moist with mutual affection and who were the refuge of happiness, have been cast into an ocean of anger. And it is said:
"He who would lead one who is unopposed and established in happiness onto the path of suffering will undoubtedly be a sufferer in birth after birth. (Pañca 1.393)

Furthermore, it is also improper that you rejoice even at a mere division [between us], because people everywhere are capable of causing harm to others, but not of benefiting them. And it has been said: "A base person knows only how to destroy another's work, not how to promote it."
The wind has the power to topple a tree, but not to lift it up.
Damanaka said: "Your Honor is ignorant of the science of political ethics (nīti-śāstra), and therefore you speak thus.
For it has been said:"
He who does not pacify an enemy or a disease as soon as they arise—even if he possesses great strength—is himself destroyed once they have grown. (Pancatantaka 1.395)
"He has become our enemy because he has seized the position of minister. And it is said:

"In this world, whoever seeks to conquer another's ancestral station held by his father and grandfather is that person's innate enemy, even if he remains in a state of friendship; he must be destroyed. (Pañca 1.396)
Therefore, I brought him here with an air of indifference by granting him safety; meanwhile, I too have been ousted from my position as his minister by him.
Or rather, it is well said:
"If a virtuous man should grant entry into his own station to a wicked person..."
Therefore, desiring his own destruction, he himself becomes capable of bringing about that ruin;
for this reason, those of vast intelligence should grant no opportunity to the base.
It is heard in the traditional texts that even a paramour may become the master of the house.
Therefore, I am devising a means to kill him,
or else to cause him to abandon his country;
and no one other than you will know of this.
Thus it has been said to you: "This was performed for your own sake. And it has also been said:

"Having made one's heart as hard as a sword-blade and one's speech as sweet as sugarcane juice, one should not entertain hesitation in this matter; one should slay the wrongdoer there. (Pañcatantra 1.398)
Furthermore, even when he is dead, he will be food for us; thus,
on one hand, there will be the accomplishment of our desired goal,
and on the other, there will be both assistance and satisfaction.
Since these three qualities have appeared in you, why do you revile me out of a state of dull-wittedness? And it is said:
"A wise man should not, like the foolish-minded jackal in the forest, seek the accomplishment of his own purpose by inflicting pain upon another. (Pañcatantra 1.399)
Karaṭaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 16.
The Story of the Lion named Vajradaṃṣṭra:
In a certain region of the forest, there lived a lion named Vajradaṃṣṭra.
He had two jackals as servants, named Caturaka and Kravyamukha, who always followed him and dwelt together with him in that very forest.

Then one day, a female camel who was near her time to give birth and had strayed from her herd was found by a lion sitting in a certain thicket of the forest, suffering from the pains of labor. Having killed her, as soon as he tore open her belly, a small young camel emerged alive.
The lion, too, together with his retinue, attained supreme satisfaction by means of the flesh of the female slave;
out of great affection, he brought the young male slave back to his home and said this: "My good man, you have no fear of death from me, nor from anyone else."
"Therefore, roam at your will in this forest;
since your ears are like spikes (śaṅku),
you shall henceforth be known by the name Śaṅkukarṇa."
When they had thus settled, all four of them remained dwelling in one place, experiencing the pleasure of various kinds of conversation with one another.
Śaṅkukarṇa, having reached the stage of youth, did not leave that lion for even a moment.
Then, on one occasion, Vajradaṃṣṭra engaged in a battle with a certain wild elephant in rut.
Because of his pride and prowess, he was so wounded by the blows of their tusks that he was unable to move.
Then, his throat parched with hunger, he said to them: "Sirs!
Search for some creature, so that even while remaining in this state, I may slay it and thereby eliminate the hunger of both myself and you."
Having heard that, all three of them wandered in the forest until the time of twilight, yet they did not encounter any living creature.
Then Caturaka reflected: "If this Śaṅkukarṇa were killed, then for several days there would be satisfaction for us all."
However, my master will not destroy him because of their friendship and because he is dependent upon his protection.
Alternatively, by means of the power of my intellect, I shall awaken the master so that he will have him killed. And it has been said:
"There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be killed, or approached, or done."
Therefore, among the intelligent people in this world, I employ that [method]. (5.400)

Reflecting thus, he said this to Śaṅkukarṇa: "O Śaṅkukarṇa, our master is currently tormented by hunger in the absence of wholesome food. Due to the loss of our master, our own destruction is also certain."
"Therefore, I shall speak a few words for the sake of my master;
let that be heard.
Śaṅkukarṇa said, "O sir, let it be announced quickly!"
"By which means I shall quickly fulfill your word without hesitation. Furthermore, O Master, when this is done for your benefit, it will be as if a hundred good deeds have been performed by me.
Then Caturaka said, "O good sir!"
