Give your own body to the master in exchange for a double profit, whereby your body becomes twofold,
while the master’s means of subsistence is secured.
Having heard that, Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"My good friend, if it is so, then let this be stated as my own business; let the master's purpose be accomplished."
"In this matter, Dharma himself is the guarantor.
Having reflected thus, they all went into the presence of the lion.
Then Caturaka said, "O King!"
Not a single being has been found;
even the Blessed One, the Sun, has set.
Therefore, if my lord will grant me a second body, [I shall go].
Then Śaṅkukarṇa offered his own body with a double interest, using Dharma as the guarantor.
The lion said, "O friend,
if it is so, then that is most excellent."
"Let Dharma be made the guarantor for this transaction.
Then, immediately after Siṃha’s words, Śaṅkukarṇa, his two flanks torn open by the wolf and the jackal, met his death.
Thereupon Vajradaṃṣṭra said to Caturaka: "O Caturaka!"
"Until I have gone to the river, performed my bath and the rites of deity worship, and returned, you must remain here vigilantly," he said, and then departed for the river.
Once he had gone, Caturaka reflected: "How will this camel become food for me alone? Having thought this, he said to Kravyamukha: "O Kravyamukha!"
"You are hungry;
therefore, until that master returns,
you should eat the meat of this camel."
"I shall prove you innocent before my master.
Having heard this, as soon as he had tasted some meat, Caturaka said: "O Kravyamukha! The master is approaching!"
"Therefore, abandon him and stand at a distance, so that he does not even consider devouring you.
When this was done, the lion arrived; when he looked at the camel, he saw that its heart had been completely removed.
Then, knitting his brows, he spoke more harshly: "Aha! By whom has this camel been brought to such a state of filth, that I must even put him to death?
When this was said, Kravyamukha looked toward Caturakamukha.
Then Caturaka laughed and said: "O friend!
Having disregarded me and devoured the meat, you now look toward my face. Therefore, taste the fruit of this tree of wicked conduct!"
Having heard that, Kravyamukha went to a distant place out of fear for his life.
In the meantime, a caravan of camels heavily laden with burdens arrived along that same path;
a large bell was tied around the neck of the lead camel.
Hearing her voice even from afar, the lion said to the jackal, "My good friend,
let it be known what this terrible sound is that is heard, never before heard.
Having heard that, [the jackal replied].
The jackal, having gone a short distance into another part of the forest, quickly returned and said, "Master,
go, go, if you are able to go!
He replied, "My good friend,"
"Why do you thus agitate me?
Tell me, what is this?
Thus addressed, Caturaka said, "Master,"
"This Dharmarāja is angry with you because this camel of mine was killed by him at an improper time; therefore,
I shall take a thousandfold camel from his presence."

Having thus resolved, he took a large stone, tied a bell around the neck of the lead camel, and taking along even his ancestors who had been attached to the condemned camels, he set out for the sake of avenging his enmity. The lion, having heard this and looking all around from afar, abandoned the dead camel and fled out of fear for his life.
Caturaka also slowly began to eat the flesh of that camel;
therefore I say: "While inflicting pain upon another... (399).
Now, after Damanaka had departed, Sañjīvaka reflected: "Alas! What have I done?"
Even one who subsists on grass has become a follower of one who eats meat.
Or rather, it is well said:
"The man who goes to those women who should not be approached and serves those who should not be served..."
He embraces death, just as a female mule conceives a fetus.
What shall I do?
Where shall I go?
How will there be peace for me?
Or rather, I shall go to that very Piṅgalaka;
perhaps he will protect me, having come to him for refuge,
and will not deprive me of my life.
As it has been said:
"If, even for those striving here for the sake of Dharma, misfortunes should somehow arise from fate,
then the wise must apply exceptional methods specifically to pacify them."

This worldly saying has attained renown throughout the entire world, for it is said that even the sprinkling of water, though beneficial, causes the growth of things already burnt by fire. (Panc 1.402)
And so it is said:
"In this world, for embodied beings who constantly rely upon the ripening of their own karma and perform actions for their own benefit,"
Whether it be merit acquired through one's state of being or even demerit, whatever is destined to happen will surely come to pass; there is no cause for deliberation in this matter.
Furthermore, even if I go elsewhere, death will come to me at the hands of some wicked, flesh-eating creature; that would be better than [dying] at the hands of a lion. And it is said:
"For one who competes with those who are great, calamity alone is more grievous."
Even when their tusks are broken, elephants remain praiseworthy for their shattering of mountains.
And so it is said:
Even a lowly person, having attained the destruction of greatness, becomes praiseworthy;
just as the honeybee, though struck by the ear of an elephant, remains intent on its quest for nectar. (Pañca 1.405)
Having thus resolved, he proceeded slowly with a cautious gait; observing the lion’s lair, he recited: "Aha!
Well said is this:
a house with a serpent lurking within, a forest with a fierce lion dwelling inside."

Like a delightful lake filled with lotuses yet infested by crocodiles, the minds of kings—though once presided over by noble people—are now inhabited by base and ignoble men who are like malicious informers slandering the virtuous; thus, they are entered with difficulty and trepidation. (Panc 1.406)
Reading thus, and seeing Piṅgalaka in the form described by Damanaka, he became terrified; with his body concealed, he sat at a great distance without even performing a prostration.
Piṅgalaka, too, observing him in such a state and believing the words of Damanaka, pounced upon him in a rage.
Then Sañjīvaka, his back torn by the animal’s sharp claws, gored its belly with his horns and somehow escaped from it; seeking to kill it with his horns, he stood ready for battle.
Then, seeing that both of them resembled flowering *palāśa* trees and were each desiring to slay the other, Karaṭaka said to Damanaka: "O you of dull intellect!
You have not acted wisely by instigating this conflict between these two;
nor do you understand the true principles of policy."
And it has been said by those learned in statecraft:
"Those skilled in policy who, out of goodwill, settle through conciliation alone tasks that are accomplished with great effort and result in severe punishment and violence—they are true ministers.
But those who, by improper means, seek through the exertion of force tasks that are pithless and yield little fruit [are not]."
Through their wicked conduct, the king's prosperity is brought to a level with that of a commoner.
Therefore, if there will be an assault upon our master, what is the use of acting according to your counsel?
Or, even if Sañjīvaka is not bound, it is still ill-fated;
for his slaughter would result from a danger to life.
Therefore, you fool,
how can you desire the position of minister?
You do not understand the accomplishment of conciliation.
Therefore, this desire of yours for punishment is in vain. And it has been said:
"The policy taught by the Self-Existent One begins with conciliation and ends with punishment; among these, punishment is the most evil, so one should employ it last. (Pañcatantra 1.408)
And thus:
"Where success is achieved through conciliation alone, a wise person should not employ punishment there;
if bile is pacified by sugar, what is the use of *paṭola*? (Pañca 1.409)
And so it is said:
"In the beginning, conciliation (sāma) should be employed by a discerning man;
tasks that are to be accomplished through conciliation never undergo failure. (Pañca 1.410)
Neither by the moon, nor by medicinal herbs, nor by the sun, nor by fire does the darkness born of enmity reach dissolution; it dissolves only through conciliation.
Likewise, that which you desire— ministerial office—
is also improper,
because you do not understand the course of a minister.
For counsel is fivefold;
and it is the means for the commencement of undertakings, as well as the excellence of the person and the materials.
The classification of place and time,
the remedy for misfortune,
and the accomplishment of the task.
Thus, this calamity has arisen and clung to either one of the two—the sovereign or the minister—or perhaps to both.
Therefore, if there is any power remaining, let a remedy for this calamity be devised;
for the testing of a minister's intellect lies in the mending of what is broken.
Therefore, you are a fool, since you possess a perverted intellect and are incapable of accomplishing that task. And it has been said:
"In the case of reconciling a breach among ministers, or in the case of a *sāṃnipātika* [complex] fever for physicians..."
Wisdom is revealed in action; for who is not wise when things go well?
And furthermore:
A base person knows only how to destroy another's work, not how to accomplish it;
a rat has the power only to overturn a basket of food, not to lift it up. (Panc 1.413)
Or rather, this is not your fault;
it is the fault of your master, who places his trust in your words. And it has been said:
Those rulers of men who follow the base and do not proceed by the path taught by the Buddha enter, therefore,
upon a road that is difficult to traverse and from which there is no exit.
The cage of misfortune, crowded with every kind of affliction.
Therefore, if you become his minister, then no other virtuous person will ever come near him. As it is said:

"Even if he is a treasury of virtues, a king is not approached if he has a wicked minister, just as a lake with clear and sweet water is avoided if it is infested with predatory crocodiles. (Pañcatantra 1.415)
And thus, even the master will meet his destruction when he is bereft of cultured people. As it has been said:
"Those kings who take their pleasure with servants whose speech is full of varied flavors but who have never had their bows drawn—their enemies revel in their prosperity. (Pañcatantra 1.416)
Therefore, what is the use of instruction for a fool?
It results only in fault, not in virtue. And it has been said: "Wood that is not supple cannot be bent; a razor cannot be fashioned from stone."
Know that the needle-mouthed [hell] is not revealed to one who is not a disciple.
Damanaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 17.
There is a story concerning a troop of monkeys.
Once, in a certain region of a mountain, there was a troop of monkeys.

At one time during the winter season, their bodies were trembling from contact with an extremely harsh wind, and they were struck by the falling torrents of thick clouds as a heavy rain of snow fell; [they could not find relief] in any way whatsoever.
He attained peace.
Then some monkeys, having gathered guñjā fruits which resembled sparks of fire, stood all around blowing upon them with the desire for fire.
Then a bird named Sucīmukha, observing their futile exertion, said to them: "O friends!"
"You are all fools!
These are not sparks of fire; these are guñjā berries.
So why this useless exertion?"
"Protection from the cold will not come from this.
Therefore, let some windless forest region, a cave, or a mountain glen be sought;
for even now, clouds with their wreaths are visible."
Then one of those elder monkeys said to him: "O fool, what is the use of this undertaking?
Therefore, let us go. And it is said:"
One who knows discernment, if he desires his own success, should not converse with a gambler who has been defeated and whose actions have been repeatedly obstructed. (Pancatanttra 1.418)
And so it is said:
"He who engages in conversation with one who hunts, who causes useless suffering, who is a fool, and who is addicted to vices, meets with defeat. (Pancatantra 1.419)

He, too, disregarding him, spoke again and again incessantly to the monkeys: "O sirs! Why this useless toil? Then, while he was still prattling on in no way ceasing, one monkey, enraged by his fruitless exertion, seized him with both wings and dashed him against a rock, whereupon he perished.
And therefore I say: "Wood that cannot be bent does not bend," and so forth. Likewise:
"Instruction for fools leads to provocation, not to peace."
For serpents, drinking milk only increases their venom.
Furthermore:
"Instruction should not be given to just any person, regardless of their nature; see how by a foolish monkey, a well-built house was turned into a ruin. (Pañca 1.421)
Damanaka asked, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 18.

In a certain forest, a pair of wild sparrows lived, having made their dwelling by hanging it from the branch of a *śamī* tree. Now once, while they were living there in comfort, a winter cloud began to rain very gently.
At that moment, a certain monkey, struck by the driving rain and with his body shivering, sat down at the foot of that *śamī* tree, playing a lute of his teeth and trembling.
Then, seeing him in such a state, the sparrow said: "O good sir!
You appear to have the form of a man, endowed with hands and feet;
why, O fool, do you not build a house when you are being pierced by the cold?"
Having heard this, the monkey said to her angrily: "O base woman, why do you not observe a vow of silence?
Oh, what audacity she possesses!
Today she mocks me."
"Needle-mouthed, ill-behaved, a widow who speaks like a scholar—she does not hesitate while prattling; why then do I not kill her? (Pañca 1.423)
Having thus lamented, he said to her: "O simple girl, what need have you for concern over me? And it is said:
'One should speak to one who possesses faith, and especially to one who asks.'"
It is said that for one devoid of faith, it is like weeping in a forest.
What need is there for much more?
While she remained in her nest, she spoke to him once again;
he then climbed that śamī tree and tore her nest into a hundred pieces.
Therefore I say: "Instruction should not be given. O fool, even though you have been instructed, you have not learned the lesson.
Or rather, it is not your fault.
For instruction leads to virtue in a person of integrity, but not in one who lacks it. And it has been said:
"What indeed can scholarship accomplish when it is applied to an improper object?"
It is like a lamp placed inside a jar shrouded in darkness.
Relying on that useless scholarship, you do not listen to my words, yet you even seek your own peace;
therefore, you are surely *apajāta*. And it is said:
"A son is born (*jāta*), one who is born after (*anujāta*), and likewise one who is born beyond (*atijāta*)."
And those who have not produced [a son] in this world should be considered as such by those learned in the scriptures.

One born with qualities equal to his mother is "born after" (anujāta); one equal to his father is "well-born" (sujāta); one superior to him is "exceedingly well-born" (atijāta); and one inferior to him is "ill-born" (apajāta), the lowest of the low.
A wicked person, rejoicing in the misfortune of others, does not even consider his own destruction;
for generally, when his head is lost at the front of battle, the headless torso dances.
Ah, this is well said:
"Both the one with a sense of righteousness and the one with a wicked mind—these two are known to me:
by a son whose scholarship was in vain, his father was killed with smoke. (Pañca 1.429)
Damanaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 20.
The Story of the Black Snake:
In a certain region, two friends named Dharmabuddhi and Pāpabuddhi lived together.
Then, at one time, Pāpabuddhi thought to himself, "I am indeed a fool and beset by poverty."
"Therefore, taking this Dharmabuddhi with me, I shall go to another country; by relying on him, I will acquire wealth, and having deceived even him, I shall live in happiness.
Then, on another day, Pāpabuddhi said to Dharmabuddhi: "O friend!
In my old age, do you remember what I have done?"
Without having seen other lands, what news of cultured people will you be able to tell? And it is said:
"For him who has wandered over the surface of the earth but has not learned the various languages, costumes, and so forth of other lands, the fruit of his birth is in vain. (Pañcāstikāya 1.430)
And so it is said:
A person does not properly acquire knowledge, wealth, or skill as long as he does not travel joyfully from one land to another upon this earth. (Pañcatantra 1.431)
Then, having heard those words of his, with a joyful heart and permitted by his elders, he set out for another country on an auspicious day along with him.
And while wandering there, through the power of Dharmabuddhi’s merit, Pāpabuddhi acquired a great deal of wealth.
Thereupon, both of them, having amassed abundant riches, departed with eager haste toward their own home. And it is said:
For those who have acquired knowledge, wealth, or arts and reside in another land,
even a stretch of ground measuring a single *krośa* will feel as if it were a hundred *yojanas*.
Then Pāpabuddhi, who was staying near his own place, said to Dharmabuddhi:
"My good friend, it is not appropriate to take all this wealth back to our home;
for our family members and kinsmen will surely demand it."

Therefore, let us deposit it right here somewhere in the thicket of the forest, take only a small portion with us, and enter our home. When the need arises again, we shall come together and carry that portion away from this place. And it is said:
"A wise man should not display his wealth to anyone, even if it be very small."
For even the mind of that Sage wavers upon seeing him.
And so it is said:
"Just as meat is devoured by fish in the water, by beasts of prey on land, and by birds in the sky, even so is the man of wealth everywhere. (Pañca 1.434)
Having heard this, Dharmabuddhi said, "My good friend, let it be done so.
When they had acted accordingly, both of them went to their own homes and lived there in happiness.
Then, on another day, at midnight, Pāpabuddhi went into the forest, took all that wealth, filled up the pit, and returned to his own dwelling.

Then, on another day, having met with Dharmabuddhi, he said: "Friend, we have a large family and are suffering due to a lack of wealth. Therefore, let us go to that place and bring back some small amount of money.
He replied: "My good friend,"
"Let it be done thus.
Then, having both gone to that place, as they were digging, they saw an empty vessel.
In the meantime, Pāpabuddhi, striking his head, said: "O Dharmabuddhi!"
"This wealth was taken by you, not by anyone else; for you have even filled the pit again. Therefore, give me half of it."
"Otherwise, I shall report this to the royal court.
He replied, "O wicked soul!
Do not speak thus!"
"I am indeed one whose mind is fixed on the Dharma;
I do not perform such a deed as theft. And it has been said:
'One should regard the wives of others as one's own mother, and the property of others as a clod of earth.'"
Those whose intellects are fixed on the Dharma regard all living beings as they do themselves.
Thus, both of them, disputing with one another, went before the judge and spoke while mutually defaming each other. Then,
as soon as they were appointed by the officials presiding over the court of justice for the purpose of undergoing an ordeal, Pāpabuddhi said:
Alas, the principle has not been correctly perceived! And it has been said:
"In a dispute, a document is sought; in its absence, witnesses;
in the absence of witnesses, the wise declare that an ordeal is to be employed. (Pañcāstikāya 1.436)
"In this matter, the deities of the trees stand as witnesses for me;
they too will determine whether one of us two is a thief or an honest man.
Then they all said, "O sir, what you have said is right. And it is said:"
When even an outcaste serves as a witness in a legal dispute, an ordeal is not appropriate there; how much less so, then, when forest deities are the witnesses?
"Therefore, we too have a great curiosity regarding this matter;
at the time of dawn, you two should also go to that forest region along with us.
In the meantime, Evil-Mind went to his own home and said to his father: "Father,"
This great wealth has been stolen by me from the Buddha of the Dharma;
and it shall come to fruition through your word,
otherwise it will depart along with my life.
He said, "My son,
speak quickly so that, having spoken, I may bring that object to a state of stability.
Pāpabuddhi said, "Father,"
In that region there is a great śamī tree;
it has a large hollow within it. Enter there this very moment.
Then, when I make the proclamation of truth at dawn, you must say, "Dharmabuddhi is the thief.
When this was carried out, at daybreak, Pāpabuddhi bathed and, preceded by Dharmabuddhi, approached that śamī tree with the judges and cried out in a loud voice:
The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and Yama;
day and night, and both twilights.
For Dharma indeed knows the conduct of a man.
"O Blessed One, O forest deity!
Tell us which of us two is the thief.
Then Pāpabuddhi’s father, staying within the hollow of a śamī tree, said: "O,"
"This wealth was taken by Dharmabuddhi.

Upon hearing this, all those royal officers, their eyes wide with astonishment, began to examine, according to the perspective of the legal treatises, the punishment appropriate for the seizure of Dharmabuddhi's property; meanwhile, Dharmabuddhi [filled] that hollow of the *śamī* tree with substances that serve as fuel for fire.

Having been wrapped around and set ablaze by fire, when it was burning, the father of Pāpabuddhi emerged from that hollow of the *śamī* tree with his body half-burnt and his eyes bulging, lamenting piteously.
Then, he was questioned by them all: "O sir, what is this?"
When this was said, [Dharmabuddhi] died, saying, "All of this evil deed has arisen because of Pāpabuddhi.
Then those royal officers, having suspended Pāpabuddhi from a branch of a *śamī* tree and praising Dharmabuddhi, said this:
"Oh, how well this is said:"
A wise person should devise a means, and likewise should also consider the potential for failure;
while the foolish crane looked on, his sons were devoured by mongooses. (Pañcatantra 1.439)
Dharmabuddhi asked, "How was that?
They replied:
"The Story 21."
The Story of the Merchant’s Son named Jīrṇadhana:
In a certain forest region there was a banyan tree inhabited by many herons;
in its hollow lived a black snake.
And he spent his time constantly devouring the young cranes, even those whose wings had not yet grown.
Then, one crane, seeing his offspring devoured by him, reached the shore of the lake out of grief for his young ones and stood there with his face cast down, his eyes overflowing with tears.
Observing him in such a state, a crab said: "Uncle, why are you weeping like this today?"
He said, "My good friend, what shall I do?
The children of my ill fortune have been devoured by a serpent dwelling in a hollow;
pained by that grief, I weep."
"Therefore, tell me if there is any means for its destruction.
Having heard this, Kulīraka reflected: "This one is indeed our natural enemy;
therefore, I shall give him such advice—part truth and part falsehood—that all the other cranes will likewise come to ruin. And it is said:
Having made one's speech as smooth as butter while keeping the mind merciless,
one should awaken the enemy in such a way that he perishes along with his entire lineage.

And he said, "My dear friend, if that is so, then throw pieces of fish-flesh from the entrance of the mongoose's burrow all the way to the snake's hole, so that the mongoose, following that path, will destroy that wicked snake.
When this was carried out, the mongoose, following the trail of the fish-flesh, killed the black snake and gradually devoured all those cranes as well who were perched upon that tree.
Therefore we say: "One should devise a means.
Thus, O fool, you have devised a calamity and not a means, like one of evil intent;
therefore, you are no virtuous person.
"You are nothing but evil-minded; I have known this from bringing about the danger to my master's life. You yourself have manifested your own wickedness and crookedness."
Or rather, it is well said:
Who could perceive, even with effort, the path by which peacocks take their food, if those very fools were not to dance when delighted by the sound of the clouds? (Pañca 1.441)
If you bring your master to such a state, what account can there be for one like me?
Therefore, you must not remain near me. And it is said:
"In a place where mice devour a balance-beam made of a thousand measures of iron..."
O King, a hawk might carry off that child there; of this there is no doubt.
Damanaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 22.
The Story of the Merchant’s Son Named Jīrṇadhana:
In a certain town there was a merchant’s son named Jīrṇadhana. Due to the depletion of his wealth, he became intent on traveling to another land and reflected:
That man who, having enjoyed pleasures in a certain country or place by means of his own prowess, should later dwell there destitute of wealth, is the lowest of men.
And so it is said:
"He who, having formerly sported for a long time joined with egoism, speaks dejectedly even in that very same situation before others, is censured. (Pañcatantra 1.444)
In his house there was a scale made of a thousand loads of metal, which had been acquired by his ancestors;
having deposited it as a pledge in the house of a certain merchant, he set out for another country.
After wandering at will through foreign lands for a very long time, he returned once more to his own city and said to that merchant: "O merchant!"
"Give me back that deposit-scale.
He replied, "Sir, that scale of yours does not exist;
it has been eaten by mice."
Jīrṇadhana said: "O merchant, there is no fault on your part if it was eaten by mice;
such indeed is this cycle of existence."
"Nothing here is permanent.
However, I am going to the river for the purpose of bathing.
Therefore, please send this child of yours named Dhanadeva with me, carrying the requisites for bathing."
He too, fearing theft and suspicious of him, said to his own son: "My child, this paternal uncle of yours is going to the river to bathe;
therefore, go with him, taking the bathing requisites."
Ah, this is well said:
"No man does anything pleasing for another out of devotion, except out of fear, greed, or for some specific purpose. (Pañca 1.445)
And so it is said:
"Wherever there is excessive devotion devoid of cause or reason, one should harbor suspicion therein, for it will bring unhappiness in the end. (Pañc 1.446)
Then that merchant’s son, taking the bathing requisites, set out with the guest with a joyful mind.
When they had proceeded thus, the merchant, having bathed, threw the boy into a river cave, blocked its entrance with a large rock, and quickly returned home.
And he was asked by that merchant: "O guest, tell me, where is my son who went to the river with you?"
He said, "He was carried off by a hawk from the riverbank.
The merchant said, "Liar!
Can a hawk ever carry off a child?"
"Therefore, hand over my son to me;
otherwise, I shall report this at the royal court.
He replied, "O speaker of truth!"

"Just as a hawk does not carry off a child, so too do mice not eat a scale fashioned from a load of iron. Therefore, give me back the scale if you have need of the boy. Thus disputing, both went to the royal court.
There, the merchant cried out in a loud voice: "O, a crime!
A crime! My child has been carried off by this thief!
Then the judges said to him: "Sir, let the merchant's son be restored."
He said, "What shall I do?
While I was looking on, the infant was carried off from the riverbank by a hawk.
Hearing that, they said, "O sir, you have not spoken the truth."
"Is a hawk capable of carrying off a chick?
He replied: "O sirs, listen to my words:
Where mice eat away at a balance-beam made of a thousand pieces of iron."
O King, a hawk might carry off the child there; of this there is no doubt.
They asked, "How was that?
Thereupon, the merchant related the entire account before the members of the assembly.
Then, they laughed and, addressing both of them to one another, satisfied them by having the child given to the scale.
Therefore I say: "A balance for a thousand loads of iron.
O fool! This was done by you because you could not endure the favor shown to Sañjīvaka.

Ah, it is well said: [The verse follows: "Better a wise enemy than a foolish friend; better a blind wife than one with eyes who is unfaithful; better a servant who speaks unpleasant truths than one who speaks pleasant lies; better a tree that yields fruit than one that is barren."
Generally in this world, those born of low families despise the well-born; the unfortunate despise the beloved of Fortune;
the miserly despise the generous; the crooked despise the upright; the poor despise those established in wealth;
those afflicted by deformity despise the beautiful-bodied; and the sinful despise those who take refuge in righteousness.
And fools always revile a man who is learned in various treatises. (Pancatantira 1.448)
And so it is said:
"The learned are hated by the foolish; the very wealthy by the poor;
those who observe vows by those of sinful character; and virtuous wives by unchaste women. (Pañcatantra 1.449)
Therefore, O fool, you have done harm even though you intended it to be beneficial. And it is said:
"A wise enemy is better than a foolish well-wisher;
the king was killed by a monkey, while the brahmins were protected by a rag. (Pañcatantra 1.450)
Damanaka said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 23.
A certain king had a monkey who was constantly devoted to him and served as his personal attendant; he was permitted to enter even the inner apartments and had become an object of great trust.
Once, while the king was asleep and the monkey was fanning him with a whisk to provide a breeze, a fly settled upon the king’s chest.
Although repeatedly warded off by the whisk, it kept returning to that very spot.
Then, that foolish monkey, naturally fickle and now enraged, took up a sharp sword and struck her;
the fly flew away,
but by that keen-edged blade the king’s chest was split asunder, and the king died.
Therefore, a king who desires long life should not keep a foolish attendant.
Furthermore, in a certain city, there was a certain Brahmin who was a great scholar, yet due to the influence of his previous birth, he was a thief.
Seeing four Brahmins who had arrived from another country selling many goods in that city, he thought: "Aha! By what means can I obtain their wealth?"
Having reflected thus, he began to serve them by reciting before them many well-spoken verses from the scriptures and speaking very dear, sweet words, thereby engendering confidence in their minds.
Or rather, it is well said:
"An unchaste woman becomes modest, and alkaline water becomes cool."
The discerning man becomes a hypocrite, and the rogue becomes a sweet-talker.
Then, while he was performing his service, those brahmins sold all their belongings and purchased precious jewels of great value.
Thereupon, having placed them inside their calves in his very presence, they made preparations to depart for their own country.
When that rogue brahmin saw those brahmins ready to leave, his mind became agitated with anxiety:
"Aha! This wealth has not fallen to me at all;
therefore, I shall go with them.
Somewhere along the way, I will administer poison to them, kill them, and seize all the jewels."
Having reflected thus, he lamented piteously in their presence and said: "O friends!
You are preparing to depart, leaving me all alone.
Consequently, my heart, bound by the tether of affection for you, has become so distressed by the very name of separation from you that it finds no stability anywhere."
"Having bestowed your favor, please take me as well as your companion along with you.
Hearing those words, their hearts softened with compassion, they set out toward their own country together with him.
Then, as the five of them were traveling through the midst of a forest village on the road, crows began to cry out: "O, O hunters!"
Run, run!
Those who possess a hundred thousand pieces of gold are passing by;
having slain them, take their wealth!

Then, having heard the words of the crows, the Kirātas went quickly; they beat those Brahmins with clubs until they were mangled, stripped off their clothes, and searched them, yet not even a little wealth was found.
Then those Kirātas said: "O travelers!"
"Never before has the word of a crow proven false.
Therefore, if there is any wealth hidden anywhere in your presence, hand it over!
Otherwise, we shall execute all of you, tear open your skins, examine every limb, and take the wealth."

Then, having heard such words from them, the thief-Brahmin thought to himself: "If these Brahmins, after killing me and searching my body, take the jewels, they will kill me anyway; therefore, I shall first offer myself as being without jewels and release them. And it is said:
"O fool, why do you fear death? Death does not spare one who is afraid."
Whether today or at the end of a hundred years, death is indeed certain for all living beings.
And so it is said:
"He who gives up his life for the sake of a cow or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, having pierced the orb of the sun, goes to the supreme goal. (Pañca 1.453)
Having thus resolved, he said: "O Kirātas!
If it is so, then kill me first and look [for the treasure].
When they had done accordingly, they saw that he was devoid of wealth, and all four others were released as well.
Therefore I say: "Even a wise man is better as an enemy.
Now, while they were thus conversing, Sañjīvaka fought with Piṅgalaka for a single moment; struck by his sharp claws, he fell lifeless upon the surface of the earth.
Then, beholding him dead, Piṅgalaka, his heart moistened by the recollection of his virtues, said: "O friend!"
"An improper deed has been committed by me, a sinner, in slaying Sañjīvaka;
for there is no action more sinful than the betrayal of trust. And it is said:
'He who betrays a friend, he who is ungrateful, and he who violates trust—'"
Those men go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
When the land is destroyed, it is indeed the destruction of the king;
or when a wise servant is destroyed, it is likewise.
For it is not right to say that these two are equal.
Even lost land is easily regained, but servants are not.
Thus, he has always been praised by me in the midst of the assembly; so what shall I say in their presence? And it is said:
"He who has previously been declared virtuous in the assembly..."
One who fears the collapse of their own thesis should not point out faults in that [position].

To him who was lamenting in this manner, Damanaka approached and said joyfully: "O Lord, this conduct of yours is the height of cowardice, that you grieve thus after having slain a grass-eater who committed an act of treachery.
This is not fitting for kings. And it has been said:"
Whether it be a father, a brother, a son, a wife, or a friend, when they seek to take one's life, they must be killed; there is no sin in this. (Pañcatantra 1.457)
And likewise:
"A compassionate king, a Brahmin who eats all things, a shameless woman, and a wicked-minded companion."
A servant who is rebellious, an official who is arrogant, a favorite who is negligent, and one who does not acknowledge what has been done for him— these should be abandoned.
Moreover:
she may be truthful or false, harsh or sweet-spoken,
cruel or compassionate, intent on wealth or generous.
The policy of kings is manifold in form, like a courtesan, bringing both great distress and the acquisition of abundant wealth. (Pancatantra 1.459)
Moreover—Even one who is great is not honored if he has committed no offense;
men worship the *nāgas*, but not Tārkṣya, the slayer of *nāgas*. (Panc_1.460)
And so it is said:
"You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not grieve for the dead or for the living. (5.46)
Thus enlightened by him, Piṅgalaka abandoned his grief for Sañjīvaka and ruled the kingdom with Damanaka as his minister.
Thus ends the section titled "The Breach of Friendship" in the *Pañcatantra* composed by Śrī Viṣṇuśarman.

The First Tantra. //1// *********************************************************************** Now follows the acquisition of friends (*mitra-samprāpti*). Herein begins the second tantra, named "The Acquisition of Friends."
Of which this is the first verse:
"Even those who lack means, if they are wise, intelligent, and well-learned, accomplish their tasks quickly, like the crow, the mouse, the deer, and the tortoise. (Pañcatantra 2.1)
Thus it is heard—
the introductory story, the account of Laghupatanaka and Citragrīva.
In the southern country there is a city named Mahilāropya.

Not far from it stands a great banyan tree, towering in height, its fruit enjoyed by various birds, its hollows covered with insects, and providing a refuge for crowds of travelers weary from the heat of the sun; indeed, this is only fitting.
That tree alone is praiseworthy: its shade provides rest for deer, its foliage is pecked at on all sides by flocks of birds,
its hollows are covered with insects, monkeys find refuge upon its trunk,
and its flowers are drunk in by bees with full confidence.
With all his limbs, he brings joy through association with many beings; he is another who has become the burden of the earth.
And there lived a crow named Laghupatanaka. Once, while setting out toward the city for the sake of finding food,
he saw a man approaching him who had a net in his hand, whose body was extremely dark, whose feet were cracked, whose hair stood erect, and who resembled a servant of Yama.

Then, seeing him, his mind filled with apprehension, he thought: "Since this evil-minded one approaches today directly toward the banyan tree that is my refuge, it is not known whether today there will be a destruction of the birds dwelling in the banyan or not.
Having reflected thus in many ways, he turned back at that very moment, went to that same banyan tree, and said to all the birds: "O friends!"
This wicked hunter approaches with a net and rice in his hand;
therefore, one must not trust him at all.
He will spread out his net and scatter the rice.
"You all must regard those grains of rice as being like the *kālakūṭa* poison," he said.
As he spoke, the hunter arrived there at the foot of the banyan tree, spread out his net, scattered the rice which resembled *sinduvāra* flowers, and went a short distance away to remain hidden.

Then, the birds who were staying there were restrained by the bolt of Laghupatanaka’s words; regarding those grains of rice as if they were sprouts of the *hālāhala* poison, they remained perfectly still.
In the meantime, a king of pigeons named Citragrīva, wandering with a thousand followers in search of sustenance,
saw those grains of rice even from afar; though restrained by Laghupatanaka, he descended to eat them out of greed for their taste,
and together with his retinue, was captured.
Or rather, it is well said:
For those who dwell in the midst of water and are addicted to the greed of the tongue, death comes unexpectedly, like that of ignorant fish. (Pañca 2.3)
Alternatively, this may happen due to the adverse course of destiny;
there is no fault in that. And it has been said:
"How could Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, not have known the fault in abducting another's wife?"
Why was the impossibility of a golden deer not perceived even by Rāma?
And why did Yudhiṣṭhira suddenly meet with calamity through the dice?
For the intellect of those whose minds are deluded by impending disaster generally fails. (Pancatantra 2.4)
And so it is said:
"The intellects of even the great, when bound by the noose of destiny and their minds struck down by fate, tend to follow a crooked course. (Pañcatantra 2.5)
In the meantime, the hunter, realizing they were bound, became joyful in mind and ran forward with his staff raised for the purpose of killing them.
Citragrīva, too, thinking himself along with his followers to be bound and seeing the hunter approaching, said to those pigeons: "Oh, do not be afraid! And it is said:"
He whose intellect does not falter even amidst all calamities reaches the further shore of them by its power; of this there is no doubt.
In prosperity as well as in adversity, the great remain uniform in nature;
the sun is red at its rising, and likewise red at its setting.
Therefore, let us all fly up together with ease, along with our snares and nets, and having gone out of his sight, attain liberation.
Otherwise, if—overcome by fear—you do not take flight with ease, then you will meet your death. And it is said:
"Threads, though long, numerous, and even, endure many strains because of their multiplicity; this is the analogy for the virtuous. (Pañca 2.8)
When this had been done, the hunter, though remaining on the ground, ran after them as they flew through the sky carrying the net. Then, looking upward, he recited this verse:
"Even these birds are going away together, carrying the net."
And as long as they shall dispute, they will undoubtedly fall.
Laghupatanaka, too, having abandoned his search for sustenance, followed after him out of curiosity, wondering what would happen there.
Then, realizing they had passed beyond the range of his sight, the hunter, becoming despondent, turned back and recited this verse:
"That which is not to be does not come to pass, and that which is destined to be occurs even without effort."
For that which is destined to perish will vanish even if it has come into the palm of one's hand.
And thus:
"If, while fate is turned away, there should somehow be an acquisition of wealth, he takes even that other thing and departs, just like the treasure of the conch. (Pañcatantra 2.11)
"Let alone the greed for the meat of birds; even my net, which served as the means for maintaining my family, has been lost.
Citragrīva, perceiving that the hunter had vanished from sight, said to them:
"O friends, that wicked hunter has turned back."
"Therefore, let all of you go while you are still safe to the north-eastern quarter of Mahilārōpya.
There, a friend of mine named Hiraṇyaka, a mouse, will cut the snares for all of you. And it is said:
'When misfortune has befallen all mortals...'"
No one other than a friend would provide assistance even with mere words.
Thus, having been enlightened by Citragrīva, those pigeons reached the fortress of Hiraṇyaka’s hole in the city of Mahilāropya.
Hiraṇyaka, too, having entered the fortress of his thousand-mouthed hole, remained there happily, free from fear from any quarter.
Or rather, it is well said:
Just as a snake deprived of its fangs or an elephant devoid of its rut becomes submissive to all, so too does a king who lacks a fortress.
And so it is said:
"That deed which kings accomplish in battle with even a single enemy from afar cannot be achieved by a thousand elephants nor by a hundred thousand horses. (Pañca 2.14)
Even a single archer standing upon a rampart can hold off a hundred; therefore, those who know the treatises on statecraft praise the fortified stronghold.
Then Citragrīva, having reached his burrow, called out in a loud voice: "O friend Hiraṇyaka, come quickly!
A great state of calamity has befallen me."
Having heard that, Hiraṇyaka, remaining within the security of his burrow, said: "O sir!
Who are you? For what purpose have you come? What is the reason?"
"What is the nature of your state of distress?
Let it be told.
Having heard this, Citragrīva said: "O friend!"
"I am Citragrīva by name, the king of pigeons, and a friend of yours. Therefore, come quickly;
there is a matter of great importance."
Hearing that, his body bristling with joy and his soul filled with delight, he departed in haste with a steady mind.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Friends who are endowed with affection are givers of joy to the eyes."
They never enter the houses of those great-souled ones who possess a home.
O dear one, the rising of the sun, betel, the story of the Mahābhārata, a beloved wife, and a good friend—these are ever-new day by day. (Pancatantra 2.17)
In whose house friends constantly assemble,
there is no happiness in the world comparable to the joy in his heart.
Then, seeing Citragrīva bound in a snare along with his followers, Hiraṇyaka said this with dejection: "O friend, what is this?
He replied: "O friend, why do you ask when you already know?
And as it is said:"
Because of which, by which, when, how, what, to what extent, and where one's own karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is performed;
therefore, by that, at that time, in that manner, and as that very thing [it ripens].
And at that very time and in that very place, by the power of destiny, he arrives.
"This bond has been incurred by me through my greed for the tongue;
now, you must quickly effect my release from the snare.
Hearing this, Hiraṇyaka said:
A bird perceives its prey from fifty leagues away, yet by fate it does not see the snare lying right at its side. (Pancaka 2.20)
And likewise: the affliction of the sun and moon by the planets,
and the binding of elephants, serpents, and birds;
And having observed the poverty even of the wise, it is my conviction that "Alas, destiny is all-powerful! (Pancatantaka 2.21).
And so it is said:
Even birds that roam exclusively in the sky meet with calamity;
and fish are caught by skillful men even from the ocean, despite its bottomless waters.
What here is ill-conducted, and what is well-done? What merit is there in attaining a high position?
Time, stretching out its hand, seizes all people even from afar.
Having spoken thus, as Citragrīva was preparing to cut his own snare, he said to him: "My good friend, do not do this!
First, cut the snares of my servants."
"And after that, it will be mine as well.
Hearing this, Hiraṇyaka became angry and said, "O sir!
What you have said is not proper."
Since servants follow immediately after their master,
he said: "My good man, do not speak thus!"
"All these wretched ones have come to me, having abandoned their own families; how then can I fail to show them even this much honor? And it is said:"
That king who always bestows excessive honor upon his dependents never loses them,
even in the absence of wealth, for they will never abandon him once they have seen his character.
And so it is said:
"Trust is the root of all prosperity; for this reason, the elephant is the leader of the herd, whereas the lion, despite his sovereignty over the beasts, is not surrounded by them. (Pañcatantra 2.24)
Furthermore, while I am cutting the snare, my teeth might break;
or perhaps a wicked hunter approaches.
That would surely mean a fall into hell. And it is said:
A master who remains at ease while his servants, who follow the conduct of the virtuous, are perishing,
goes to hell and suffers both in this world and the next.
Hearing that, Hiraṇyaka was delighted and said: "O friend, I know the duty of kings;
however, I merely conducted an examination of you."
Therefore, I shall first cut the bonds for all of them;
you too shall come to have a large retinue of pigeons. And it is said:
"Compassion and the sharing of one's own portion are seen in the way one treats one's dependents."
By this very mind of yours, even lordship over the three worlds might be doubted.
Having spoken thus and severed the bonds of them all, Hiraṇyaka said to Citragrīva: "Friend, you may now go to your own abode;
you should come together again when misfortune befalls us once more."
Having dispatched them, he entered the fortress once more;
Citragrīva also returned to his own abode with his retinue.
Or rather, it is well said:
Since one who possesses friends accomplishes even those goals that are difficult to achieve,
one should therefore make friends who are equal to oneself.

Laghupatanaka the crow, having observed the entire liberation of Citragrīva’s kinsmen, reflected with a mind full of wonder: "Oh, the intelligence and power of this Hiraṇyaka, as well as his fortifications!
Such indeed is the nature of the binding and liberation of these birds ordained by fate."
"And I do not trust anyone, for my nature is fickle; nevertheless, I shall make him my friend. For it is said:
'The wise should make friends even with those who are already full.'"
Even when completely full, the lord of rivers awaits the rising of the moon.
Having reflected thus, he descended from his perch, went to the entrance of the hole, and called out to Hiraṇyaka with a voice like Citragrīva’s: "Come, come, O Hiraṇyaka, come!
Hearing that sound, Hiraṇyaka thought: "Is there some other pigeon remaining in captivity who calls out to me?
And he said: "O sir, who are you?"
He said, "I am a crow named Laghupatanaka.
Hearing this, Hiranyaka, who was especially wary, spoke from within his hiding place: "O sir!
Depart quickly from this place!"
The crow said, "I have come to your side on a matter of great importance;
why then do you not grant me an audience?
Hiranyaka replied, "I have no need for association with you."
He said, "O friend, I have witnessed Citragrīva’s release from his snare at your hands;
because of that, great joy has arisen within me.
Therefore, should I ever fall into captivity, my liberation will surely come about through your assistance."
"Therefore, let friendship be formed between you and me.
Hiraṇyaka said, "Oh, you are the eater,
and I have become your food!"
Therefore, what friendship can there be between you and me?
So, depart!
How can there be friendship when there is a state of enmity? And it has been said:
Only between those whose wealth is equal and whose lineage is equal should there be friendship and marriage, but not between the prosperous and the destitute. (Pañcatantra 2.29)
And so it is said:
"The fool of wicked intellect who makes a friend for himself that is unsuitable—whether inferior or superior—becomes an object of ridicule. (Pañcatantra 2.30)
"Therefore, you may go.
The crow said, "O Hiraṇyaka!
Here I am, sitting at the entrance of your fortress."
"If you do not show me friendship, then I shall perform the sacrifice of my life before you;
otherwise, I shall sit in fasting unto death.
Hiraṇyaka said, "O sir!"
"How can I cultivate friendship with you, my enemy? For it has been said:
"One should not enter into an alliance with an enemy, even through a most firmly cemented treaty;
for water, however scalding, still extinguishes fire. (Pañcatantra 2.31)
The crow said:
"O sir, there is not even a sight of you with me; how then could there be enmity?"
"So why do you say this is improper?
Hiraṇyaka replied, "Enmity is of two kinds:
innate and acquired."
Therefore, you are our natural enemy. And it has been said:
"Artificial enmity perishes quickly through artificial virtues;
however, innate enmity does not come to an end except by the giving up of life. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.32)
The crow said:
"O sir, I wish to hear the characteristics of the two kinds of enmity;
let that be told."
Hiraṇyaka said:
"O friend, that which is artificial is rendered ineffective by its cause;
it perishes because it cannot perform the specific service appropriate to it."
Furthermore, their natural enmity never ceases,
as in the case of mongooses and snakes,
or of grass-eaters and claw-armed predators.
Of water and fire,
of gods and demons,
and of dogs and cats.
Of those who are masters and those who are poor, of rival wives,
and of lions and elephants.
Of hunters and deer,
of Vedic scholars who have fallen away from their duties, and of fools and learned men.
Among faithful wives and unchaste women, or among the virtuous and the wicked,
no one has ever been killed by anyone else.
Nevertheless, they cause their own lives to suffer.
The crow said:
"O friends, this is without cause."
Listen to my words:
one becomes a friend because of a cause, and one becomes an enemy because of a cause.
Therefore, in this world, a wise person should cultivate friendship and not enmity.
"Therefore, enter into a union with me for the sake of friendship, dharma, and wealth. Hiraṇyaka said: "O friend, listen to the very essence of political wisdom (nīti):"
He who desires to reunite with one who has once proved treacherous, even if that person was beloved,
embraces death just as a female mule conceives a foal.
Or perhaps [he thinks], "I am virtuous;
no one will inflict vengeance upon me.
This too is not possible. And it has been said:
A lion took the life of Pāṇini, the author of grammar;
an elephant suddenly crushed the sage Jaimini, the author of Mīmāṃsā;
and a sea-monster killed Piṅgala, a treasury of knowledge in prosody, on the shore of the ocean.
What is the use of virtues for animals whose minds are shrouded in ignorance and who are overcome by excessive rage? (Pancadaśī 2.35)
The crow said: "That is so;
nevertheless, listen—because of their benefit to the world, and as signs for deer and birds."
The friendship of fools arises from fear and greed, whereas that of the virtuous arises from the mere sight [of one another].
A wicked person is like a clay pot: easy to break but difficult to repair;
a good person, however, is like a golden vessel: difficult to break and easy to mend. (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 2.37)

Just as there is a gradual excellence of flavor in every successive joint of a sugar-cane starting from the tip, so too is the friendship of the virtuous; but for those who are its opposite, it is the reverse.
And so it is said:

"The friendship of the wicked and the virtuous is like the shadow of the day—divided into its first and latter halves; heavy at the beginning and gradually diminishing for the wicked, while for the virtuous it was small at first and subsequently increases. (Pañcatantra 2.39)
"Therefore, I am well-disposed;
moreover, I shall make you fearless by means of oaths and the like.
He replied, "I have no confidence in your oaths. And it has been said:"
One should not place trust in an enemy, even if he has been bound by oaths;
it is heard that Vṛtra was slain by Śakra after having made a solemn oath.
An enemy cannot be overcome even by the gods without instilling trust;
through trust, the womb of Diti was split open by the Lord of the Thirty-three.
And furthermore: Even one wiser than Bṛhaspati should not place his trust in this;
if he desires his own intelligence, long life, and happiness. (Pancatantra 2.42)
And so it is said:
"Even by entering through a very minute opening, an enemy, having gained the interior, will gradually destroy [his host] afterwards, like a flood of water destroying a boat. (Pañcatantra 2.43)
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place full trust even in the trustworthy;
for danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots.
For one who does not trust is not bound, even if weak, by those who are powerful;
whereas those who trust are quickly bound, even if they are strong, by those who are weak.
The successful policy of Viṣṇugupta, the acquisition of allies by Bhārgava, and Bṛhaspati’s counsel on mistrust—thus policy and alliance are established in three ways. (Pañcatantra 2.46)
And so it is said:
"He who places his trust in enemies, even when they offer a great abundance of wealth, or in wives who are utterly devoid of affection—his life ends with them. (Pañcatantra 2.47)
Having heard that, Laghupatanaka, being at a loss for a reply, reflected: "Aha! What brilliance of intellect he possesses regarding the matter of policy;
or rather, it is simply his partiality toward me out of friendship."
He said: "O Hiraṇyaka!
Wise people say that friendship among the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together;
therefore, since you have attained the status of a friend, listen to these words of mine. (Pancatantra 2.48)
"Even while staying in a fortress, you must always engage in conversation with me—discussions concerning virtues, faults, and refined speech—if you do not trust me at all times.
Having heard this, Hiraṇyaka reflected: "This Laghupatanaka appears to be eloquent and his words are truthful; therefore, it is fitting to form a friendship with him."

However, you must never, under any circumstances, set foot upon my fortress. As it is said: "An enemy, once long ago creeping very slowly with great trepidation, later glides along the ground with ease, like the hand of a lover upon a woman. (Pañcatantra 2.49)
Having heard that, the crow said, "My good friend,
let it be so.
From that time forward, both of them remained enjoying the pleasure of conversations on elegant sayings.
Having rendered service to one another, they passed their time.
Laghupatanaka, out of affection, would bring pieces of meat—pure, remnants of offerings, or other special cooked foods—for the sake of Hiraṇyaka.
Hiraṇyaka, too, having brought rice and other special kinds of food at night for the sake of Laghupatanaka, would offer them to him when he arrived at that time.
Alternatively, this [description] applies to both as well. And it has been said:
"He gives and he receives, he tells secrets and he asks questions;
he eats and he is fed—this is the sixfold characteristic of affection. (Pañca 2.50)
Without some benefit, affection can never arise in anyone toward anyone; for it is by means of granting what has been prayed for that the gods bestow what is desired.
Affection remains in the world only so long as gifts are being given;
when the milk is exhausted, the calf abandons its mother. (Pancavimshati 2.52)
Behold the majesty of giving, which produces immediate conviction;
by its power, even hatred turns into friendship in that very instant.
I consider that gift indeed dearer even than a son, though he be a beast devoid of discernment,
by whom all the milk was given when the rogue was fed.
Behold, the queen, together with her son, gives [alms] constantly! (5.54)

In short: Having established an unbreakable and constant affection, like that between the nail and the flesh, the mouse and the crow indeed attained the state of artificial friendship. (Pancatantra 2.55)
Thus, that mouse, delighted by his kindness, became so full of trust that he entered into the midst of the bird's wings and held conversation with him at all times.

Then, on another day, the crow approached with eyes filled with tears and said to him in a faltering voice: "My dear Hiraṇyaka, a sense of detachment has now arisen in me toward this country; therefore, I shall go elsewhere."
Hiraṇyaka said, "My good friend, what is the cause of your detachment?
He replied, "My good friend, listen.
In this region, a famine has arisen due to a great drought."
Due to the famine, people are so afflicted by hunger that no one offers even a mere morsel of food as an offering.
Furthermore, in every house, hungry folk have prepared snares for the purpose of catching birds.
As for me, having been caught in a snare due to the remainder of my lifespan, I have now been rescued.
"This is the cause of my detachment; therefore, I shed tears because I have set out for a foreign land. Hiraṇyaka said, "Where, then, are you going?"
He said, "In the southern region, in the midst of a dense forest, there is a great lake.
There dwells a tortoise named Mantharaka, who is a supreme friend even dearer to me than you;
he will give me pieces of fish-flesh."
By eating that, I shall enjoy the pleasure of conversing with him on elegant sayings and pass my time in happiness;
I do not wish to see the destruction of birds here through the binding of snares. And it is said:
"When the land is struck by drought and the crops have gone to ruin..."
Blessed, O dear one, are those who do not witness the ruin of their country or the destruction of their lineage.
What is too heavy for the capable? What is distant for the industrious? What is a foreign land for those possessed of knowledge? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? (Pancatantra 2.57)
Scholarship and kingship are never equal;
a king is honored in his own country, but a scholar is honored everywhere.
Hiraṇyaka said, "If that is so, then I too shall go with you;
I also suffer great distress.
The crow said, "O sir!"
"What is your sorrow? Tell me.
Hiraṇyaka said, "O sir!"
"There is much to be said on this matter;
having gone there myself, I shall explain everything in full detail.
The crow replied, "As for me, I am one who travels through the sky."
"So how can I go with you? He replied, "If you would save my life, then mount me upon your back and carry me there; otherwise, I have no means of going."
Hearing this, the crow said with joy: "If that is so, then I am blessed that I may spend my time there together with you.
I know these various modes of flight, such as the *sampāta* and others;
therefore, mount upon my back."
"By which means of happiness shall I cause you to reach that lake?
Hiraṇyaka said, "I wish to hear the names of those who have flown away.
He replied:
Sampāta, viprapāta, mahāpāta, nipātana, vakra, tiryak, and likewise ūrdhva; the eighth is known as laghu.
Hearing that, Hiraṇyaka ascended upon him at that very moment. He too, taking him up very slowly, set out by flying into the air and in due course reached that lake.
Then, seeing Laghupatanaka mounted by the mouse, Mantharaka—knowing well the requirements of place and time—realized from afar that this was no ordinary crow, and quickly plunged into the water.
Laghupatanaka, too, having left Hiraṇyaka in a hollow of a tree standing on the bank and climbed to the tip of a branch, spoke in a loud voice: "O Mantharaka! Come, come!
I am your friend, the crow named Laghupatanaka; I have arrived after a long time, full of longing."
Therefore, come and embrace me. And it is said:
"What need is there for sandalwood with camphor, or for cool snows?
All of these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the body of a friend. (Pañcaviṃśati 2.60)
And so it is said:
"By whom was this nectar created—the two syllables 'Mitra' (friend)—the protection against calamities and the medicine for the fever of grief? (Pañcatantra 2.61).

Having heard that and recognized him more clearly, Mantharaka quickly emerged from the water; with his body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of joy, he said: "Come, come, friend!
Embrace me!
After a long time, you were not properly recognized by me."
Therefore, I entered into the water. And it was said:
"One should not form an association with one whose prowess, lineage, and conduct are unknown," so declared Bṛhaspati. (Pañcatantra 2.62)
When this was said, Laghupatanaka descended from the tree and embraced him.
Or rather, it is well said:
"What is the use of streams of nectar that can only serve to wash the body?"
This embrace of a long-lost friend is something that cannot be priced.
Thus, both of them, having embraced one another with their bodies covered in horripilation, sat down beneath the tree and related the accounts of their own adventures.
Hiraṇyaka, too, having offered his salutations to Mantharaka, sat down near the crow.
Then, observing him, Mantharaka said to Laghupatanaka: "O friend, this is a mouse named Hiraṇyaka."
He is like a second life to me, as dear as my own friend.
So what need is there for many words?
He is like the showers of rain from a cloud, or like the stars in the sky.
Just as grains of sand and dust are beyond the reach of calculation.
Just as the qualities are devoid of number, so it is with this Great-Souled One;
having attained supreme world-weariness, he has come into your presence.
Mantharaka asked, "What is the cause of his world-weariness?
The crow replied, "I questioned him, but this was what he said:"
"As for what must be said at length,
I shall explain it once I have gone there;
it was not even reported to me."
"Therefore, my dear Hiraṇyaka,
let the cause of your own world-weariness now be explained to both of us.
He replied:
Story 1: The Story of Hiraṇyaka and Tāmracūḍa.
There is a city named Mahilāropya in the southern region.
Not far from that place was a monastery dedicated to the Blessed Lord Mahādeva,
where a wandering mendicant named Tāmracūḍa resided.
Having gone about the city for alms, he sustained his life by means of that food.
Having placed the remains of his alms-food right there in that same alms-bowl and hanging that bowl on a peg, he later sleeps during the night.
At dawn, having given that food to the laborers, he properly orders the sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and decorating of that very temple.
On another day, my kinsmen informed me: "Master," [they said].
"In the monastery, cooked food, out of fear of mice, is always kept right there in an alms-bowl, suspended on a peg.
We are unable to eat it;
moreover, when our master returns, there is nothing left."
"So what is the use of wandering elsewhere? Having gone there today, let us eat as we please through your favor.
Hearing this, I was immediately surrounded by my entire troop and went there at that very moment.
Having flown up, I alighted upon that alms-bowl;
there, having given various kinds of food to my attendants, I myself ate afterwards.
When everyone was satisfied, I returned once more to my own home.
In this way, I constantly eat that food,
while the wandering mendicant also protects it to the best of his ability;
however, whenever he is interrupted by sleep, [I take it].
Then, having climbed up there, I shall perform my own task.
Now, at one time, he made a great effort for the sake of protecting me;
he brought a withered bamboo pole.
Therefore, even while asleep, he strikes my alms-bowl out of fear of me;
and I too, though no food has been offered, withdraw out of fear of being struck. Thus, as I remain intent on conflict with him throughout the entire night, the time passes by.

Then, on another day, a wandering mendicant named Bṛhatsphiṅ, a friend of his who had arrived as a traveler on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, came to his monastery. Upon seeing him, [the host] honored him with the ritual of rising to greet him and engaged him in the hospitable rites due to a guest. Then, at night, both lay down to sleep upon a single bed of *kuśa* grass and began to tell religious discourses.

Then, during conversations and assemblies concerning large buttocks, that Tāmracūḍa, his mind distracted by the fear of the mouse, struck his alms-bowl with a worn bamboo stick and gave him a vacant reply; absorbed in that thought,
he did not say anything at all.
Then that guest, having fallen into a state of great anger, said to him: "O Tāmracūḍa!
You have not been properly recognized as a friend;
therefore, you do not converse with me joyfully."

Therefore, even during that night, I shall leave your monastery and go elsewhere to sleep. And it is said: "Come, come! Sit down upon this seat; why have you been seen after such a long time? What news do you bring? You are very weak; is all well? I am delighted by the sight of you.
Those who thus address their friends with respect when they arrive—it is proper for them always to go to their mansions with an unhesitating mind. (Pañcatantra 2.66)
When a householder, seeing someone arrive, looks toward the directions or even downward,
those who enter his home are bulls devoid of horns.
Where there is no act of rising to greet others, no sweet-syllabled conversation,
and no discussion of virtues or faults— there one should not go, even if it be a palace.
Thus, you have become arrogant merely by obtaining a single monastery;
you have abandoned affection for your friends. You do not realize that, under the pretext of taking refuge in a monastery, you have earned rebirth in hell. And it is said:
If your mind is set on hell, then perform the duties of a royal priest; for one year, what need is there for anything else? Attend to the affairs of the monastery for just three days.
"That is your face; you, who have become arrogant, ought to be grieved for.
Therefore, I shall abandon your monastery and depart.
Then, having heard this, Tāmracūḍa, his mind terrified with fear, said to him: "O Blessed One!"
Do not speak thus;
there is no other friend of mine equal to you.
However, hear the reason for this slackening of our conversation.
This wicked mouse, having leaped up, climbs even onto the alms-bowl placed in a high position and eats the remnants of the alms remaining there.
Because of its absence, even the act of sweeping in the monastery does not take place. That mouse—
"I strike him again and again;
there is no other reason.
Behold this further marvel of that wicked-souled one: even cats, monkeys, and the like are put to flight by his leaping."
Bṛhatsphiga said, "Now it is known that his burrow is in a certain location.
Tāmracūḍa said, "Venerable sir, I do not know precisely.
He replied, "Surely his burrow is upon a treasure-trove."
One exults through the heat of a treasure-store. And it is said:
"Even the mere warmth arising from wealth brings an increase of vitality to embodied beings;
how much more so its actual enjoyment when it is accompanied by the virtue of renunciation! (Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 2.70)
And so it is said:
"O Mother, Śāṇḍilī does not sell sesame seeds for sesame seeds without a reason;
since they are different from those that were plucked out, there must be a cause for this. (Pañca 2.71)
Tāmracūḍa asked, "How was that?
He replied—
The Second Story.
The Story of the Sale of Sesame Flour:

Once, during the rainy season, I requested a certain Brahmin for lodging at a particular place so that I might observe a religious vow. Thereupon, having been served by him according to his word, I remained there happily, devoted to the worship of the gods.
Then, on another day at dawn, having woken up, I listened with close attention to a conversation between a Brahmin and his wife.
Therein, the Brahmin said: "O Brahmin lady, at dawn tomorrow the sun will enter its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana-saṅkrānti), which yields infinite fruit for gifts."
"Therefore, I shall go to another village for the purpose of receiving alms.
You must give some food to a certain Brahmin on behalf of the Blessed One Sūrya.
Then, having heard this, the Brahmin woman, reviling him with even harsher words, said: "How can you, who are stricken by poverty, obtain food?"
Why then do you feel shame in speaking thus? Moreover, while clinging to your hand, I have never found any pleasure, nor have I tasted any sweet food.
Nor [should there be] ornaments for the hands, feet, neck, and so forth.
Having heard that, the Brahmin, though terrified with fear, spoke very slowly: "O Brahmin lady, it is not proper to say this. And it has been said:
Why is even half of that portion not given to those who seek it?
When will anyone possess wealth sufficient to satisfy their every desire?
It is not heard in the scriptures that a poor man should obtain, with a mere cowrie shell, that same fruit which the lords indeed obtain through abundant giving.
A giver, though small, is worthy of service, whereas a miser, though great in wealth, is not;
a well with sweet water within brings joy to the world, but not the ocean.
And so it is said:
"What is the use of the title 'King of Kings' for those whose greatness lies in not having renounced anything?
The wise do not honor Maheśvara as the protector of treasures. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.75)
Moreover:
A lordly elephant is indeed praiseworthy when its body is constantly worn down by giving; for a donkey, even if its limbs are stout, is surely contemptible if it does not give.
Even one who is well-behaved and of good conduct sinks downward due to a lack of giving, like a water-jar;
whereas even a hunchback or a one-eyed woman rises upward through giving, like a karkaṭī fruit.
Even a cloud, by bestowing water, becomes beloved to all the world;
whereas the sun, though its rays are constantly extended, cannot even be looked upon.
Knowing this, even those overcome by poverty should give, however small or even smaller, at the proper time and to a worthy recipient. And it has been said:
"When a worthy recipient, great faith, and the appropriate place and time are present, that which is given by those who possess discernment conduces to infinity. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.79)
And so it is said:
"One should not practice excessive craving, yet one should not abandon craving entirely;
for one who is overwhelmed by excessive craving, a crest-jewel remains upon the head. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.80)
The Brahmin woman asked, "How was that?
He said—
Story 3.
The Story of the Śabara and the Boar:
In a certain forest region there was a certain Pulinda;
he set out toward the woods to practice the hunt.
Then, as he was moving forward, he encountered a great boar shaped like the peak of a mountain of black collyrium.
Upon seeing it, he struck it with a sharp arrow drawn back to his ear.
The boar, its mind possessed by rage, tore open the hunter's belly with its tusk, which shone with the luster of the crescent moon; thus, the Pulinda fell lifeless upon the earth.
Then, having killed the hunter, the boar also passed away due to the pain of the arrow-wound.
In the meantime, a certain jackal whose death was imminent, wandering here and there afflicted by hunger, arrived at that place.
As soon as he saw both the boar and the hunter, he was overjoyed and thought: "O!..."
Favorable is destiny for me;
therefore, even this food has presented itself unexpectedly.
Or rather, it is well said:
Even when no effort is made by men, the fruit— whether auspicious or inauspicious— produced in another birth comes to them, ordained by destiny.
And so it is said:

"In whatever place and at whatever time, and by whatever age, whatever action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—was performed, that is experienced by that very person in that same manner. (Pañca 2.82)
Therefore, I shall eat in such a way that my sustenance lasts for many days;
first, I will eat this sinew-tether attached to the tip of the bow. And it has been said:
"One's own earned wealth should be consumed very gradually."
It should never be treated with levity by the wise, as if it were a mere elixir.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he thrust the tip of the bow into his mouth and proceeded to eat the sinew.
Then, as the noose snapped, the tip of the bow pierced through the region of his palate and emerged from the middle of his head;
he too, in that very instant, died by this means.
Therefore I say: "Excessive craving should not be indulged in.
He spoke again: "O Brāhmaṇī, have you not heard this?"
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even the manner of death—
these five are indeed created for the embodied being while still residing in the womb.
Then, having been thus awakened by him, the brahmin woman said: "If it is so, there is a small heap of sesame seeds in my house;
therefore, having crushed the sesame seeds, I shall feed the brahmin with sesame powder.
Having heard those words, the brahmin went to the village.
She, too, having crushed the sesame seeds with warm water and kneaded them, placed them in the heat of the sun.
In the meantime, while she was occupied with her household chores, a certain dog made a voiding of urine amidst the sesame seeds.
Seeing this, she thought: "Oh, behold the ingenuity of Fate, which has turned its back!"
"Since these sesame seeds have been rendered unfit for consumption,
I shall take them and go to someone's house to exchange those that have been plucked out for those that have not.
By this method, everyone will give [me their seeds]."
Then, in the house where I had entered for the sake of alms, she too entered with sesame seeds to sell them. She said: "Let someone take the shelled sesame seeds for the unshelled ones.
Now, as soon as she entered that householder's house and began taking the shelled for the unshelled, her son, having studied the *Kāmandakī-śāstra*, exclaimed: "Mother!"
"These sesame seeds are indeed ungraspable;
one cannot grasp those that have been plucked by means of those not yet plucked.
There must be some underlying cause."
Therefore, she gives those who have plucked out their hair in exchange for those whose hair has already been plucked.
Having heard that, those sesame seeds were abandoned by Ayā. Thus I say: "Not without cause, O mother of Śāṇḍilī."
Having said this, he spoke further: "Now, is his path of movement known?
Tāmracūḍa replied, "Venerable sir, it is known;
for he does not come alone."
However, surrounded by an incalculable multitude of followers, he was seen by me wandering here and there, coming and going together with all the people.
A visitor asked, "Is there any small shovel?
He replied, "Certainly, there is."
"This is a ring made of all kinds of metals, fastened on my own hand.
The guest said, "In that case, you must stay with me at dawn,
so that we both may follow his tracks upon the ground defiled by the feet of the people."
Having heard those words, I too thought: "Alas, I am ruined, for his words are heard to be full of intent.
Surely, just as he has discovered the treasure, he will also discover our fortress."
It is known precisely from this intention. And it has been said:
"Even by seeing a man but once, the wise understand his essential worth;
even with the balance of their hands, the skilled discern the weight in palas. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.85)
Desire itself indicates beforehand the future—
whether auspicious or inauspicious— that is born of another body for men;
this is known even from an infant who has not yet developed the marks of his [future] lineage.
The peacock, moving away from those who had come forward to meet him, remained straightforward.

Then, my mind terrified with fear, I and my retinue abandoned the difficult path and set out to travel by another way. As I was proceeding ahead with my attendants, a large-bodied cat suddenly appeared before us;
seeing the troop of mice, it leapt up into their midst.
Then those mice, seeing me treading upon a wrong path, reproached me; and the survivors, having drenched the earth with blood, entered that very same fortress.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Having cut the snare, cast off the trap, and forcibly broken through the net..."

Having emerged from the forest far away, his body matted with a mass of flames from the surrounding fire, the deer sprang up and ran with speed even beyond the range of the hunters' arrows; yet, having fallen into the middle of a well, what can human effort achieve when fate is adverse? (Pancatantra 2.87)
Then I went elsewhere alone;
the rest, out of folly, entered that very same fortress.
In the meantime, that wicked wandering mendicant, seeing the ground smeared with drops of blood, arrived and stood there by way of that same fortress path.
That a mortal is always full of energy and overcomes other people, and that he speaks words with arrogance—all that is the power born of wealth. (Pañcatantra 2.88)
Then, having heard that, I was overcome with anger and leaped up specifically toward my alms-bowl; before I could reach it, I fell to the ground.
Hearing this, my enemy laughed and said to Tāmracūḍa:
"O, look, look at this wonder! And he said:
Everyone is powerful through wealth; he who is endowed with wealth is wise.
Behold this mouse, who, though born of the same species, is considered equal [to us] despite being useless.
Therefore, sleep soundly, free from fear;
that which was the cause of its flight has now fallen into our hands.
Or rather, it is well said:
Just as a snake deprived of its fangs or an elephant devoid of its rut,
