so too a man bereft of wealth here is merely a bearer of a name.
Having heard that, I reflected in my mind: "Since there is not even the power to leap a mere finger's breadth, fie upon the life of a man devoid of wealth! And it is said:
"For a man of small intelligence who is bereft of wealth..."
All activities are cut off, like small streams in the summer heat.
Just as "crow-barley" is called, or as "wild sesame" is spoken of—being merely names and not actualities—so too are men devoid of wealth. (Pancatanttra 2.92)
For even the virtues of others do not shine for a poor man;
prosperity is the illuminator of virtues among living beings, like the sun.
In this world, a person who is poor by nature is not so greatly afflicted as one who, having acquired wealth, remains in misery when deprived of it. (Pancavimshati 2.94)
Better is the birth of even a tree that is withered, hollowed by insects, scorched on all sides by fire, and situated in barren soil, than that of one who is a seeker of worldly gain.
For poverty, being devoid of power, is everywhere to be suspected;
indeed, even when one has arrived to offer assistance, a person leaves a pauper behind and departs.
Rising again and again only to fall back down right there, the desires of the poor fall futilely upon their hearts, like the breasts of a widow.
Even though the day has clearly dawned, he who is perpetually shrouded by the darkness of poverty is not seen by anyone here, despite being present right before them, even with effort.
Having lamented thus, my enthusiasm broken, I saw that treasure used as a pillow and returned to my own fortress at dawn.
Then, as my servants were departing in the morning, they whispered among themselves, "Oh,
he is incapable of filling our bellies!"
There are only calamities, such as those from cats and the like, for those who cling to his back; so what is the use of propitiating him? And it has been said:
A master from whom no gains are obtained and from whom there are only calamities—such a master should be abandoned from afar, especially by his dependents. (Pañcatantra 2.99)
Having heard their words in this manner, I entered my own fortress. While no one approached me face-to-face, I thought: "Fie upon this poverty!
Or rather, it is well said:
A poor man is as if dead; sexual union without offspring is as if dead;
a funeral rite performed by one ignorant of the Vedas is as if dead; and a sacrifice without a priestly fee is as if dead. (Pañcatantra 2.100)
People who are high-born but destitute of wealth cause great distress to the minds of others through hundreds of their mere desires, just like widows, despite their noble lineage. (Pancatantra 2.101)
Poverty is a suffering for embodied beings that causes supreme humiliation;
because of it, people consider themselves as if dead even while they are alive. (Pañca 2.102)
He becomes a vessel for wretchedness, the ultimate state of humiliation, a constant refuge for calamities, and is defiled by misfortune. (Pancatikā 2.103)
Relatives feel ashamed of him and conceal their connection to him;
even friends turn into enemies for one who possesses no coins. (Pancatantra 2.104)
This poverty is indeed the personified lightness of misfortunes; it is the abode of calamities and the very synonym for death for embodied beings. (Pancatantra 2.105)
Like the dust of a goat avoided by those who are frightened, like the dust from a broom by people,
or like the shadow cast by a lamp-stand, a person without wealth is shunned.
There may be some use for clay in certain circumstances even after it has been used for purification;
however, there is no use at all for a person who is destitute.
Even a poor man who desires to give, when he arrives at the house of the wealthy, is thought of as a beggar; alas, what a curse is poverty for embodied beings! (Pañca 2.108)
For the ancestors do not accept even the handful of water offered by that man who, seeing his own wealth being seized, protects only his life. (Pancaka 2.109)
And likewise:
"For one who gives up his life in battle for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, or for the sake of protecting a woman or wealth, eternal worlds are attained. (Pañcatantra 2.110)
Having thus resolved, I went there at night and made a hole in the chest while he was under the influence of sleep; meanwhile, the wicked ascetic woke up,
and I somehow escaped with my life after being struck on the head with a splintered bamboo staff.
Nor is he dead; and it has been said:
"A man obtains the wealth that is destined to be obtained;
even a god is not able to bypass it."
Therefore, I do not grieve, nor do I feel astonishment;
for that which is ours does not indeed belong to others.
The crow and the tortoise ask: "How was that?
Hiraṇyaka says: Story 4.
The Story of Sāgaradatta:
In a certain city, there was a merchant named Sāgaradatta. His son purchased a book being sold for a hundred coins.
And it is written therein:
"A human being obtains the wealth that is to be obtained;
even a god is not able to thwart it."
Therefore, I do not grieve, nor is there any wonder for me,
for that which is mine does not indeed belong to others.
Having seen that, Sāgaradatta asked his son: "Son, for what price was this book purchased? He replied: "For a hundred rūpakas."
Having heard that, Sāgaradatta said: "Shame on you, fool!
Since you accept a single written verse for a hundred rūpakas, how will you acquire wealth with such an intellect?"
"Therefore, from this day forward, you must not enter my house.
Having been thus rebuked, he was expelled from the home. Out of despondency, he went to a distant foreign land and, having reached a certain city, settled there.
Then, after a few days, he was asked by a certain resident of that city: "From where have you come? What is your name?
He replied: "A man obtains whatever is destined to be obtained."
Then, when questioned by another person as well, he gave the same answer.
Thus, because he had attained his desired object in the midst of that city, the name "Prasiddha" (Renowned) became established for him.
Now, the king’s daughter named Candravatī, endowed with fresh beauty and youth, was looking about the city on a certain day of great festival, accompanied by a female friend.

And at that very place, a certain prince, endowed with exceeding beauty and charming, somehow came within the range of her vision. At the very moment she saw him, struck by the arrows of the flower-bowed god, she said to her own friend: "Friend, you must strive today so that there may indeed be a union with him."
Having heard this, the friend went quickly to her presence and said: "I have been sent to you by Candravatī.
She has spoken thus regarding you: 'By the sight of you, my heart has been brought to its final state by the god of love.
Therefore, if you do not come to me very soon, then death shall be my only refuge.'"
Having heard this, he said: "If I must certainly go there, then tell me by what means I am to enter?
Then his friend replied: "At night, you should climb up there by means of a strong rope suspended from the palace."
He said, "If this is your firm resolve, then I shall do exactly that.
Having made this decision, the friend went into the presence of Candravatī.
Then, when night had fallen, the prince thought to himself, "Alas, this is a great misdeed! And it is said:
In this world, they call that man a slayer of a Brahmin who approaches the daughter of his guru, the wife of a friend, or the wife of his master’s servant. (Pañcatantra 2.112)
Furthermore:
One should not perform that action by which ill-repute is gained, by which one falls into a lower rebirth, or by which one is deprived of one's own welfare. (5.113)
Having reflected thus correctly, he did not go into his presence.
Then Prāptavyamartha, while wandering about, saw a rope suspended at night near the Dhavalagṛha; with a heart filled with curiosity, he grasped it and climbed up.
And that princess, her mind reassured by the thought, "This is indeed he," [attended to him] with bathing, food, drink, clothing, and other necessities.

Having honored him, she reclined upon the bed with him; her body bristling with horripilation from the thrill born of the touch of his limbs, she said: "I have surrendered this self of mine, for I am enamored by the mere sight of you.
No other than you shall be my husband, even in my thoughts."
"Why do you not speak with her?
He replied: "A man obtains whatever wealth is destined to be obtained.
When this was said by her, thinking, "This is someone else," he was cast out from the white house and released.
But that *daṇḍapāśaka* arrived;
meanwhile, he went to the household of Khaṇḍadeva and fell asleep.
Then, while he was there with an appointment made by a certain unchaste woman, the *daṇḍapāśaka* arrived.
Just then, he saw someone who had previously been asleep and, for the sake of guarding his secret, addressed him: "Who are you? He replied: "A man obtains whatever is destined to be obtained.
Having heard this, the staff-bearer said: "This temple is empty."
"Therefore, go to my place here and sleep. Having agreed to this, Mati, due to his confusion, slept on another's bed.
Now, that protector’s daughter, named Vinayavatī—endowed with beauty and youth and infatuated with a certain man—had given him a rendezvous and was sleeping there upon that very bed.

Then, seeing him arrive, she thought, "This is indeed my beloved," and being deluded by the thick darkness of night, she rose up, had food and clothing provided, and married herself to him by the Gāndharva rite.
Resting upon the bed with him, her lotus-face blossoming with joy, she said to him: "Why do you still not speak with me with confidence?"
He said, "A man obtains whatever wealth is destined to be obtained.
Having heard this, she thought, "Such is the ripening of the fruit for that action which is performed without due reflection.
Reflecting thus, she sent him away with sorrow.
As he was proceeding along the street, a bride named Varakīrti, a resident of another district, arrived with a great sound of musical instruments.
Prāptavyamartha also began to go along with them.

Then, as the auspicious moment for the wedding approached, there stood at the gate of a merchant’s house near the royal road a merchant’s daughter, dressed in garments adorned with festive and auspicious decorations, upon a platform erected within a pavilion.
Intoxicated by rut, he killed the elephant-driver and reached that very spot, throwing the world into confusion with the clamor of fleeing people.
Upon seeing him, all the bridegroom’s followers fled along with the groom and scattered in every direction.
Then, at this moment, perceiving the maiden alone and her eyes trembling with fear, [he said]: "Do not be afraid!"

Having steadied himself with great courage, thinking "I am my own protector," and grasping the elephant's right trunk, he—possessing the audacity of one who has attained his goal through human resolve—rebuked the elephant.

Then, by a stroke of fate, when the elephant had somehow retreated, Varakīrti arrived with his friends and kinsmen at the very moment the auspicious hour had passed; seeing that the maiden had already gone into another's hands, he said:
"O sir, you have acted contrary to what is right, in that having promised her to me, you have given the maiden to another!"
He said, "O friend, I too fled out of fear of the elephant and have come here with you; I did not know what had happened. Having spoken thus, he began to question his daughter:
"My child, you have not done well."
"Tell me then, what is this story?
He replied, "Since I have been saved from the danger to my life by him,
no one else shall take my hand while I am alive, except for him."
By means of this exchange of news, the night passed away.
Then, in the morning, when a great crowd had gathered there, the princess arrived at that spot upon hearing the news.
Having heard it through the succession of whispers, the daughter of the police officer also came to that very place.

Then, having heard of that great assembly of people, the king also came to that very place. Addressing the matter that was to be accomplished, he said: "O sir, speak with confidence; what kind of news is this?"
Then he said, "A man obtains that which is destined to be obtained.
The princess, having reflected, said, "Even a god is not able to bypass that.
Then the daughter of the police officer said, "Therefore, I do not grieve, nor is there any wonder for me."

Having heard that entire account of the world's affairs, the merchant’s daughter said, "What belongs to us does not indeed belong to others. Then, having granted the boon of safety and learned each individual's story, the king— having understood the truth— respectfully gave his own daughter, along with a thousand villages and accompanied by all her ornaments and retinue, to him for the wealth he had obtained.
Having declared, "You are my son," he publicly proclaimed this throughout the city and consecrated him as the crown prince.
Daṇḍapāśaka also, honoring his own daughter according to his means with gifts of clothing and other items, gave her to Prāptavyamartha for the sake of their union.
Then Prāptavyamartha also brought his own father and mother, surrounded by their entire family, into that city with great honor.
Then he too, enjoying various pleasures together with his own kinsmen, remained in a state of happiness.
Therefore I say: "A man obtains the wealth that is destined to be obtained.
Having experienced all this pleasure and pain, he fell into great despondency and was brought into your presence by this friend.
"This, then, is the cause of my detachment.

Mantharaka said, "My good friend, he is undoubtedly a true friend who, though emaciated by hunger, carries you— who have become his enemy— on his back as if you were food, and does not devour you even on the way."
And as it has been said:
"The mind of one whose wealth never undergoes change at any time shall be a friend at all times; therefore, one should cultivate such an excellent friend. (Pañca 2.114)
In this matter, the wise have declared that the testing of friends by these signs is undoubtedly performed by the learned, just as the examination of a sacrificial fire is done by experts. (2.115)
And so it is said:
"When a time of calamity has arrived, he alone is a true friend;
but when a time of prosperity has arrived, even a wicked person may become a friend. (Pañca 2.116)
Therefore, even in me, confidence has now arisen regarding this matter, since this friendship between water-dwellers and flesh-eating crows is contrary to political wisdom.
Or rather, it is well said:
"No one is anyone's friend, nor is anyone an eternal enemy."
An enemy is recognized by the ruin of a task that was once accomplished through a friend's assistance.
"Welcome to you!
Please stay here on this lake-shore as if it were your own home.
You should not feel any distress regarding the loss of wealth and residence in a foreign land that has occurred in that country. And it is said:"
The shadow of a cloud, the friendship of the wicked, the earth at the edge of the ocean, youth, and wealth—all these perish in an instant. (Pañcatantra 2.118)
For this very reason, those who possess discernment and have conquered their own minds do not harbor desire for wealth. And it has been said:
"Though well-accumulated, well-guarded like one's own life, and never parted from even one's own body,"
Even for a man departing for the realm of Yama, these cruel riches do not grant him even five steps.
And furthermore:
Just as meat is devoured by fish in the water, by beasts of prey on the earth, and by birds in the sky, so too is the man of wealth preyed upon everywhere. (Pancatantra 2.120)
O wealthy one, a king may charge even the faultless with faults;
yet one who is destitute, though he has incurred faults, remains free from harassment everywhere. (Pañca 2.121)
The acquisition, increase, and protection of wealth must be undertaken;
for even Mount Sumeru diminishes if it is consumed without being replenished. (Pancatantira 2.122)
If this foolish person, seeking wealth, were to endure even a hundredth part of the hardships he endures for the sake of liberation, he would attain liberation. (Pancatikā 2.123)
What is considered one's own territory or what is considered a foreign land for a wise and resolute man?
Whatever country he takes refuge in, he makes that very place his own through the prowess of his arms—
just as a lion plunges into the forest with his fangs, claws, and tail as his weapons.
With the very blood of the slain lordly elephants, he cuts off his own thirst for it. (Pancavimśati 2.124)
One who is devoid of wealth, even when gone to a foreign land, does not come to grief in any way if he possesses wisdom. And it has been said:
"What is too heavy for the capable? What is too far for the resolute? What is a foreign land for the well-skilled? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? (Pañca 2.125)
Therefore, you are a treasury of wisdom and are not equal to an ordinary man. Or rather:

Fortune herself desires to dwell with one who is endowed with energy, who is not dilatory, who knows the proper method of action, who is unattached to vices, who is brave, grateful, and firm in friendship. (Pañcatantra 2.126)
Furthermore, even wealth that has been acquired perishes through the force of past karma;
thus, for all these days it was yours,
yet not even for a moment can it be enjoyed as something that does not belong to you.
Even that which comes to one of its own accord is taken away by fate;
having acquired wealth, an unfortunate man does not enjoy it, just as the fool Somilaka did after reaching the great forest. (Pancatantra 2.127)
Hiraṇyaka said, "How was that?
He replied—
Story 5.
The Story of Somilaka:
In a certain town there lived a weaver named Somilaka.
He constantly produced garments suitable for kings, dyed with various patterns of woven silk.

However, although he was skilled in the manufacture of many kinds of fine fabrics, he could not by any means acquire even enough wealth for food and clothing. Now, there were other ordinary weavers there who were experts in producing coarse cloth and possessed great prosperity.
Seeing them, he said to his wife: "My dear," he said.
"Behold these coarse-cloth weavers, so prosperous with wealth and gold! Therefore, this place is not for me to remain in; I shall go elsewhere to acquire wealth."
She said: "O beloved, this is a false lamentation, that wealth belongs to those who have gone elsewhere, but not to one in one's own place. And it is said:"
Even when birds fly up into the sky or descend upon the surface of the earth, that which is not given does not come to them by their mere reaching. (5.128)
And so it is said:
"That which is not to be brought into being does not come into being, yet that which is to be brought into being comes into being even without effort."
But for one whose destiny is not to be, even that which has come into the palm of their hand perishes.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does previously committed karma follow after its doer.
It lies down together with that which lies down; it follows him as he goes.
The past karma of men, however, remains together with the self.
Just as shadow and sunlight are always closely connected to one another,
so too are action and the agent joined together with each other.
The Kaulika said: "My dear, you have not spoken correctly. Without resolve, action does not bear fruit. And it has been said:"
Just as a clap cannot be produced with only one hand,
so it is taught that no fruit results from an action devoid of effort.
Behold how, by the power of karma, even food obtained at the time of eating cannot enter the mouth in any way without the raising of the hands. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 2.134)
And so it is said:
Fortune approaches the industrious lion among men; "it is to be given by fate," say the cowards.
Overcoming fate, exercise human effort through your own power; if success is not achieved despite the exertion, what fault is there in that?
And so it is said:
"For undertakings are accomplished through exertion, not by mere wishes;
indeed, deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion."
"O King, without effort, one's desires are not fulfilled; those who speak thus are cowards. Whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass. (Pañca 2.137)
If an action performed with one's own power does not yield success,
the person in that case— whose human effort has been thwarted by destiny— is not to be blamed.

Having resolved, "Therefore, I must certainly go to another land," he went to the city of Vardhamāna; staying there for three years, he acquired three hundred gold pieces and set out once more for his own home.
Then, while he was traveling on the road, as he was wandering through a forest, the blessed sun reached its setting.
There, out of fear of wild beasts, he climbed onto the thick trunk of a banyan tree and remained fast asleep. Then, at midnight, he heard two men of fierce appearance conversing with one another.
One of them said: "O Karta! Do you not know perfectly well that this Somilaka possesses no wealth beyond his food and clothing?
Why then have you given him three hundred gold pieces?"
He said, "O Kārman, I must certainly give to those who are industrious; however, its final outcome in that matter depends upon you.
Then, as soon as that weaver woke up and looked at the bundle of gold, he saw it was empty.
Thereupon, he reflected with indignation:
"Alas, what is this?
Wealth acquired with great hardship has vanished somewhere in an instant! Now, my labor rendered futile and myself destitute, how shall I show my face to my wife and my friends?"
Having thus resolved, he went to that very city.
There, having earned five hundred gold pieces in barely a year, he set out once more toward his own home.

When he was halfway there, having entered the forest again, the blessed sun went to its setting; then, out of fear of losing his gold, though utterly exhausted, he did not rest, feeling only a longing for home.
He was walking quickly.
In the meantime, he heard two men of that same appearance approaching within his field of vision, conversing with one another;
there, one of them said: "O Creator!"
"Did you give him five hundred pieces of gold?
Do you not know that he has nothing more than food and clothing?
He replied, "O Karma!"
I must certainly give to those who are industrious;
the outcome of that, however, depends on you.
So why do you reproach me?
Having heard that, as soon as Somilaka examined the knot, he found no gold.
Thereupon, overcome by grief, he thought: "Alas! What is the use of life for me, destitute of wealth?
Therefore, having hanged myself from this banyan tree, I shall give up my life."

Having thus resolved, Somilaka prepared a rope of darbha grass, placed a noose around his neck, and tied himself to a branch; just as he was about to throw himself down, a man standing in the air said this: "O Somilaka!
Do not commit such a rash act!"
"I am the robber of your wealth; I will not tolerate even a single cowrie beyond what you have for food and clothing.
Therefore, go back to your own home.
Furthermore, I am pleased by your audacity."
"Thus, my meeting with you would not be in vain;
therefore, let some desired boon be requested.
Somilaka said, "If that is so, then give me abundant wealth."
He said: "O sir, what will you do with wealth that is devoid of enjoyment, since you do not even obtain more than food and clothing? And it is said:
'What is the use of that fortune which, like a bride, belongs to one man alone; it is not like a courtesan, who is enjoyed by travelers as common property? (Pañcatantra 2.139)"
Somilaka said: "Even if there is no enjoyment [from it], let there still be wealth for me. And it is said:
Even if he is miserly and of low birth, that man is always served by those dependent on him in this world, provided he possesses an accumulation of wealth. (Pañca 2.140)
And so it was:
"O blessed lady, for fifteen years I have watched them as they fell, sometimes loose and sometimes well-fastened, yet never falling."
The man asked: "What is this? He replied: "A story. (6)
The Story of the Sharp-Horned Jackal:
In a certain locality there lived a great bull named Tīkṣṇaviṣāṇa (Sharp-Horn).
Out of excessive pride, he had abandoned his own herd and became a forest-dweller, tearing up the riverbanks with his two horns and eating at will the grass that resembled emeralds.
Now, in that very forest, there lived a jackal named Pralobhaka.
Once, he was sitting comfortably on the bank of a river together with his wife.
In the meantime, a sharp-horned animal descended onto that same sandbank for the sake of water.
Then, seeing his testicles hanging down, the jackal was addressed by the female jackal:
"Master, look at these two lumps of flesh belonging to this bull, hanging down as they are;
in a moment or perhaps within an hour, they will fall."
"Knowing this, you must act as one who follows behind.
The jackal said, "My dear,
it is not known whether these two will ever fall or not."
So why do you employ me for a futile labor?
Staying right here, I shall devour the mice that come for water along with you,
since this is their path.
Moreover, if I leave you and go upon the back of this bull with its sharp horns, then someone else will come and take possession of this place;
it is not right to do this. And it has been said:
"He who abandons what is certain and pursues what is uncertain..."
His stable things perish, and that which is unstable is already lost.
The female jackal said: "O you coward, you find satisfaction even with whatever little you have obtained. And it is said:
A small stream is easily filled; the paws of a mouse are easily filled;
likewise, a coward is easily satisfied, for he finds contentment even with very little. (Pañcatantra 2.143)
Therefore, a person should always be possessed of enthusiasm. And it has been said:

"Where there is the undertaking of effort, where there is the restraint of laziness, and where there is the union of policy and valor, there prosperity is certainly and immovably established. (Pañcatantra 2.144)
Thinking "that is fate," one should not abandon personal effort;
for without processing, oil is not produced from sesame seeds.
Moreover:
Even if Fortune were bestowed upon that person of dull intellect who is content with only a little, she would be wiped away from that man devoid of merit. (Pañcatantra 2.146)
And as for what you say—
that these two will fall or not—
that too is incorrect. And it has been said:
Those who have reached firm resolve are worthy of veneration; mere height is of no use.
What is this wretched *cātaka* bird, for whom even Indra is but a water-carrier?
Furthermore, I am weary of mouse-flesh,
and these two lumps of meat appear to be on the verge of falling.
Therefore, this must not be done otherwise under any circumstances.
Then, having heard that, he abandoned the place where the mouse was found and followed after Tīkṣṇaviṣāṇa.
Or rather, it is well said:
"In this world, a man may remain his own master in all his affairs only so long as—"
As long as he is not forcibly restrained, he will be trampled by the goad of a woman's words.
Impelled by the words of women, a man considers what should not be done as what ought to be done, what is inaccessible as easily accessible, and what is inedible as edible. (Pancavimśati 2.149)
Thus, wandering behind him with his wife, he spent a long time;
yet neither of them fell.
Then, out of despondency, in the fifteenth year, the jackal said to his wife: "Loose yet well-fastened," and so forth.
After that, there will be no further falling for the two of us;
let us go back to our own respective places.
Therefore I say: "Both loose and well-bound. (141)
The man said: "If that is so, then go once more to the city of Vardhamāna.
Two sons of merchants dwell there;
one is Guptadhana."
The second has already spent his wealth.
Therefore, having ascertained their true natures, you should request a boon from one of them:
"If you have need for wealth that has not been consumed, then I shall make even you one whose wealth is hidden."
"Or rather, if you have need of wealth that can be given and enjoyed, I shall make that wealth available for your enjoyment.
Having said this, he vanished from sight.
Somilaka, his mind filled with wonder, returned once more to the city of Vardhamāna.
Then, at the time of twilight, exhausted, he somehow reached that city; inquiring for the house of Guptadhana, he entered it with great difficulty after the sun had set.
Thereupon, being scolded by Guptadhana along with his wife and son, he forcibly entered the house and sat down.
And then, at the hour of the meal, some food devoid of respect was given even to him.
Then, having eaten there, while he was asleep at midnight, he saw those two men conversing with one another.
One of them said: "O Karta!
Why have you caused such an excessive expenditure for this Guptadhana, that he has given food to Somilaka?"
"What you have done is improper. He replied, "O Karma, the fault is not mine in this matter."
"I must grant the man the attainment of his gain;
its transformation, however, depends upon you.
Then, as soon as he rose, Guptadhana, suffering from cholera and overcome by pain, remained there for a moment.
Then, on the second day, due to that fault, he (Somilaka) became one who had observed a fast.
At dawn, Somilaka also departed from that man's house and went to the house where his wealth had been consumed.
He too was honored by [the host] with a formal rising to greet him, and having been provided with food, clothing, and hospitality, he lay down and slept upon a comfortable bed in that very house.
Then, at midnight, as he looked, he saw those same two men consulting with one another.
There, one of them said: "O Karta!
By this person, who is performing a service for Somilaka, a great expense has been incurred."
"Therefore, tell me how the method for its extraction shall be;
all of this has been brought here by him from the house of the litigant.
He said, "O Karma!"

"This is my duty; however, the final outcome depends upon you. Then, at the time of dawn, a royal official arrived bringing wealth born of the king's favor and handed it over for the enjoyment of the one who had consumed the funds.
Seeing that, Somilaka reflected:
"Better is this man who has enjoyed his wealth, though he is devoid of accumulation, than that miser who guards his wealth. And it is said:
'The fruit of the Vedas is the Agnihotra sacrifice; the fruit of sacred learning is virtuous conduct.'"
A wife has as her fruit pleasure and offspring; wealth has as its fruit giving and enjoyment.
"May the Creator therefore make me one who has given away and spent his wealth;
I have no need for hidden riches.
Thereupon, Somilaka became one whose wealth had been given away and spent.
Therefore I say: "Having acquired wealth... If we were wealthy by means of that very wealth buried in the middle of our house, would we not then be wealthy? (Pañca 2.151)
Therefore, my good friend Hiraṇyaka, knowing this, you should not feel distress regarding wealth.
Furthermore, even wealth that exists should be considered as non-existent if it is incapable of being enjoyed. And it has been said:
"For the very relinquishing of acquired riches is their true preservation."
Like an overflow for waters contained within the belly of a pond.
And so it is said:
"For wealth that has been acquired, renunciation is indeed its preservation, just as an overflow channel is for the waters contained within a reservoir. (Pañca 2.153)
Furthermore:
Giving, enjoyment, and loss—these are the three destinies of wealth.
For one who neither gives nor enjoys it, the third destiny occurs. (Pancatantira 2.154)
Knowing this, a person of discernment should not strive to acquire wealth for the sake of maintaining it, since that leads only to suffering. As it has been said:
"Those fools who, harboring hopes for happiness, remain attached here to wealth and such things, seek out fire for the sake of coolness in the heat of a scorching summer. (Pañcāstikāya 2.155)
Snakes drink only air and yet they are not weak;
forest elephants become strong by eating dry grass;
and the best of sages pass their time on bulbs and fruits.
Contentment alone is the supreme treasure for a person.
Where is that happiness of those with peaceful minds, who are satisfied by the nectar of contentment,
for those greedy for wealth who run hither and thither?
For those who drink contentment as if it were nectar, there is supreme bliss;
for men who possess discontent, however, there is incessant suffering.
When the mind is ceased, all the sense-faculties are likewise ceased;
just as when the sun is covered by clouds, its rays become obscured.
The peaceful great seers have declared that the cessation of desire is true well-being;
desire does not turn back by means of objects, just as thirst is not quenched by fanning a fire.
Mortals censure even the blameless and loudly praise the unworthy; for the sake of wealth, what indeed will they not do? (Pancatantira 2.161)
Even for one whose desire for wealth is for the sake of Dharma, that desire does not bring about what is auspicious;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
There is no other treasure equal to generosity,
nor is there anything else on earth more supreme than greed;
there is no ornament equal to ethical conduct, nor any other like it.
There is no wealth equal to contentment.
The supreme form of poverty is the deficiency of the wealth of honor;
yet Śiva, whose only riches are an old bull, remains the Supreme Lord.
"Knowing this, O good sir, you should practice contentment.
Having heard Mantharaka’s words, the crow said: "Good sir, whatever Mantharaka says in this manner must be kept in your heart.
Or rather, it is well said:"
O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to such words, are both rare.
Those who speak even unpleasant words that are beneficial to people here in this world are declared to be true friends; others are merely bearers of the name.
Now, while they were thus conversing, a deer named Citrāṅga, terrified by a hunter, entered that very lake. Then, seeing him approaching in great haste, Laghupatanaka climbed a tree,
and Hiraṇyaka entered a thicket of reeds.
Mantharaka was staying in his watery retreat.
Then Laghupatanaka, having correctly identified the deer, said to Mantharaka: "Come, come, friend Mantharaka!
This deer, afflicted by thirst, has arrived here and entered the lake."
"This sound is not produced by a human being.
Having heard this, Mantharaka said what was appropriate for the time and place: "O Laghupatanaka!

I myself shall personally subdue this wicked-souled one who has taken the side of the enemy," he said,
and having spoken thus, he climbed upon him.
Having slain him with swift peckings of its beak and having drenched him with the blood it had drawn, the crow went with his followers to Mount Ṛṣyamūka as directed by him.
In the meantime, Kṛkālikā, who had become a spy for the enemy, reported all of that—the calamity of the minister and that he had departed somewhere with his retinue.
Then the lord of the owls, having heard this, set out at the time of sunset with his ministers and attendants for the purpose of slaying the crow.
And he said: "Hurry! Hurry! A frightened enemy intent on flight is obtained through merit. And it is said:
"When an enemy is in motion, one who creates a single opening and another place of refuge becomes subject to the control of those serving the king during his state of agitation. (Pañca III.125)
Speaking thus, he stood surrounding the banyan tree on all sides from below;
and as soon as not a single crow was to be seen, Arimardana, having ascended to the tip of a branch with a joyful mind while being praised by bards, said to those attendants: "Aho!"
Let their path be discovered;
by which way have the crows vanished? Before they take refuge in a difficult place, [let them be found].
At that very moment, they follow from behind and strike them down. And it has been said:

"Even an enemy who has taken refuge in one's livelihood should not be slain by one desiring victory; how much less so one who has taken refuge in a fortress and is endowed with supreme resources? (Pañca 3.126)
Now, on this occasion, Sthirajīvin reflected: "If these enemies of mine depart just as they came, having failed to obtain news of me, then nothing will have been accomplished by me.
And it is said:
'The non-commencement of undertakings is the first mark of wisdom.'"
Bringing to completion what has been begun is the second characteristic of intelligence. //Panc_3.127//
"It is better not to begin at all than to have one's undertaking frustrated.
Having reflected thus, "I shall reveal myself after letting them hear this sound," he made a very soft noise.
Hearing that, all those owls set out to kill him.
Then he said: "Alas!
I am named Sthirajīvin, the minister of Meghavarṇa;
it was by Meghavarṇa himself that I have been brought to such a state."
Let him report this to his own master;
he has much to discuss with him.
Then, having been informed by them, that king of owls, overcome with astonishment, went to his presence at that very moment and said: "Ho there! Ho there!"
"Why have you fallen into this state?
Please tell me.
Sthirajīvin replied, "O King!"
Listen to the cause of that situation:
On the day past, that wicked Meghavarṇa, seized by anger and grief due to the suffering of the many crows slain by you, set out for battle against you.
Then I said, "O Master!"
It is not proper for you to go against them;
they are powerful, while we are weak. And it has been said:
One who desires prosperity should not, even in thought, seek conflict with one more powerful than himself;
for one who adopts the conduct of a reed is not destroyed in this world.
It is evident that there is the destruction of the moth's way of life.
Therefore, a peace treaty is indeed appropriate for him by granting him a means of livelihood. And it has been said:
"Seeing a powerful enemy, a wise man should protect his life even by giving away his entire property; for with his life protected, he may acquire wealth once again. (Pañcatantra 3.129)
Having heard that, I have been reduced to this state by one provoked by wicked people who suspected me of being a partisan of yours.
Therefore, your feet are now my refuge;
what is the use of further entreaty?
"As long as I am able to move, I shall lead you to his dwelling and bring about the destruction of all the crows.
Then, having heard this, Arimardana consulted with his ministers who had come down through the succession of his fathers and grandfathers;
and he had five such ministers.
Namely: red-eyed, cruel-eyed, and blazing-eyed.
Vakranāsa and Prākārakarṇa.
Therein, he first asked Raktākṣa: "My good man!"
"Thus, this minister of that enemy has fallen into my hands;
so, what should be done?
Raktākṣa replied, "O King!"
What is there to deliberate upon here?
This man must be slain without hesitation, for: "An inferior enemy must be destroyed before he becomes powerful."
Having subsequently attained the strength of one's own manly effort, one becomes difficult to conquer.
Furthermore, there is a popular saying in the world that "Fortune, having come of her own accord, curses when she is rejected. And it has been said:
"For Time comes but once to a man who awaits his time; it is difficult for him to encounter it again if he wishes to perform the deeds of Time. (Pañcatantra 3.131)
And it is heard as follows:
"A certain cruel hunter, resembling Death itself to living beings, roamed through the great forest, a terrible man of vile conduct. (Pañca 3.132)
Arimardana asked, "How was that?
Raktākṣa related:
Story 5.
The Story of the Brahmin and the Snake:
In a certain town there lived a brahmin named Haridatta.
As he was engaged in agriculture, his time passed away constantly without any fruit.

Then one day, at the end of the hot season, that brahmin, afflicted by the heat, fell asleep in the shade of a tree in the middle of his field; seeing nearby, upon an anthill, a terrifying serpent with its large hood spread out, he thought:
"Surely this is the deity of the field whom I have never worshipped."
"Therefore, this work of my cultivation is becoming fruitless;
thus, today I shall pay her honor.
Having resolved this, he requested milk from somewhere, poured it into a shallow bowl, approached the vicinity of the anthill, and said: "O Guardian of the Field!"
"For so long a time, I did not know that you were dwelling here;
therefore, no worship was offered.
Please forgive me for this now."
Having spoken thus and offered the milk, he set out toward his home. Then, when he returned in the morning and looked,
he saw a single dīnāra in a shallow dish.
And so, coming alone every day, he gave milk to him and took one dīnāra each.
Then, on one day, having appointed his son to bring the milk, the Brāhmaṇa went to another village.
The son also took the milk there, set it down, and returned home.
On another day, having gone there and seen a *dīnāra* coin, he picked it up and thought, "Surely this anthill is full of gold *dīnāras*.
Therefore, having killed him, I will take everything all at once. Having thus resolved, on the following day, while giving the milk, the Brahmin’s son struck the snake with a staff.

Then, by some stroke of fate, though his life was not yet departed, he bit that very man with such intense venom out of rage that the man immediately met his death. And he was cremated by his own kinsmen with piles of wood not far from the field.
Then, on the second day, his father arrived;
having heard from his own kinsmen the cause of his son’s destruction, he accepted it as such and said:
"He who does not show favor to spirits that have come to him for refuge..."
His true goals perish, just as swans vanish from a lotus grove.
The men asked, "How was that?
The Brahmin related:
Story 6.
There is a story of a golden swan.
In a certain city there was a king named Citraratha.
A lake named Padmasaras, well-guarded by his soldiers, belonged to him; and therein dwelt many swans made of Jāmbūnada gold.
Every six months, they each discard one of their feathers.
Then, a large golden bird arrived at that lake,
and they said to him, "You must not dwell among us."
For this reason, we took possession of this lake by giving one feather each at the end of six months;
and so, what need is there to say more?
A mutual conflict has arisen.
Having gone for refuge to the king, he said:
"Your Majesty, these birds say: 'What will our king do?'"
"We do not give lodging to anyone.
I said, "What you have said is not right;
I shall go and inform the king."
This being the case, Your Majesty is the authority.
Thereupon the king said to his servants: "Ho there!
Go, kill all the birds and bring them back quickly."
Immediately after the king's command, they set out.
Then, seeing the king's men with clubs in their hands, one aged bird there said: "O kinsmen, an ill fortune has befallen us!"
"Therefore, all must fly up with one mind.
And they did exactly that. It is for this reason that I say: "He who does not show favor to living beings... (133).
Having spoken thus, the brahmin again took milk at dawn, went there, and praised the serpent with a loud voice.
Then the serpent, remaining hidden for a long time within the opening of the anthill, replied to the brahmin: "You have come here out of greed, even abandoning grief for your son;
therefore, from now on, affection between you and me is no longer appropriate."
"I was struck by your son out of the intoxication of youth; I have seen him.
How can I forget that blow from the club?
And how can you forget the sorrow and suffering caused by the death of your son? Having said this again, he entered the interior of the hole.
The Brahmin, having taken the jewel and censuring the notion that it was his son, returned to his own home.
Therefore I say: "Behold the funeral pyre aflame!
Thus, once he is slain, the kingdom will belong to you without effort and free from all thorns.
Having heard these words of his, he asked Krūrākṣa: "My good man, what do you think?
He replied: "O King!"
"What he has said is heartless; for it is well known that one who has come for refuge must not be killed—
this indeed is the established tradition."
For it is heard that a pigeon, when his enemy came to him for refuge,
honored him according to the rules and invited him with his own flesh.
Arimardana asked, "How was that?
Krūrākṣa relates:
Story 7.
The Story of the Dove and the Fowler:
A certain fowler of cruel conduct, resembling Death itself to living beings, roamed through the great forest—a terrible hunter of birds. (Pancavimshati 3.135)
He has no friend at all, no relative, and no kinsman;
he is abandoned by all of them because of that terrible deed.
Alternatively:
Those who are cruel and evil-minded, who destroy the lives of living beings, become like predatory beasts, causing terror among all creatures. (Pañca III.137)
Taking his cage, as well as his snare and club,
he would go daily to the forest, a harmer of all living beings.
One day, as he was wandering in the forest, a certain female pigeon fell into his hand; he placed her inside a cage.
Then, as he stayed in the forest, all directions became dark with thick clouds,
and a great wind and rain fell like at the time of universal destruction.
Then, with a terrified heart and trembling again and again,
seeking protection, he approached a great tree.
As long as he gazes for a moment at the sky filled with clear stars, he reaches a tree and speaks thus: "Whoever is staying here..."
"I have come to him for refuge; may he protect me," [he thought], as he was being pierced by the cold and deprived of consciousness by hunger. (3.143)
Then, on the trunk of that tree, a pigeon who had lived there for a very long time remained, separated from his wife; being deeply distressed, he lamented.
There was a great wind and rain, yet my beloved does not come;
for deprived of her, this house of mine is empty today.
Devoted to her husband, regarding her husband as her very life, and intent upon the pleasure and welfare of her husband—that man on earth who possesses such a wife is truly blessed. (Pañca III.146)
They do not say that a house is a home; rather, the wife is called the home. A house devoid of a wife is considered to be like a wilderness.

Then, having heard her husband’s words filled with sorrow while she remained in the cage, the female dove was deeply satisfied and spoke these words: pañjara-sthā tataḥ śrutvā bhartur duḥkhānvitaṃ vacaḥ / kapotikā susantuṣṭā vākyaṃ cedam athāha sā //Panc_3.148//
She should not be considered a woman with whom her husband is not pleased;
when the husband is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied for women.
Like a flowering creeper scorched by a forest fire,
may that woman be reduced to ashes upon whom her husband is not pleased.
For a father gives only a limited amount, a brother gives a limited amount, and a son gives a limited amount;
who would not revere her husband, the giver of the unlimited?
And he spoke again:
"Listen attentively, my beloved, to what I shall say for your benefit:
one who has come for refuge must always be protected by you, even at the cost of your own life. (Panc_3.152)
This fowler lies here, having taken refuge in your dwelling;
afflicted by cold and tormented by hunger, offer him honor.
And it is heard in scripture:

"He who does not honor a guest who has arrived in the evening to the best of his ability—having given that person his own misdeeds, he takes away the guest's merit. (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 3.154)
And do not harbor hatred toward him, thinking, "My beloved has been bound by this man";
for I am bound only by the fetters of my own past actions.
Poverty, disease, suffering, bondage, and calamities—
these are the fruits for embodied beings of the tree of their own transgressions.
Therefore, having abandoned the hatred born of my bondage and having fixed your mind upon the Dharma, worship this according to the prescribed rite.
Having heard those words of hers, which were endowed with righteousness and logic, the pigeon, approaching him, then spoke timidly to the hunter: *Pancatantra 3.158*
"O noble one, a very warm welcome to you! Tell me, what may I do for you?
You should not feel any distress; you are staying in your own home."
Having heard those words of his, he replied to the bird:
"O pigeon, it is indeed cold for me; let protection from the frost be provided."
Having gone and brought charcoal, he cast it into the fire;
then he quickly kindled it with dry leaves.
Having then set it ablaze, he said to him who had come for refuge:
"Heat your own limbs here with confidence, free from fear."
We forest-dwellers all subsist on what has been cast up;
we possess no wealth whatsoever by which we might satisfy your hunger.
One person supports a thousand, another a hundred, and yet another ten;
but for me, who have performed no merit and am so base, even my own self is difficult to support.
What is the fruit for one who dwells in a house filled with manifold afflictions, yet lacks the power to give even a single morsel of food to a guest? (Pancatantaka 3.165)
Therefore, I shall bring this body, which lives in suffering,
to such a state that I shall never again say "it does not exist" when meeting with those who seek my help.
He reproached himself, but not the hunter again;
he said, "I shall satisfy you; wait for a moment."
Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one, with a joyful inner self,
circumambulated the fire and entered it as if it were his own home.
Then, seeing that pigeon fallen into the fire, the hunter was deeply afflicted by compassion and spoke these words: *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, 3.169.
The man who commits evil does not have a self that is truly dear to him;
for the evil committed by oneself is experienced by oneself alone.
Thus, being of evil mind and always delighting in evil deeds, I shall fall into a most terrible hell; of this there is no doubt.
Surely a true reflection has been shown to me, a cruel man,
by that great-souled pigeon who offered his own flesh.
From this day forward, I shall again wither my own body, deprived of all enjoyments, just as the summer heat dries up even a small amount of water.
Enduring cold, wind, and heat, with emaciated limbs and soiled body,
I shall practice the supreme Dharma through various kinds of fasting.
Then the hunter broke the staff, the stick, the net, and likewise the cage, and he released that wretched female pigeon.
Then, released by the hunter, the female pigeon saw her husband fallen into the fire;
with a mind tormented by grief, she lamented in distress.
"O Lord, there is no purpose for my life today without you;
what is the fruit of life for a wretched woman who is bereft of her husband? (Panc 3.177)
Pride, arrogance, self-conceit, noble lineage, and honor among kinsmen, as well as authority over servants and employees—all these perish through widowhood. (Pancatantra 3.178)
Having lamented thus many times piteously and being deeply afflicted by grief,
that devoted wife entered that very same blazing fire.
Then, wearing celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments,
that female pigeon beheld her husband situated upon a celestial chariot.
He too, having assumed a divine body, spoke these words according to the truth:
"O auspicious one, you have done well by following me. (Pancavimshati 3.181)
For as many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
so long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
In the form of a pigeon, he experienced happiness every day at sunset;
his former existence as a pigeon was due to the beneficial power arising from his past merit.
Then, overcome with joy and filled with profound world-weariness, the hunter entered the forest,
having completely abandoned the harming of living beings.
There, seeing a forest fire, he entered it with a mind free from desire;
having been cleansed of all defilements, he attained the bliss of heaven.
Therefore I say: "It is heard that by a pigeon... and so forth.
Having heard that, Arimardana asked Dīptākṣa: "This being the case, what do you think?
He replied: "O King, he must certainly not be killed; for—
She who was always anxious for me now embraces me;
O doer of what is pleasing, may you be blessed—take whatever belongs to me.
And Coreṇa also said:
"I see nothing that you should take; yet if there is something to be taken, I shall come again, provided this [woman] does not embrace me."
Arimardana asked: "Who is it that embraces the ship? And who is this thief?
I wish to hear the details."
Dīptākṣa relates:
Story 8,
the Story of the Merchant Afflicted by Lust.
In a certain place, there was an old merchant named Kāmātura. His mind being overcome by passion,
and his wife having died, he [approached] a certain daughter of a poor merchant.
Having given him abundant wealth, she was married to him;
then, overwhelmed by suffering, she was not even able to look upon that old merchant.
And this is only right:
That very white spot upon the head, the place where the hairs grow, which is the ultimate object of contempt for men,
people avoid and depart from once it has become a vessel for fragments of bone.
Young women [avoid] it from afar, as if it were a well belonging to a caṇḍāla.
And so it is said:
"The body is hunched, the gait has faltered, the teeth have perished, the vision wanders, the form is impaired, and the mouth drools."
Relatives do not heed one's words at all, the wife does not show obedience, alas, what misery! A man overcome by old age is even despised by his own son. (Pancatantira 3.189)
Then once, while she was lying on the same bed with him turned away from him, a thief entered the house.
Seeing the thief, she, overwhelmed by fear, firmly embraced her husband even though he was old.
He too, his entire body covered in horripilation out of astonishment, thought: "Aha! Why does she embrace me today?"

As he looked with increasing acuteness, he saw a thief in a corner of the house and thought: "Surely she embraces me out of fear of him. Realizing this, he said to the thief: "She who is terrified of me," and so forth.
Upon hearing this, the thief also said: "I see nothing that should be stolen from you," and so forth.

"Therefore, even for a thief, assistance is considered a merit; how much more so for one who has come for refuge? Furthermore, this man, having been mistreated by them, will serve our own enrichment and provide us with an opportunity to see their vulnerabilities. For these reasons, he must not be killed.
Having heard this, Arimardana questioned another minister, Vakranāsa: "My good sir," he said.
"Now that this is the case, what should be done?
He replied, "Your Majesty, he is not to be slain; for—"
Even enemies may dispute with one another for the sake of mutual benefit;
thus, life was given by a thief, and a pair of oxen by a rākṣasa.
Arimardana asked, "How was that?
Vakranāsa relates:
Story 10.
The Story of the Brahmin named Droṇa:

In a certain town there was a poor Brahmin named Droṇa; though his wealth consisted solely of gifts received, he was constantly deprived of the enjoyment of fine garments, ointments, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, betel, and other such luxuries.
With his hair, beard, nails, and body hair grown long and thick,
his body withered by cold, heat, wind, rain, and other elements,
he was given a pair of young oxen by some donor out of compassion.
And from his childhood, the Brahmin had reared and well-nourished him by providing him with requested offerings of ghee, oil, fodder, and so forth.
Seeing this, a certain thief suddenly thought, "I shall steal this pair of oxen from this Brahmin.
Having thus resolved, he took a binding noose at night and—

As he was proceeding, he saw on the way someone with a row of sparse, sharp teeth, a prominent bridge of the nose, eyes with clearly visible red corners, limbs stretched out by a network of thick sinews, hollow cheeks, and a beard, hair, and body as tawny as a well-fed sacrificial fire.
Seeing him, the thief, terrified by intense fear, said: "Who are you?
He replied: "I am a thief of cruel deeds; I have set out to steal a pair of oxen from a poor Brahmin.
Then the Rākṣasa, having gained confidence, said: "Good sir!"
"I am one whose meal-time is the sixth part of the day;
therefore, I shall devour that very brahmin today.
Then, having gone there, the two of them stood in a secluded spot, searching for a dog.

Seeing the Rākṣasa set out to devour that Brāhmaṇa while he was asleep, the thief said, "Good sir, this is not right; since I have already stolen the pair of oxen, you should eat this Brāhmaṇa afterwards. He replied, "Perhaps this Brāhmaṇa might wake up at the sound of the oxen; in that case, my effort would be in vain."

The thief also said: "If even a single obstacle should arise for you when you have approached to devour him, then I too shall not be able to steal the pair of oxen. Therefore, once the pair of oxen has first been stolen by me, only then should the Brahmin be devoured by you."
Thus, as the two of them were disputing with one another, "I first! I first!", a conflict arose; and due to the sound of their voices, the brahmin woke up.
Then the thief said to him, "Brahmin, this rakshasa wishes to devour you!"
The *rākṣasa* also said, "O Brahmin,
this thief wishes to steal your pair of oxen.

Having heard this, the Brahmin rose up, became alert, and protected himself from the *rākṣasa* and his pair of oxen from the thief by means of meditation on the mantra of his chosen deity while wielding a raised club.
Therefore I say: "Even enemies are for the sake of one's welfare.
Then, having taken his words to heart, Arimardana asked Prākārakarṇa once more: "Tell me, what do you think of this?"
He said:
"O King, this one is indeed not to be killed;
for if he is protected, time may perhaps pass happily through mutual affection. And it has been said:"
Those living beings who do not protect one another’s vital points meet their destruction, like snakes within the belly of an anthill.
Arimardana asked, "How was that?
Prākārakarṇa relates: Story 10.
The Story of the Serpent within the Belly of an Ant-hill:
In a certain city there was a king named Devaśakti.
His son’s every limb began to waste away day by day due to a serpent that had taken up residence in an ant-hill within his belly.

Although he was treated by excellent physicians with numerous medical procedures and according to the methods of medicines prescribed in authentic treatises, he did not attain health. Then, out of despondency, that prince went to another land;
having wandered for alms in a certain city, he spent his time in a great temple.
Now, in that city there was a king named Bali,
and he had two daughters who were in the prime of their youth. Every day at sunrise, they would come into the presence of their father and pay him homage.
And there one said, "Be victorious, O Great King!
By whose grace all happiness is obtained.
But the second said, "Enjoy what has been ordained, O Great King!"
Thus she spoke.
Having heard this, the king became enraged and said: "O ministers!
Give this wicked-speaking girl to some foreigner; in that way, she shall experience the consequences of her own actions."
Then, having agreed, saying "So be it," that young woman with a small retinue was presented by the ministers to the prince who resided in the temple.
She too, with a joyful heart, accepted him as her husband like a god and departed for another region.

Then, in a certain distant part of the city, having stationed the prince on the bank of a pond to guard their dwelling, she herself went for the purpose of purchasing ghee, oil, salt, rice, and other provisions.
She departed with her retinue.
Having completed her buying and selling, as she was returning, the prince was fast asleep with his head placed upon an anthill;
from his mouth, a serpent had extended its hood and was inhaling air.
And from that very anthill, another snake emerged and remained there in the same manner.
Then, as the two of them looked at one another with eyes bloodshot with rage, the snake staying within the anthill said: "O you wicked soul!
How can you thus torment this prince whose every limb is so beautiful?"
The enemy situated in the mouth said, "O, O you wicked soul! How was this pair of jars filled with gold defiled by you in the midst of this anthill? Thus they both exposed each other's secrets.
Then the snake residing in the anthill said, "O wicked soul!"
"This remedy of yours—does no one know that you meet your destruction by drinking old, fermented gruel mixed with mustard seeds?
Then the serpent within the belly said, "Does no one know this remedy of yours as well—that your destruction would come about through hot oil or very hot water?
And so, the princess, hidden behind a branch, having overheard their mutual conversation concerning their vital secrets, carried out exactly what they had suggested.
Having restored her husband to health and freedom from disease, and having obtained a supreme treasure, she set out toward her own country.
Honored by her father, mother, and kinsmen, and having secured all enjoyments, she lived there in happiness. Therefore I say: "The vital secrets of one another... etc.
Having heard that, Ariṣṭanemi himself also agreed accordingly, and it was carried out in that manner.
Seeing him hidden within, Raktākṣa laughed and spoke again: "Alas!"
"You have unjustly destroyed this master of yours. And it is said:
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped, and there is disrespect toward those worthy of worship, three things prevail there: famine, death, and fear. (Pañca 3.192)
And so it is said:
"Even when a sin has been committed before one's very eyes, a fool pacifies it with conciliation;
the chariot-maker carried his own wife along with her lover upon his head. (Pañcatantra 3.193)
The ministers asked, "How was that? Raktākṣa related:
Story 11.
The Story of Vīravara the Carpenters and His Wife:
In a certain city there was a carpenter named Vīravara;
his wife was Kāmadamanī.
That unchaste woman was beset by public scandal.
He, too, for the sake of testing her, reflected: "Now I must put her to the test. And it is said:
"If fire were to become cold, or if the moon were to become hot..."
The chastity of women would only exist if wicked people were well-disposed toward them.
And I know her to be unchaste from the talk of the world; for it is said:
"Whatever is not seen or heard in the Vedas or the scriptures—all that which exists within the universe, this world knows. (Pañcatantra 3.195)
Having reflected thus, he said to his wife: "My dear, at dawn I shall go to another village;
I will stay there for a few days."
"Therefore, you must prepare some suitable provisions for my journey.
Hearing these words, she too was delighted at heart;
out of eagerness, she abandoned all her other duties and prepared food consisting primarily of ghee and sugar.
Or rather, it is well said:

"On a foul day, in dense darkness, when the clouds are raining in a great forest and the like, there is supreme pleasure for the woman of loose morals while her husband has gone abroad. (Pañcāstikāya 3.196)

Then, having risen at dawn, he departed from his own house; she too, perceiving that he had set out, adorned her face and limbs with a smile and managed to pass that day somehow. Then, going to the house of a former acquaintance, a libertine, she said to him: "That wicked husband of mine has gone to another village;
therefore, you must come to our house while the people are fast asleep."
When it had been carried out accordingly, that carpenter spent the day in the forest and, at nightfall, entered his own house by a side door and remained hidden beneath the bed.
In the meantime, Devadatta arrived and sat down upon that bed.
Seeing him, the carpenter’s mind was overcome with rage, and he thought: "Shall I rise up and kill him?"
Or rather, shall I kill both of them with ease while they are fast asleep?
But first, let me observe her movements and listen to her conversation with him.
In the meantime, having quietly closed the door of the house, she ascended to the surface of her bed.
As she was climbing up there, her foot became caught on the body of the carpenter.
Then she thought: "Surely this must be that wicked carpenter, who has come for the purpose of testing me."
"Therefore, I shall employ some stratagem to understand the conduct of women.
While she was thinking thus, Devadatta became eager for physical contact.
Then, with her hands joined in reverence, she said: "O noble sir!"
"You must not touch my body, for I am a devoted wife and a great virtuous woman;
otherwise, having cast a curse upon you, I shall reduce you to ashes.
He said, "If that is so, then why were I summoned by you?"
She said: "O sir, listen with a one-pointed mind.
Today at dawn, I went to the temple of Caṇḍī for the purpose of seeing the deity. There, suddenly, a voice arose in the sky: 'Daughter, what shall I do?
You are devoted to me.'"
"But within six months, by the decree of fate, you will become a widow.
Then I said, "O Blessed One, as you know this calamity,"
Likewise, you also know the remedy for that.
Is there some means by which my husband may become a hundred-year-liver? Then she said: "Daughter,"
"Even though it exists, it does not exist,
because that remedy depends upon you.
Having heard this, I said, "O Queen!"
"If that can be accomplished by my life, then give the command so that I may do it.
Then the queen said: "If today you ascend one bed with another man and embrace him, then the untimely death attached to your husband will pass over to him;
and your husband, moreover, shall live for another hundred years."
Therefore, you have been entreated by me;
so do whatever it is you intend to do.
For it is certain that the word of the deity shall not be otherwise.
Then, with a face half-smiling and half-blooming, he acted as was appropriate for the occasion.
That foolish carpenter, too, upon hearing her words, his body bristling with horripilation, emerged from beneath the bed and said to her: "Excellent, O devoted wife!
Excellent, O delight of your family!"
"With my heart suspicious due to the words of wicked people, I made the pretext of going to another village and remained hidden beneath the bed for the purpose of testing you.
Therefore, come here and embrace me;
you are the foremost among women devoted to their husbands."
"Since you have thus observed this vow of Brahman even in the company of another,
and since you have acted in this way for the sake of prolonging life and destroying untimely death—
having spoken thus, he embraced her with affection."
Having placed her upon his own shoulder, he said to Devadatta: "O noble one!
By my merits you have come here;
through your favor, I have obtained a lifespan measuring a hundred years."
Saying, "Therefore, you too must embrace me and climb onto my shoulder," he forcibly lifted Devadatta onto his own shoulder despite the latter's reluctance.

Then, having performed a dance and saying, "O foremost among those who uphold the vow of Brahman, you have also rendered me a service," and so forth, he set him down from his shoulder; wherever he wandered—such as at the doors of the houses of his kinsmen—he would describe the virtues of both of them.
He did so;
therefore I say: "Even when a sin has been committed before one's eyes" (193).
Thus, we have been utterly uprooted from our foundation and are ruined.
This is indeed well said:
"For those who reject beneficial advice and instead follow what is contrary to it are considered by the wise to be enemies in the guise of friends. (Pañcatantra 3.197)
And so it is said:
"Even existing matters perish when obstructed by place and time, having encountered unwise ministers, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (Pañca 3.198)
Then, disregarding those words, they all began to lift up Sthirajīvin to bring him to their own fortress.
As he was being carried away, Sthirajīvin said, "O King,
what is the use of taking me along when I am in this condition and can be of no service today?"

"For the reason that I desire to enter the blazing fire, you ought to rescue me by providing the fire. Then, having understood Raktākṣa's inner intention, he said: "For what purpose do you wish to fall into the fire?"
He said, "I have been brought to this calamity on your account by Meghavarṇa;
therefore, I wish to become an owl for the sake of taking revenge upon them.
Hearing that, Raktākṣa, who was skilled in royal policy, said, "My good friend!"
"You are crooked and clever at using deceptive speech;
even though you have entered the womb of an owl, you still hold your own crow-womb in high esteem.
And this story is heard:"

The ministers asked, "How was that?
Raktākṣa relates:
Story 11.
The Story of the Mouse Protected by Śālaṅkāyana:
In a certain town, there lived an ascetic named Śālaṅkāyana who had gone to the Ganges to bathe.
While he was performing his devotions to the sun in that place, a certain mouse was seized by a hawk with the tips of its very sharp claws.
Seeing this, the sage, his heart moistened with compassion, cried out, "Release! Release! and hurled a piece of stone at him.

Struck by that stone, his senses overwhelmed, the cat fell to the ground, its grip lost. The mouse, too, terrified with fear and not knowing what to do, cried out, "Protect me! Protect me! and crouched down near the sage's feet.
Even the hawk, having regained consciousness, said to the sage:
"O Sage,
it was not proper that you committed this act, since I have been struck by you with a stone."
"Do you not fear unrighteousness?
Therefore, surrender this mouse to me;
otherwise, you will incur a great sin."
To the hawk speaking thus, he replied: "O lowest of birds!
The lives of living beings must be protected;
the wicked must be punished."
The virtuous are to be honored;
the teachers are to be revered;
the gods are to be praised.
"Why do you prattle such nonsense?
The hawk replied, "O Sage,
you do not understand the subtle Dharma."
For here, while creating all living beings according to the law, food was also ordained.
Therefore, just as you have your food, so too were mice and others ordained for us. Why then do you reproach me, who am desiring my own food? And it has been said:
If that which is prescribed for him as food is not available, it does not cause him defilement;
however, there would be great fault in consuming what is unfit to eat; therefore, one should not engage in such transgression.

O twice-born one, just as what is edible for the twice-born becomes inedible for those who drink liquor, and as the sacrificial oblation becomes inedible for others, so too does it happen for other classes. (3.201)
"It is better to eat what is fit to be eaten; to eat what is unfit is a great sin.
Therefore, O man of vain conduct, how can you deserve to punish me? (Pancavimshati 3.202)
Furthermore, this is not the dharma of sages, since by them—having seen and heard—that which is unheard of is praised: freedom from greed and freedom from enmity. And it has been said:
"Equal toward enemy and friend, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same;
impartial toward well-wishers, friends, neutrals, and those who are indifferent, as well as toward the hateful and kinsmen."
One who possesses an even mind toward both the virtuous and the wicked is preeminent.
"A yogi, remaining in solitude, should constantly engage the self in the company of the virtuous—those who are blameless and whose conduct is always rooted in right practice.
By this action, you have become one whose ascetic merit has fallen away. And it is said:
"Release! Release! cries one as he falls; "Do not release! cries the second.
Seeing both fall, silence is the means to accomplish all goals. (Pañcatantra 3.205)
Śālaṅkāyana said: "How was that?
Śyena said:
"The twelfth story."
On the bank of a certain river, three brothers who were sages named Ekata, Dvita, and Trita were performing austerities.
By the power of their asceticism, their washed garments remained suspended in the air, moist from bathing and without support, out of fear of touching the ground.
Now, one day, a certain little frog of mine was forcibly carried off by a vulture.
Then, seeing that it had been caught, the eldest among them, whose heart was moist with compassion, cried out like you, "Release it! Release it!
In that interval, it fell from the sky onto the ground along with his washed cloth.
Seeing it fallen, the second one, distressed by fear of that [punishment], cried out, "Do not release it! as soon as he spoke, it fell upon him as well.
Then the third one, seeing that the cleaning-cloth had fallen to the ground for both of them, remained silent.
Therefore I say: "Release, release! One falls," and so forth.
Having heard this, the sage laughed and said: "O foolish bird!"

In the Kṛta-yuga, that was the state of dharma, because in the Kṛta-yuga even from sinful speech sin arose; thus, when a washed garment fell, it was not due to the fault of an improper word or a false accusation. But this, moreover, is the Kali-yuga.
In this case, even every evil-doer [is purified]; that karma committed does not cling as sin. And it has been said:
"Sins committed by embodied beings in other ages wander here [in this world]."
But in the Kali age, which is joined with evil, he who performs [an action] becomes defiled by it.
And it is said:
"From sitting, from lying down, from traveling in a vehicle, from social contact, and even from eating—once committed, evil spreads like a drop of oil upon water. (Pañca 3.207)
So why this useless prattle? Go away! Otherwise, I shall have you punished.
Then, after the hawk had departed, the mouse said to the sage: "Venerable sir, lead me to your own abode;
otherwise, some other wicked bird will kill me."
"Therefore, I shall spend my time right there in that hermitage, subsisting on handfuls of food given by you.
That compassionate and kind-hearted man thought: "How can I take this mouse by holding it in my hand? It would cause public ridicule.
Therefore, I shall lead her away after turning her into a young girl."
In this way, the girl was prepared.
When it had been carried out accordingly, the wife, seeing the sage accompanied by the girl, asked:
"Venerable sir, from where has this girl come?"
He said: "This mouse, seeking refuge out of fear of the hawk, has been brought to your house in the form of a maiden.
Therefore, she must be protected by you with great care;
furthermore, I shall turn her back into a mouse."
She said, "O Blessed One, do not do this!
You are her father in the Dharma. And it is said:
The progenitor, the one who performs the initiation, the one who imparts knowledge,
the giver of food, and the protector from fear— these five are remembered as fathers.
Therefore, you have granted her life;
furthermore, I too have no offspring.
Consequently, she shall become my daughter.
When she had been treated in this manner, that maiden grew day by day like a digit of the moon during the bright fortnight.
As she performed service for that sage and his wife, she quickly attained youth.
Then, seeing her approaching the bloom of youth, Śālaṅkāyana said to his wife: "My dear," he said.
"This girl has reached the threshold of youth;
she is no longer fit to dwell in my house. And it is said:
"If an unmarried daughter reaches her menses within the house of one [who fails to marry her]..."
Even those ancestors of his who reside in heaven fall down because of those [unwholesome] qualities.
A maiden chooses a bridegroom; her mother desires wealth; her father desires learning;
her kinsmen desire noble lineage; and other people desire sweet food. (Pancatantra 3.210)
And so it is said:
"As long as a girl does not feel shame, as long as she plays in the dust,
and as long as she remains on the path of the cattle— during that time, one should marry her."
The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses.
Having examined these seven qualities— lineage, moral conduct, having a protector, learning, wealth, physical form, and age— one should bestow [the gift].
The maiden is for the wise; the remainder is not to be contemplated.
Therefore, whatever pleases him, I shall summon the Blessed Sun and bestow it upon him. And it has been said:
"If a suitor is undesirable to a maiden, even if he is endowed with beauty, a girl who desires her own welfare should not be given to him. (Pañca 3.214)
She said, "What fault is there in this matter?
Let it be done thus.
Then the sage summoned Ravi.
By the power of the invocation with Vedic mantras, the Sun appeared at that very moment and said, "O Blessed One, speak quickly; for what purpose have I been summoned?
He replied, "This daughter of mine stands here."
"If she chooses you, then marry her.
Having said this, the Blessed One revealed himself to her and said,
"Daughter!"
"Do you like this Blessed One, the lamp of the three worlds?
She replied, "Father,
he is of a nature that burns excessively."
"I do not desire him;
let someone even more excellent than he be summoned.
Then, having heard those words of hers, Bhāsvara, recognizing her to be a mouse, spoke to him without desire: "O Blessed One!"
"Is there also a cloud superior to me, by whom being covered my very name is not known?
Then the sage, having summoned the cloud as well, said to the maiden: "Does this one please you?
She replied: "This one is black in color and dull-witted."
"Therefore, give me someone else who is more eminent than this.
Then the sage also asked Megha:
'O, is there anyone even superior to you?'"
He said, "There is something even greater than me: the wind. Struck by the wind, I am shattered into a thousand pieces.
Having heard that, the sage summoned the wind.
And he said: "Daughter, does this wind appear to you as the best for marriage?
She replied: "Though powerful, this one is fickle;
let someone even more excellent than this be summoned."
The sage said, "O Wind, is there anyone superior even to you?
He replied, "There is one superior even to me: the mountain, by which I, though powerful, am held fast."
Then the sage, having summoned Parvata, showed him the girl and said, "Little daughter,
shall I give you to him?
She replied, "Father, he is harsh-natured and arrogant."
"Therefore, give me to another.
Then he was asked by the sage:
"O King Parvata!"
"Is there anyone even superior to you? He replied, "There are mice even superior to me, who forcibly tear my body apart on all sides."

Having heard that, the sage summoned the mouse and showed him to her, saying: "Daughter, here is the king of mice for you, by whom that which is appropriate shall be performed. Seeing him and thinking, "He is of my own kind," she spoke with her body adorned by the bristling of horripilation: "Father!"
"Make me into a mouse and give me to him, so that I may perform the domestic duties ordained for my own species.
Having heard this, he, who was skilled in the ways of women, turned her into a mouse and gave her to the rat.
Therefore I say: "Having abandoned the sun as a husband," and so forth.
Then, disregarding the words of Raktākṣa, they led him to his own fortress for the destruction of their own lineage.
As he was being led away, Sthirajīvī laughed inwardly and thought:
