"Let him be killed—he who spoke thus as an advisor for the benefit of his master."
He alone among all here is the knower of the true essence of the meaning of the treatises on ethics.
If they had followed his advice, not even the slightest misfortune would have befallen them.
Then, having reached the gate of the fortress, Arimardana said: "O you well-wishers, grant this Sthirajīvin the place he desires."
Having heard that, Sthirajīvin reflected: "I must devise a means for their slaughter.
This cannot be accomplished by me while remaining neutral;
for if they observe my gestures and other signs, they too will become vigilant."
"Having stationed myself at the gate of this fortress, I shall accomplish my purpose.
Having thus resolved, he said to the lord of the owls: "O Lord, what has been spoken by our master is indeed appropriate."
Furthermore, although I am knowledgeable in policy and devoted to you, and though I am pure, even so, dwelling in the middle of a fortress is not fitting. Therefore,
staying right here at the gate of the fortress, my body purified by the dust of your lotus feet, I shall perform service to you every day.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," those servants of the king of owls daily provided Sthirajīvin with abundant food and, by the command of the owl-king, gave him excellent meat.
Then, within just a few days, he became as strong as a peacock.
Now, seeing Sthirajīvin being thus nourished, Raktākṣa was filled with wonder and said to the ministers and the king: "Aha! These ministers and you yourself are fools. Thus [he spoke].
I understand. And it has been said:
"First, I was a fool; second, the one who bound the animal.
Then there is the king and the minister—indeed, the entire circle is composed of fools. (Pañcatantra 3.216)
They asked, "How was that?
Rakshaka relates:
Story 13.
The Story of the Gold-Spitting Sindhuka Bird:
In a certain region of a mountain there was a great tree,
and in it lived a certain bird named Sindhuka.
Gold was produced from its excrement. Then, on one occasion, a certain hunter arrived with that bird in mind;
and the bird discharged its excrement right before him.

Then, seeing that it had turned into gold at the very moment of its fall, the hunter was struck with amazement. Thinking, "Aha! Though I have been addicted to bird-catching since my childhood for eighty years, I have never once seen gold in bird droppings," he set a snare on that tree.
Thereupon, that foolish bird, trusting as before, sat down in that very spot and was caught by the snare at that very instant.
The hunter, having released him from the snare and placed him in a cage, led him to his own dwelling. Then he reflected: "What shall I do with this bird, which is fraught with danger?
If ever someone..."
"Even if he were to discover this and report it to the king, my life would surely be in danger.
Therefore, I shall report the bird to the king myself.
Having reflected thus, he acted accordingly.
Then the king, too, upon seeing that bird, his lotus-like eyes and face blossoming with joy, attained supreme satisfaction and spoke thus: "O guards! Protect this bird with great care!"
"And provide him with food, drink, and so forth as he desires.
Then the minister said: "What is the use of this bird, which has been accepted solely on the basis of the words of an untrustworthy hunter?
Could gold ever possibly exist in the droppings of a bird?"

"Let this bird be released from its confinement in the cage. At these words of the minister, the king set the bird free; it perched upon the archway of the high gate, voided golden excrement, and having first recited the verse beginning with "First, I was a fool," it departed through the path of the sky as it pleased.
Therefore I say: "First, I was indeed a fool.
Then, however, because of adverse fate, they disregarded even Raktākṣa’s beneficial words and once again nourished him with various foods, including abundant meat and other delicacies.
Thereupon, Raktākṣa summoned his own faction and spoke to them in private: "O!"
This much alone is the welfare and the fortress of our king;
that which has been advised by me is what the hereditary minister declares. Therefore, we shall now take refuge in another mountain fortress.
And it has been said:
"He who acts for the future prospers;
he who does not act for the future grieves."
While dwelling in the forest, he reached old age; indeed, the voice of a cave was never heard by him.
They asked, "How was that?
Raktākṣa relates:
Story 14.
The Story of the Lion Kharanakharā:
In a certain region of the forest there lived a lion named Kharanakharā.
Once, while wandering here and there, his throat emaciated by hunger, he did not encounter even a single living creature.
Then, at the time of sunset, having reached and entered a great mountain cave, he thought: "Surely some creature must come to this cave at night;
therefore, I shall remain hidden.
In the meantime, its owner, a jackal named Dadhipuccha, arrived.
As he looked further, he saw that the trail of lion's footprints had entered the cave and did not emerge;
thereupon he thought, "Alas, I am ruined!"
"Surely there must be a lion dwelling within this;
so what shall I do?
How shall I find out?"
Having reflected thus, standing at the entrance, he began to holler: "O hole!
O hole!
Having said this, he became silent, and then spoke again in the same manner: "O sir!"
Do you not remember the agreement that was made between us,
that when I have returned from outside, I am to be spoken to by you, and I am to be received by you?
"Therefore, if you do not call out to me, then I shall go to the second cave.
Having heard this, the lion thought: "Surely this cave always calls out to him whenever he arrives;
however, today it says nothing at all out of fear of me."
Or rather, it is well said:
"In those whose minds are terrified by fear, activities such as moving the hands and feet may or may not proceed; their speech ceases, and trembling becomes excessive. (Pañcaviṃśatikā 3.218)
"Therefore, I shall call out to him so that, having entered in accordance with that call, he will become my food.
Having thus reflected, the lion made his call.
Then, by the sound of the lion, the cave was filled with echoes, terrifying even other forest-dwellers situated at a distance.
The jackal, as he was fleeing, recited this verse: "He who prepares for the future shines," and so forth.
Having reflected thus, [the lion said], "Therefore, you must go with me.
Having spoken thus, Raktākṣa departed for a distant land, followed by his own retinue of attendants.
Then, when Raktākṣa had departed, Sthirajīvī, with a most joyful mind, reflected: "Aha!
Prosperity has come upon us, since Raktāṃśa has gone—he was far-sighted—while these others are of deluded minds."
Consequently, they became easy for me to eliminate;
and as it is said:
"That king who does not have ministers capable of long-sighted vision..."
For one who has come [to this state] by gradual stages, its destruction will surely occur before long.
Or rather, it is well said:
"For those who, abandoning sound policy, follow a contrary course, should be regarded by the wise as enemies in the guise of ministers. (Pañcatantra 3.220)
Reflecting thus, he would drop a single piece of forest wood into his own nest day after day for the purpose of setting the cave on fire;
yet those foolish owls did not realize that he was causing their nest to grow for the sake of burning them.
Or rather, it is well said:
A man struck by fate makes an enemy his friend, hates and harms a friend, perceives evil as good, and regards sin as auspicious. (3.221)
Then, when a heap of wood had been piled at the entrance of the fortress under the pretext of building a nest,
and at sunrise,
while the owls had become blinded, Sthirajīvin quickly went to Ṛṣyamūka and said to Meghavarṇa: "My Lord!"
"The enemy caves have been rendered combustible.

Therefore, you, along with your followers, must assemble and each take a single burning piece of forest wood; throw it at our nest at the entrance of the cave, so that all the enemies may die in agony resembling the Kumbhīpāka hell."
Having heard that, Meghavarṇa was delighted and said: "Father, tell me your own story!
After a long time, you are seen today."
He said, "My son,
this is not the time for speaking;
for it may happen that some spy of that enemy will report my arrival here."
"Since the blind man will flee elsewhere upon gaining knowledge of this, let us hasten. And it is said:
'The man who delays in matters requiring swift action...'"
Without a doubt, the deities will obstruct that person's undertaking out of anger.
And so it is said:
"For whatever specific task has reached fruition, if it is not performed quickly, time drinks up its fruit. (Pañcaka 3.223)
"When you have entered that cave and your enemy has been slain, I shall relate everything to you in full detail and with complete composure.
Then, having heard those words, he, along with his followers, took a single glowing piece of forest wood in the tip of his beak,
reached the entrance of the cave, and dropped it into the nest of Sthirajīvin.
Then all those night-blind ones, remembering the words of Raktākṣa and unable to escape because the door was closed, fell into the fate of being boiled in a cauldron within the cave and died.
Having thus brought his enemies to total destruction, Meghavarṇa once again went to that very fortress of the banyan tree.
Then, seated upon his throne in the midst of the assembly, with a joyful mind, he asked Sthirajīvin: "Father!"
"How have you spent all this time while dwelling in the midst of enemies? We have a great curiosity regarding this matter;
please tell us. For it is said:"
For those of meritorious deeds, a plunge into a blazing sacrificial fire is preferable,
yet they would not associate with a person of hostile intent even for a moment.
Having heard that, Sthirajīvin said: "My good friend, out of desire for future rewards, a servant does not even perceive hardship. And as it is said:"
In view of the task at hand, even poison consumed becomes like nectar for all living beings; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Panc 3.225)
Whatever path may lead to the removal of fear and bring about one's welfare, that very path should be followed with discerning intelligence, whether it be great or humble.

Did not the wearer of the diadem (Arjuna) fashion his arms—resembling the trunks of elephants, scarred by the bowstring, and skilled in the use of mighty weapons—into bracelets like those of a woman? 3.226

Even though he is capable and wise, a person must indeed dwell among base and wicked folk— whose speech is as harsh as a thunderbolt— who look toward a later time for their own advantage, and who have ladles in hand, are soiled by smoke, and are full of toil.
Why was Bhīma, possessed of exceeding strength, not made to dwell as a cook in the palace of the Matsya king?
Whether it be good or censurable, a wise man who has fallen into adversity should perform the action held in his heart, awaiting the right time.
What need is there for one whose hand is hardened by the striking of the great string of the vibrating Gāṇḍīva bow?
Nor was there Savyasācin, who sports with the playful dancing of his girdle.
A wise person seeking success, though possessed of courage and vigor, should restrain his own brilliance and gradually maintain steadfastness toward the decrees of fate,
even if accompanied by brothers equal to Indra, Kubera, and Yama.
Why did the illustrious son of Dharma remain afflicted for so long in the palace of Virāṭa?
Endowed with noble form and lineage, the two sons of Mādrī, possessed of great strength,
entered into service under Virāṭa in the occupation of tending and protecting cattle.
She who was like the goddess Śrī herself— possessing peerless beauty, the virtues of youth, birth in a noble family, and radiant splendor— has, through the passage of time,
come to this state of being addressed with prideful disdain by young women as "Sairandhrī."
Was it not indeed boldly applied by Draupadī with sandalwood paste in the palace of the King of Matsya?
Meghavarṇa said:
"Father, I consider this dwelling with an enemy to be like the vow of walking upon the edge of a sword.
He replied: "O King!"
So it is;
however, nowhere have I ever seen such a gathering of fools,
nor have I seen anyone so wise as Raktākṣa, who possesses great insight and a mind peerless in many treatises.
For that reason, he has understood my mind exactly as it is;
whereas other ministers are great fools who live merely on the designation of being "ministers," being unskilled in reality, and by whom even this was not known. For:
A servant who has come from afar, being wicked and devoted to associating with him,
is corrupted because he shares the nature of a spy and is constantly anxious.
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, or with regard to drinks, food, and possessions—seeing an opening among those who are heedless, enemies strike at their foes. (Pañca 3.233)
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person, being attentive, should protect himself— the abode of the three aims of life— for through negligence one perishes.
And it is well said:
"Whom do diseases not torment who eats unwholesome food?
Whom do the faults of policy not overcome who follows bad counsel?"
Whom does prosperity not intoxicate? Whom does death not strike down?
And whom do the objects of the senses, once accepted, not torment?
The fame of the greedy perishes; the friendship of the backbiter is lost; the virtue of one who neglects his duties and is intent on wealth is destroyed;
the fruit of knowledge belongs to the addicted; and happiness belongs to the miserly.
The kingdom of a lord of men whose ministers are negligent.
Therefore, O King, as for what you have said—that I have practiced the "sword-edge vow" (asidhārāvrata) because of association with enemies—that has been experienced by me directly. And it is said:
"Placing dishonor in front and casting pride behind one's back..."
A wise person should rescue their own interest, for the ruin of one's purpose is indeed folly.
A wise person, having found the right time, may even carry an enemy on his shoulder;
many frogs were killed by a great black serpent.
Meghavarṇa asked, "How was that?
Sthirajīvī related: Story 15.
The Story of the Slowly Poisonous Snake:
In a certain region near Mount Varuṇādri, there lived an old black snake named Mandaviṣa (Slow-Poison).
He reflected thus in his mind: "How indeed may I maintain my livelihood by means of an easy method?"
Then, having approached a pond containing many frogs, he showed himself as if overcome by dejection.
While he remained thus, he was questioned by a certain frog who had gone to the edge of the water:
"O Noble One, why do you not move about today for the sake of food as you did before?"
He said: "My good friend, how could there be any desire for food for one as unfortunate as I?
For this reason: today, at the very onset of night, while I was wandering about in search of food, I saw a single frog."
To capture him, I prepared a trap;
but he, seeing me, fled through the midst of some Brahmins intent on their Vedic recitations out of fear of death, and I could not discern where he had gone.
With my mind deluded by his likeness, I bit the thumb of a certain Brahmin’s son as it lay within the water at the edge of a lake.
Then he immediately met his death.
Thereupon, his grieving father cursed me, saying: "O wicked soul!
By you my innocent son was bitten."
"Therefore, because of this fault, you shall become the vehicle for frogs;
I shall live by a livelihood obtained through their favor. Thus, I have come here for the purpose of being your vehicle.
And he informed all the frogs of this;

then, with hearts full of joy, they all went and made this report to the frog-king named Jalapāda. Thereupon, the king, surrounded by his ministers and considering this to be most wonderful, ascended the pond in great haste and mounted the hood of the mildly venomous serpent.
The others also mounted upon his back according to their seniority.
What need of more? Those who could not reach a place on top ran after him, following closely at his heels.
Even Mandaviṣa, for the sake of pleasing them, displayed various kinds of extraordinary movements.
Then Jalapāda, having obtained comfort, said to him:
"Neither by elephant, nor by horse, nor by chariot,
nor even by a human vehicle is there such a journey for me as that which has been made with slow poison."
Then, on another day, Mandaviṣa began to crawl very slowly under a pretext;
seeing this, Jalapāda said, "My good friend Mandaviṣa!"
"Why is it not carried as before today?
Mandaviṣa replied, "O King, due to a deficiency in food today, I have no strength to carry it.
Then he said, "My good man!"
"Eat the small frogs!
Upon hearing this, Mandaviṣa, his entire body thrilled with joy, spoke with agitation: "I am indeed subject to this Brahmin’s curse;
therefore, I am pleased by these words of permission from you."
Then, by eating frogs continuously, he became strong within just a few days.
Delighted, he laughed inwardly and said this:
"Indeed, these various frogs have been secured through a ruse."
For how long would they remain unexhausted, even while being eaten by me?
Even Jalapāda, his mind utterly deluded by the new armor produced by the mild venom, did not perceive anything at all.
In the meantime, another large black snake arrived at that spot;
seeing him being carried along by the frogs, he was filled with amazement.
And he said: "Friend, how can you be carried by those whose food is ours?
This is contradictory."
Mandaviṣa said:
"I understand all this—that I am being deceived by frogs—yet I shall wait for a little while, like the Brahmin who was blinded by ghee. (Pancatantra 3.241)
He asked, "How was that?
Mandaviṣa relates:
Story 16.
The Story of the Ghee-blind Brāhmaṇa:
In a certain town there was a Brāhmaṇa named Yajñadatta.

His wife was unchaste, her mind intent on another man; she would constantly prepare oil-cakes and ghee-filled cakes with pieces of meat for a paramour and give them to him by stealing them from her husband.
Then, on one occasion, her husband saw this and said, "My dear,
what is this being cooked? And where are you constantly taking this?"
"Tell me the truth.
Then she, having conceived a clever wit, spoke to her husband with fabricated words: "Not far from here is the temple of the Blessed Goddess;
there, having fasted, I take offerings and various special foods."
Then, seeing that [object], she took it all and set out toward the temple of the Goddess;

for she thought that when this was offered to the Goddess, my husband would think: "While my Brahmin wife has gone down into the river to bathe for the sake of the Blessed One, her husband has also arrived by another path at the Goddess’s [shrine]."
He stood behind her, invisible.

Then that brahmin woman, having bathed and come to the temple of the goddess, performed the rites of bathing, anointing, offering garlands, incense, and oblations; and having bowed to the goddess, she petitioned her: "O Blessed One, by what means will my husband become blind?"
Hearing that through the change in his voice, the Brahmin standing behind the queen said, "If you continue to give that husband of yours food such as ghee-filled cakes and the like,
he will soon become blind.
But that unchaste woman, her mind deceived by those feigned words, gave that very same food to the Brahmin every day.
Then on another day, the Brahmin said, "My lady,
I cannot see at all.
Hearing this, she thought to herself, "This is a favor bestowed upon me by the Queen."
Now, her heart’s beloved paramour, thinking "This blind Brahmin will do me no harm," came to her side every day without hesitation.
Then one day, seeing him entering and approaching close by, she seized him by the hair and beat him with blows from clubs and heels until he met his death.
She also cut off the nose of that stout wife and sent her away.

Therefore I say: "One should carry even an enemy on one's shoulder," and so forth. Now, O King, just as the frogs were destroyed by me through my dull poison and my power of intelligence, so too have all my enemies been slain.
And this is well said:
A fire blazing in the forest protects its roots while burning them;
whereas the wind, though gentle and cool, may uproot them entirely.
Meghavarṇa said: "Father, this is indeed true.
Those who are great-souled are beings of great substance; even when fallen into calamity, they do not abandon what they have begun."
And as it has been said:
"This is the greatness of the great who wear the ornament of policy:
that they do not abandon what has been undertaken, even in the face of hardship or the onset of calamity. (Pañca 3.243)
And so it is said:
"The base do not indeed begin an undertaking out of fear of obstacles; the mediocre, having begun, desist when thwarted by obstacles."
Even when struck by obstacles multiplied a thousandfold,
those of superior virtue do not abandon what they have begun.
My kingdom has been rendered free of thorns by you, who have brought my enemies to total extinction;
or rather, this is precisely what those who know statecraft consider appropriate.
For it has been said:
A wise person does not come to grief when they have completely eliminated the remainder of a debt, the remainder of a fire, the remainder of an enemy, and likewise the remainder of a disease. (3.245)
He said: "O King,
you alone are fortunate, for everything you have undertaken has been completely successful."
Thus, it is not valor alone that accomplishes a task;
rather, only that which is performed with wisdom leads to victory. And it has been said:
"Enemies slain by weapons are indeed not truly slain."
But enemies destroyed by wisdom are truly well-slain;
a weapon slays only a man's single body, whereas wisdom destroys his family, his prosperity, and his fame. (3.246)
Thus, for one endowed with both wisdom and human effort, the accomplishment of tasks occurs without exertion. And it has been said:
"The intellect expands at the commencement of an undertaking, mindfulness becomes firm, and counsel, bringing forth its own objectives, does not fall into confusion."
Reasoning becomes fruitful, the mind attains exaltation, and a man destined for success finds delight in praiseworthy action. (Pañcāstikāya 3.247)
And thus, sovereignty belongs to a man endowed with policy, generosity, and valor. As it has been said:
"A person who delights in association becomes virtuous when associating with one who is generous, brave, and wise;
from the virtuous comes wealth, from wealth comes prosperity, from prosperity comes authority, and from that, sovereignty. (Pañcatantra 3.248)

Meghavarṇa said: "Surely the treatises on political ethics bear fruit immediately, since you, by entering [the enemy's service] through disguise, have utterly destroyed the crusher of foes along with his retinue.
Sthirajīvin said:
"Even that objective which is attainable only through the employment of harsh means..."
For him as well, it is first proper to rely upon a worthy person;
for the lordly tree, lofty in its summit and the very essence of the forests, is felled only after being honored and worshipped.
Or rather, my lord,
what is the use of saying that which, in the immediate situation, is devoid of action or difficult to accomplish?
And this is well said:
"By those who are indecisive, fearful of commitment,
and whose purpose is the pleasure of conversing as they please,"
In this world, words that fail to correspond with their results become objects of ridicule.
Furthermore, the wise should not show disregard even for tasks that are minor; for it is said:
"Thinking, 'I am able to do this small thing, which can be accomplished without effort,' those who neglect a duty out of such disregard [perish]."
Some men, with heedless minds, undergo the suffering of remorse, which is easily encountered through the occurrence of calamities.
Therefore, today my lord, having conquered his enemies, will obtain sleep as before.
And it is said:
"One sleeps happily in a house that is either free of snakes or where the snakes have been bound."
But for one who constantly sees snakes, sleep is obtained only with great difficulty.
And so it is said:

"Of those undertakings which are to be accomplished by extensive effort, which possess great magnitude, which are accompanied by affectionate blessings, which rise through both policy and daring, and which ascend to the heights of one's desire..."
For one who is addicted to the prowess of pride and arrogance, as long as they have not reached the further shore,
how can there be peace while the heart remains a domain for resentment?
Therefore, my heart seems to find rest now that the undertaking of my duties has been concluded.

Thus, having now eliminated all thorns [from your path], devote yourself to the protection of your subjects and enjoy for a long time this kingdom—where the glory of your royal umbrella and throne remains unshakable through the succession of sons and grandsons. Moreover:
"A king who does not delight his subjects with qualities such as protection and the like [is no true king]."
Like the fleshy protuberance on a camel's neck, his kingdom is utterly useless.
That king who has passion for virtues, disregard for calamities, and delight in good servants,
enjoys for a long time the kingdom where the silken fly-whisks are ever-wavering.
The royal glory, adorned with the white parasol.

And you must not, thinking "I have obtained the kingdom," allow yourself to be corrupted by the intoxication of power (*śrī-mada*). For this reason: the prosperities of a king are indeed fickle; the royal fortune (*rājya-lakṣmī*) is as difficult to ascend as a bamboo pole, and it is prone to falling in an instant.
Though maintained with hundreds of efforts, it is difficult to hold;
though propitiated with praise, it deceives in the end;
like the race of monkeys, its mind is scattered and restless.
Like a lotus petal, it is not joined by any fastening; like the movement of the wind, it is exceedingly fickle;
like association with the ignoble, it is unstable.
Like a venomous serpent, she is difficult to serve;
like a streak of twilight clouds, her passion lasts but a moment; and like a row of water bubbles, she is fragile by nature.
It is as ungrateful as the nature of the body,
and as fleeting as a heap of wealth obtained in a dream, seen for a moment and then vanished. Moreover,
at the very moment one is consecrated in the kingdom—
At that very moment, one's intellect should be applied to misfortunes;
for at the time of a king's consecration, jars indeed pour forth calamity along with the water.
And there is indeed no calamity that cannot be encountered; as it has been said:
"The wandering of Rāma in the forest, the dwelling of the sons of Pāṇḍu in the woods, the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, and the fall of King Nala from his kingdom."
Reflecting on the fall of Arjuna, who was a master of dramatic arts, at the hands of the Lord of Laṅkā, all people here must endure it under the power of time; who can protect whom?
Where has that Daśaratha gone, having become a friend of Mahendra in heaven? Where is King Sagara, who bound the shore of the ocean?
Where is Vainya, born from the palm of the hand? And where is Manu, whose body was the sun?
Surely these have been awakened and then closed back up by powerful Time.
Where has Māndhātṛ gone, the conqueror of the three worlds? Where is King Satyavrata?
Where has Nahuṣa, the king of the gods and master of the true scriptures, gone, O Keśava? They were thought to occupy the throne of Śakra, accompanied by chariots and excellent elephants.
They were indeed imitated by the Great Soul in due time, and they were exiled by Time itself.
Moreover: That king, those ministers, those women, and those groves and forests—
both he, they, and those things— have perished, as seen by Kṛtānta.
Thus, having obtained the royal fortune—which is as fickle as the ear of an elephant in rut—enjoy it while remaining solely devoted to justice.
Thus ends the third book, titled "The Crows and the Owls," in the *Pañcatantra* composed by Śrī Viṣṇuśarman. //3//
Now begins the fourth tantra, named "The Loss of What Was Gained" (Labdha-praṇāśa).
Thus commences this fourth tantra called "The Loss of What Was Gained."
Of whom this is the first verse:
"He whose intellect does not falter when tasks arise—he alone crosses over the difficult passage, just like the monkey staying in the water. *Pañcatantra* 4.1.
As it is heard in tradition— the introductory narrative of the story concerning the monkey and the crocodile.
On a certain seashore there was a great jambu tree that bore fruit at all times. There lived a monkey named Raktamukha.
Once, beneath that tree, a makara named Karālamukha emerged from the waters of the ocean and settled on the shore, which was covered with very soft sand.
Then Raktamukha said to him:
"O sir, you are a guest who has arrived;
therefore, please eat these jambu fruits given by me, which are like nectar. And it is said:
Whether he is dear or hateful, whether he is a fool or a scholar,
one who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who serves as a bridge to heaven.
Manu has declared that one should not inquire about the guest's conduct, lineage, learning, or family at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite or during a śrāddha ceremony.
He who honors a guest who has arrived at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering, weary from the fatigue of a long journey, attains the supreme goal.
When a guest departs from someone's house unhonored and sighing in frustration,
that person's ancestors turn their faces away and depart along with the deities.
Having spoken thus, he gave him rose-apples (*jambū-phala*).
He too, having eaten them and enjoyed the pleasure of conversation with him for a long time, returned once more to his own abode.

In this manner, those two—the monkey and the crocodile—remained constantly in the shade of the rose-apple tree, spending their time in the company of various scriptural discussions, living in happiness.
That makara, too, would go home and give the remaining jambu fruits he had eaten to his wife. Then, on one occasion, she asked him: "My lord, where do you obtain such nectar-like fruits?"
He said: "My dear lady, I have a dear friend, a monkey named Raktamukha;
he gives me these fruits out of affection."
Then she said, "The heart of one who always eats such fruits as these, which are like nectar, will become composed of nectar.
Therefore, if you have need of a wife,"
"Therefore, give me his heart,
so that by eating it, I may be free from old age and death and enjoy pleasures with you. He said, "O lady,"
Do not speak thus;
for he has accepted us as his brothers,
and moreover, he is the giver of fruit.
Therefore, it is impossible to cause harm;
abandon this false attachment. And it has been said:
"A mother gives birth to one [body], but speech gives birth to a second."
They spoke words that were even more excessive than those of a blood relative.
Then Makarī said: "You have never once acted contrary to my word;
therefore, she must surely be that female monkey, since you spend the entire day there out of affection for her."
Thus you have been correctly understood by me; for— You do not offer me a word with joy, nor do you grant anything I desire; generally, you sigh rapidly during the nights like the flame of a fire.
That you are lax in embracing my neck and that you do not kiss me with passion— O rogue, it is because some other beloved dwells in your heart, just as my own does.
He too, having clasped his wife’s feet and placed them upon his lap, spoke very dejectedly to her as she was at the height of her anger:
“O beloved of my life, since I have fallen at your feet and have become your servant, why, O wrathful one, do you maintain your anger? (Pañca 4.8)
Having heard those words, she, her face bathed in tears, said to him:
"O rogue, that very same beloved of yours, charming with her artificial affectations, remains in your mind along with hundreds of your desires."
There is no possibility whatsoever for us here; therefore, enough with these mockeries of prostrating at your feet.
Furthermore, if she is not dear to you,
why do you not kill her even though I have told you?
Or, if that monkey is dear to you, then what kind of affection do you have for him?
So what need is there for much?
Know this: if I do not devour his heart, then consider my fast unto death already accomplished.
Having thus understood her resolve, his heart agitated with anxiety, he said: "Or rather, it is well said:
'The diamond-smear, the fool, women, and the crab share one and the same grip; likewise do the fish, indigo, wine, and milk. (Pañcatantra 4.10)
"What shall I do? How can he be slain by me?
Having reflected thus, he went to the side of the monkey.
The monkey also, seeing him arrive after a long time looking anxious, said: "O friend! Why have you come so late today? Why do you not speak with joy?"
"You do not recite the well-spoken words.
He said, "Friend, I have been addressed with exceedingly harsh words by your brother's wife: 'O ungrateful man!'"
Do not show me your own face,
for you live off your friend every day,
yet you do not even return his favor by showing him your home.
Therefore, there is no atonement even for you. And it has been said:

"For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, the breaker of vows, and the rogue—atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement. (Pañcatantra 4.11)
"Therefore, for the sake of repaying my kindness, take my brother-in-law today and bring him home;
otherwise, there will be no meeting with you for me in the next world.
Having been addressed thus by her, I have come into your presence.
Therefore, such a long time has passed while I have been quarreling with her today on your account. So come to my house;

your brother’s wife is waiting there in eager anticipation, having prepared the fourfold offerings, arranged appropriate ornaments of cloth, gems, rubies, and the like, and hung a garland of salutation at the doorway.
The monkey said: "O friend, what my brother’s wife has said is correct. And it is said:
A man who is even more wise should avoid a friend who has the character of a weaver."
The greedy one who constantly draws [objects] toward himself as if they were right before his eyes.
And thus:
"He gives and receives, he tells secrets and asks questions, he eats and causes [the other] to eat; this sixfold manner is the mark of affection. (Pañca 4.13)
"However, we are forest-dwellers, and your home is at the edge of the water;
therefore, how is it possible to go there?
For that reason, bring even my brother's wife here, so that I may bow down and receive her blessing."
He said, "O friend, there is our home on a very beautiful stretch of sand in the middle of the ocean; mount my back and go there comfortably, free from fear.
Having heard this, he also spoke joyfully, "My good sir!"
If this is so, why delay? Make haste!
Here I am, mounted upon your back.
When it had been done so, seeing the crocodile moving through the fathomless ocean, the monkey, his mind terrified with fear, said: "Brother!
Proceed very slowly;
my body is being submerged by the waves of the water."
Hearing this, the crocodile thought: "He has reached the bottomless water and has come under my control;
having mounted my back, he cannot move even so much as a sesame seed.
Therefore, I shall tell him my own intention."
By means of which he performs the recollection of his chosen deity.
And he said: "Friend, you were brought by me to be executed, having been made to trust through the words of your wife."
"Therefore, let your chosen deity be remembered.
He said, "Brother,
what wrong have I done to her, or even to you, that a means for my execution has been devised?"
The crocodile said:
"O sir, a longing has arisen in you to eat her heart, which is as sweet as the taste of the juice of nectar-fruits;
for that reason, this was done."
The monkey Pratyutpannamati said:
"My good sir, if that was the case, why did you not tell me right then and there?
For this reason, I have always kept my own heart well-hidden within the hollow of a rose-apple tree."
"I shall entrust that to my brother's wife.
Why have you brought me here with a vacant heart?
Hearing this, the crocodile said joyfully, "My good friend!"
"If that is so, then give me your heart,
so that my wicked wife may eat it and rise from her fast;
I shall lead you back to that very Jambu tree."
Having spoken thus, he turned back and went to the base of the rose-apple tree (*jambū*).
The monkey, too, having somehow performed various offerings and worship to the deities with his chatter, reached the shore.
Then, after walking back and forth for a very long time, he climbed that same rose-apple tree and thought: "Aha!"
Life has indeed been regained;
or rather, it is well said:
"One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one trust even the trustworthy."
Fear born from misplaced trust cuts away even one's very roots.
"Today this has become for me like a day of rebirth," he thought;
then the crocodile said, "O friend,
give up that heart so that your brother's wife, having eaten it, may rise from her fast."
Then, laughing and reproaching him, the monkey said to him: "Fie, fie upon you, fool, betrayer of trust!
Does anyone possess two hearts?
Therefore, depart at once to the foot of the rose-apple tree; you must never come here again."
And as it has been said:
"He who desires to reunite with a friend who has once proved treacherous embraces death, just as a female mule conceives a foal. (Pañcatantra 4.15)
Having heard that, the crocodile thought with great embarrassment: "Alas!
What have I, in my extreme folly, revealed of my own inner intention to him?
Therefore, if he should somehow regain his confidence once more..."
Therefore, I shall inspire confidence in you once more;
and he said: "Friend, I inquired after your intentions in jest."
"She has no need for you in her heart;
therefore, come to our house as a guest.
The monkey said, "O wicked one!"
"Go;
I shall not come now. And it is said:
"What sin will a hungry man not commit?"
"People who have lost their wealth become pitiless.
Tell Priyadarśana, O blessed lady, that Gaṅgadatta will not return to the well again. (Pancaka 4.16)
The crocodile asked: "How was that?
He replied:
"Story 1."
The Story of Gaṅgadatta and Priyadarśana:
In a certain well there lived a king of frogs named Gaṅgadatta.
Once, being harassed by his kinsmen, he climbed up the rope of a water-wheel and emerged.
Then he thought: "How can I retaliate against those heirs? And it is said:

"I consider that man to have been born all over again who, having wronged both of these—the one who did him harm in times of misfortune and the one who mocked him in difficult circumstances—does so once more. (Pañca 4.17)
Thinking thus, he saw a black snake entering the hole.
Upon seeing it, he thought once more: "I shall take this [snake] to that well and bring about the destruction of all my kinsmen. And it is said:
"One should employ an enemy against an enemy, and a stronger one against a strong one."
Since there would be no suffering whatsoever here for one's own purpose upon the destruction of that [body]. (4.18)
And so it is said:
"A wise man should uproot an enemy by means of a sharp enemy, just as one extracts a painful thorn with another thorn for the sake of comfort. (Pañcatantra 4.19)
Having thus reflected, he went to the entrance of the cave and called out to him: "Come, come, Priyadarśana! Come!
Hearing this, the serpent thought: "He who calls me thus is not of my own kind."
Since this is not the voice of a serpent,
and I have no alliance with anyone else in the mortal world, I shall remain right here in this fortress for now to discover who he might be. And it is said:
"One should not form an association with one whose conduct, lineage, and refuge are unknown," so said Bṛhaspati.
Perhaps some practitioner of spells or one skilled in medicinal herbs will summon me and cast me into bondage;
or perhaps some person, harboring enmity, summons me for the purpose of devouring someone.
And he says: "Ho! Who are you?"
He said, "I am Gaṅgadatta by name, the lord of frogs; I have come into your presence for the sake of friendship.
Having heard that, the serpent said, "O friend! This is incredible—that there should be a union of grass with fire. And it is said:"
He who is destined to be killed by another does not, under any circumstances, even in a dream, approach that person; so why do you prattle on in this way?
Gaṅgadatta said: "O sir!
This is true;
you are our natural enemy."
"Having suffered successive humiliations, I have come into your presence. And it has been said:
'When total ruin has occurred and even one's life is in jeopardy, one should protect one's life and wealth even by bowing down before an enemy. (Pañca 4.22)
The serpent said, "Tell me, why have you been insulted? He replied, "By my kinsmen. The serpent asked further, "Where is your dwelling—in a pond, a well, a lake, or a pool?"
"Therefore, tell me your own abode.
He replied, "In a well constructed with a heap of stones.
The serpent said, "Alas! We are footless."
There is such a place, and I have access to it; yet for one who has entered, there is no place where,
while staying, I might destroy your heirs.
Therefore, let it be so. And it has been said:
"One who desires prosperity should eat that which is capable of being swallowed, which, once swallowed, is digested, and which is wholesome upon digestion. (Pañcatantra 4.23)
Gaṅgadatta said: "O sir, come along;
I shall cause you to enter there by an easy means."
Likewise, in the middle of that place, near the water's edge, there is a most delightful hollow;
staying there, you shall kill your kinsmen with ease.
Having heard this, the serpent reflected: "I am, after all, advanced in years."
"Perhaps at some time, by some means, I might catch a single mouse;
this is a source of happiness and a means of livelihood shown to me by this wretch of a kinsman.
Therefore, I shall go and eat those frogs."
Or rather, it is well said:
"For that wise person who has his life-breath exhausted and is deprived of companions should indeed arrange a livelihood consisting of all means for happiness. (Pañca 4.24)
Having reflected thus, he said to him: "O Gaṅgadatta,
if it is so, then go ahead,
so that we may both go there."
Gaṅgadatta said: "O Priyadarśana!
I shall lead you there by an easy means and show you the place; those very ones are to be eaten."
The snake said: "Now you have become my friend;
therefore, you must not fear.
By your word, those heirs of yours shall be eaten."

Having spoken thus, he emerged from his hole, embraced him, and set out with him. Then, upon reaching a well, the snake was led by that man through the path of the water-wheel buckets to his own dwelling.
Gaṅgadatta said: "My good friend!"
"How can you perform the duty of a friend?
Therefore, go now by this very path of the water-clock.
The snake said, "O Gaṅgadatta!"
"You have not spoken correctly.
How shall I go there?
My own cave-fortress will have been occupied by another."
"Therefore, give one frog from your own kind to me while I remain here;
otherwise, I shall devour them all.
Hearing this, Gaṅgadatta, his mind distressed, reflected: "Alas, what have I done by bringing this serpent!"
Therefore, if I were to reject him, he would devour everyone;
or rather, it is rightly said:
"He who makes an enemy his friend when that enemy is superior to himself in prowess..."
He performs it without doubt, for he himself consumes poison.
Therefore, I shall grant him one friend each day. And it has been said:
"Wise men, when faced with an enemy intent on seizing all their possessions, satisfy him with small gifts, just as the ocean satisfies the submarine fire (bāḍava). (Pañcatantra 4.26)
And so it is said:
"He who, though weak, when entreated even by a powerful person, does not yield even the slightest thing, even through conciliation,"
He does not give even when it is being shown to him;
instead, he gives a khārī of powder.
And so it is said:
"When total ruin has arisen, the wise man abandons half;
with the remaining half he accomplishes his purpose, for total ruin is difficult to overcome. (Pañca 4.28)
A wise man should not destroy a great deal for the sake of a small thing;
for this indeed is wisdom: that one protects the great by means of the small.
Having reflected thus, he constantly assigns one [victim] at a time;
and having devoured that one, he devours others as well when he is out of sight.
Or rather, it is well said:
For just as one sits anywhere at all with soiled clothes,
so too does one whose wealth has been squandered fail to protect what remains of that wealth.

Then, on another day, after he had eaten other frogs, he devoured Yamunādatta, the son of Gaṅgadatta. Thinking him to have been eaten, Gaṅgadatta, intent on lamenting "Woe! Woe! in a loud voice, did not cease his outcry by any means. Thereupon, he was addressed by his own wife:
Why do you cry out, O you whose cries are ill-timed, you who cause the destruction of your own side?
Once the destruction of your own side has occurred, who will be our protector?
Therefore, even now, consider your own escape and the means for his slaughter.
Then, as time passed, the entire family of frogs was devoured;
only Gaṅgadatta remained.
Then Priyadarśana said, "O Gaṅgadatta!
I am hungry;
all the frogs have been eaten up."
"Therefore, let some food be given to me, for I have been brought here by you.
He replied, "O friend,
while I am staying here, you need not worry about this matter at all."
"Therefore, if you send me, I shall inspire confidence in the frogs residing in other wells and bring them here.
He said, "As for me, you are not to be eaten; you stand in the place of a brother. If you do this, then you truly become my father."
"Therefore, let it be done thus.
Having heard this, he too, having resorted to the water-wheel at the well and having offered prayers and performed worship with various articles provided for the deities, emerged from that well.
Priyadarśana also remained there, waiting in expectation of him.
Then, when Gaṅgadatta had not returned for a long time, Priyadarśana said to a monitor lizard living in another hollow: "My dear lady, please provide some small assistance;
for Gaṅgadatta has been a close acquaintance of yours for a long time."
Therefore, go to his presence and, having searched for him at some reservoir, deliver my message so that he may come very quickly even alone, if other frogs do not arrive;
for I am unable to remain here without you.
Likewise, if I have acted against you, that misdeed has been held by me within my own merit.
At those words, the iguana also searched for Gaṅgadatta even more swiftly and said, "O noble Gaṅgadatta!
That friend of yours, Priyadarśana, remains here watching the path for your return."
Therefore, come quickly!
Furthermore, he has kept a favor done for you in his heart regarding the making of you deformed; so come together with a mind free from apprehension.
Having heard that, Gaṅgadatta said:
"What sin will a hungry man not commit?
When their resources are exhausted, men become devoid of compassion."
"Tell Priyadarśana, O blessed lady,
that Gaṅgadatta will not return to the well again."
Having spoken thus, he dismissed her.
"O wicked aquatic creature!
Just like Gaṅgadatta, I shall by no means go to your house."
Having heard that, the crocodile said, "O friend!
Otherwise, I shall give up my life upon you by means of fasting.
The monkey said, "Fool!"
Am I a fool with long ears?
Even having seen the danger, I go there myself and destroy myself.
He who has come and gone, and having gone, comes back again—[what is his fate]?
The fool, whose heart was not attentive, met his death right there.
The crocodile said: "My good sir, who is this Lambakarṇa?
How is it that he has died even though his downfall was witnessed?"
"Therefore, let it be related to me.
The monkey said:
"The Second Story."
The Story of Karālakeśara:
In a certain region of the forest, there lived a lion named Karālakeśara.
He had a jackal named Dhūsaraka who was always his follower and attendant.
Then, on one occasion, while he was fighting with an elephant, severe blows were inflicted upon his body;
by these, he was unable to move even a single step.
And because of his inability to move, Dhūsaraka became weak, his throat emaciated by hunger.
On another day, he said to him: "Master, I am tormented by hunger;
I am not even able to move a single step."
"So, how shall I serve you? The lion said,
"My friend, go and search for some creature."
"By this means, even though he has reached such a state, I shall kill him.
Having heard this, the jackal, while searching, reached a certain nearby village.
There, he saw a donkey named Lambakarna, who was with difficulty tasting sparse sprouts of dūrvā grass at the edge of a pond.
Then, having approached him, he said: "O uncle, please accept this salutation from me;
it has been a long time since we last saw one another."
"Therefore, tell me, why has he come to such weakness?
He replied, "O sister's son,
what shall I say?"
The washerman torments me with excessive cruelty and an unbearable burden; he does not even give me a handful of fodder.
I eat nothing but sprouts of dūrvā grass mixed with ashes.
"How then can there be nourishment for my body?
The jackal said, "Uncle,
if that is so, there is a most delightful region, abounding in grass as green as emeralds and graced by rivers."
"Having come there, remain with me, enjoying the pleasure of a conversation on well-spoken words.
Lambakarṇa said, "O son of my sister,
what you have said is appropriate."
"But we are mere village animals, fit to be slain by those who roam the forest; so what is the use of that auspicious place?
The jackal said, "Uncle!"
Do not speak thus;
that region is protected by the cage of my own arms.
No one else has entry there.
"Furthermore, because of this very same fault, we three orphaned she-asses have been tormented by the washerman;
now that they have grown fat and are full of youthful vigor, they said this to me: 'If you are truly our maternal uncle, then go to some other village and bring us a husband suitable for us;
for that purpose, I shall take you there.'"
Then, having heard the words of the jackal, his body tormented by desire, he said to him: "My good sir, if it is so, then go ahead so that I may follow;
or rather, as it is well said:"
There is neither nectar nor poison whatsoever, with the sole exception of a woman of shapely hips;
for by union with her one lives, and by separation from her one dies.
And so it is said:

"If even by their names alone desire might arise without seeing them or meeting them, how is it that one's curiosity does not melt upon actually obtaining the sight and company of those very women? (Pañca 4.35)
When that was carried out, he returned to the presence of the lion together with the jackal.
As soon as the lion, agitated by pain, saw him and rose up, the donkey began to flee.
Then, as he was fleeing, the lion struck him with a blow of his paw.
And that [blow] proved as futile as the effort of an unfortunate man.
In the meantime, the jackal, overcome with anger, said to him: "O sir, why was such a blow dealt by you?"
Since even a donkey passes before you by force,
how will you fight with an elephant?
Thus has your strength been seen.
Then the lion, with a meaningful smile, said: "O sir, what can I do?
I had not prepared my stride."
"Otherwise, even an elephant, when stepped upon by my stride, cannot move.
The jackal said, "Even now, I will bring him to you once more;
however, you must remain with your stride prepared."
The lion said, "My good sir,
how could he who has departed after seeing me face-to-face ever come here again? Therefore, search for some other creature."
The jackal said, "What business have you with this?
You simply remain standing with your limbs ready.
When this was done, the jackal also proceeded along the path of the donkey.
While he was still wandering in that very place, he was spotted.
Then, seeing the jackal, the donkey said: "O son of my sister!
You have led me to a fine place."
"I have swiftly fallen under the power of death.
Therefore, tell me: what creature was it that, by a blow from a hand like an exceedingly fierce thunderbolt, I was released?
Hearing this, the jackal said with a laugh, "My good sir!"
Seeing you approaching, the she-ass rose up with passion to embrace you;
but you, out of cowardice, fled.
She, however, was unable to remain without you.
She, however, extended her hand for the sake of supporting you as you were falling,
and for no other reason;
therefore, come.
For your sake, she remains seated in a fast unto death.
She says this: "If Lambakarṇa does not become my husband, then I shall enter fire or water;
I cannot endure separation from him again."
Therefore, show favor and come there;
otherwise, you will incur the sin of killing a woman, and furthermore, the Blessed One will direct his wrath toward you. And it has been said:

Those fools of perverted intellect, seeking false fruits, abandon the female consort (*strī-mudrā*) of the Makaradhvaja— the victorious one who bestows all prosperity and half of everything— and depart;
yet they are struck down by that very same [consort] with extreme ruthlessness, stripped naked and shorn bald.
Some are clad in red robes, some have matted hair, and others are Kāpālikas.
Then, having heard those words as something worthy of trust, he set out once more with him.
Or rather, it is well said:
even though a man knows better, he commits a censurable act through the power of fate.
What kind of action in this world is censured by some, and how is it pleasing to others? (5.37)
In the meantime, that long-eared one was killed by the lion according to his prepared plan.
Then, having slain him and appointed the jackal as guardian, the lion himself went to the river to bathe.
Out of greed and eagerness, the jackal also devoured his ears and heart.

In the meantime, just as the lion was returning after bathing, performing worship to the gods, and offering libations to the ancestors, he found the donkey standing there, deprived of its ears and heart.
Seeing him, the lion, his soul overcome with rage, said to the jackal: "Wretch!
Why have you committed such an improper act?"
"Since he has been rendered into a state of leavings by this one's devouring of his heart," the jackal said with humility, "My lord,
do not speak thus!"
"Because this donkey was previously deprived of his ears and heart,
he has come here, beheld you, and returned once more.
Then, considering your words to be trustworthy, the lion shared [the meat] with him and, his mind free from suspicion, devoured him.
Therefore I say: "He has come and he has indeed gone. O fool, you have practiced deception!
But it was destroyed by Yudhiṣṭhira himself through his word of truth.
Or rather, it is well said:
"That deceitful person of very dull intellect who speaks the truth while abandoning his own interest—"
He will surely fall away from his own welfare, like another Yudhiṣṭhira.
The crocodile asked: "How was that?
He replied:
"The third story."
The Story of the Potter named Yudhiṣṭhira:
In a certain town there lived a potter.
Once, due to negligence, he fell with great force upon the sharp edge of a half-submerged potsherd while running.
Then, his forehead split by the tip of a spear, his body drenched in blood, he rose with great difficulty and returned to his own abode.
Subsequently, due to his indulgence in unwholesome food, that wound became agonizing; however, with great effort, he was restored to health.
Later, when a certain region was afflicted by famine, the potter—his throat parched with hunger—went to another land along with some royal servants and became a servant to a king.
The king, too, seeing the terrible wound from the blow upon his forehead, reflected:
"This must be some heroic man; surely he has struck him a direct blow upon the surface of his forehead."
Therefore, he looked upon him with a special favor in the midst of all the princes by means of his equal treatment and other marks of distinction.
Those princes, seeing that excessive favor shown to him, bore a sense of supreme envy; yet, out of fear of the king, they said nothing.

Then, on another day, while the king’s estimation of his heroes was being carried out, as war was imminent, elephants were being prepared, horses were being harnessed, and warriors were being arrayed—
While he was being treated by that king, the potter was questioned by him in private, in accordance with the occasion: "O prince, what is your name? What is your caste?
In which battle did this wound strike upon your forehead?"
He said, "O King, this was not a blow from a weapon;
I am a potter by nature named Yudhiṣṭhira. In my house there were many shards."
Then once, having drunk liquor, he went out and fell upon a potsherd while running;
this wound from that blow on my forehead has thus become so hideous.
Hearing this, the king said with shame, "Alas! I have been deceived by this potter who imitates the son of a king!"
"Therefore, let half of this moon be given to him immediately.
When this was done, the potter said, "Do not do so!
Behold my manual dexterity in battle!"
The king said: "You are endowed with every virtue;
nevertheless, you must go. And it is said:
'O son, though you are a Śūdra and have encountered obstacles, you are handsome to behold.'"
In the family in which you were born, O elephant, no one is killed there.
The potter asked: "How was that?
The king related:
Story 4.
The Story of the Lion Couple:
In a certain region, a lion couple lived together.
Then, the lioness gave birth to two sons.
The lion, too, habitually killed deer and gave them to the lioness;
however, on another day, he did not obtain anything at all,
so that even as he wandered about, the sun set.
Then, as he was returning to his own home, he encountered a jackal cub.
Thinking, "This is but a young child," he carefully placed it between his teeth and handed it over to the lioness while it was still alive.
Thereupon, the lioness said: "O beloved!"
"Have you brought any food for us?
The lion said, "My dear,
today I have not encountered any creature at all, having let go of this jackal cub."
And because I considered him a mere child—and especially because he was of my own species—I did not kill him. For it is said:
"One should never strike women, those with false marks, or children, even when their lives are at stake, and especially those who are trusting. (Pañcārakṣā 4.40)
"Now, eat this and make yourself well;
at dawn I shall procure something else.
He said, "O beloved!"
Thinking, "This is but a child," you did not kill him;
so how could I destroy him for the sake of my own belly? And it is said:
"One must never perform an improper act, even when the loss of one's life has arrived."
And one's duty must not be abandoned; this is the eternal law.
"Therefore, this shall be my third son.
Having said this, she also brought him to the highest state of nourishment with the milk from her own breast.
Thus, those three children, unaware of their mutual differences in birth, spent their childhood together in identical conduct and activities.
Then, once while wandering in that forest, a wild elephant arrived.
Upon seeing him, both lion cubs set out toward him with angry faces; just then, the jackal cub said, "Aha!
This elephant is the enemy of your lineage."
"Therefore, you must not go toward him.
Having said this, he ran home;
the two of them, too, having lost heart due to the failure of their elder kinsman, became dispirited.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Even by a single man who is very steadfast and full of enthusiasm for battle, the entire army becomes enthusiastic; but when he is broken, they meet with defeat. (Pañcatantra 4.42)
And so it is said:
"For this very reason, kings desire warriors who possess great strength, who are brave, heroic, and full of zeal; they avoid those who are cowardly. (Pañca 4.43)

Then, having both reached home, they related before their parents the actions of their eldest brother—how he had fled even upon seeing the elephant from afar. Upon hearing this, his mind overcome with anger, his sprout-like lips quivering, his eyes copper-red, and knitting his brows into a three-pronged frown, he rebuked them and spoke words of extreme harshness. Thereupon, he led the lioness away to a secluded spot.
He was thus awakened: "My child, never speak in such a manner again;
these two are your younger brothers."
Then, overcome with great anger, he said to her: "Am I inferior to these two in heroism, beauty, study of the sciences, or skill, that they mock me? Therefore, I must certainly kill them."
Hearing this, the lioness, desiring his life, laughed within herself and said: "Listen well to this:
you are the son of a jackal;
out of compassion, I have brought you to growth with the milk from my own teats."
Therefore, as long as these two sons of mine do not recognize you as a jackal because of their childhood, go very quickly and join your own kind;
otherwise, slain by them, you will enter the path of death.
Having heard those words, his mind agitated by fear, he slowly withdrew and joined his own kind.
Therefore, you too must depart as quickly as possible before these princes recognize you as a potter.
"If I do not die after receiving this mockery from them," [the crow thought].
Having heard that, the potter also quickly fled.
Therefore I say: "The hypocrite who abandons his own interest... (38).
"Fie upon you, fool!
That you have begun to undertake this task for the sake of women.
One should never place trust in women under any circumstances. And it is said:"
She for whose sake my own family was abandoned and half of my life was lost—she now abandons me without affection; what man can trust women?
The crocodile asked: "How was that?
The monkey said:
"The Fifth Story."
There is a story concerning a brahmin in a certain town;
he had a wife who was dearer to him than his own life.
He, too, did not rest, quarreling with his family every single day.

That brahmin, unable to endure the strife yet out of affection for his wife, abandoned his own family and went with the brahmin woman to a distant foreign land. Then, in the middle of a great forest, the brahmin woman said: "Noble son!"
"Thirst torments me;
search for that water somewhere.
Then, immediately after those words, as he returned carrying as much water as he could find, he saw her dead.
While he was lamenting, overcome with despair due to his great affection, he heard a voice in the sky:
"O Brāhmaṇa, if you give half of your own life, then your wife shall live.
Having heard this, the Brāhmaṇa purified himself and gave half of his own life with three utterances.
And that Brahmin woman died at the very moment she spoke those words.
Then, having drunk water and eaten forest fruits, the two of them began to proceed.
Subsequently, in due course, having entered a flower garden in the vicinity of a certain city, the Brahmin said to his wife: "My dear,"
"Until I return having taken my meal, you must remain here," said the brahmin, and with these words he went into the center of the city. Now,
in that flower garden, a cripple was playing with a water-wheel and singing a song in a divine voice.
Having heard that, the Brahmin woman, tormented by the arrows of the flower-armed god (Kāma), went into his presence and said: "My good man, if you do not desire me,
then the sin of killing a woman committed against me will fall upon you."
The lame man said, "What will you do with me, who am seized by disease?
She replied, "What is the use of saying this?
I must certainly have union with you."
Having heard that, he did exactly so.
After the act of love, she said: "From this moment forth, for as long as I live, I have given myself to you.
Knowing this, may you also come with us."
He replied, "So be it. Then the brahmin, having taken his food and returned, began to eat together with her. She said, "This lame man is hungry;
therefore, give him even a few morsels as well."
When this had been carried out, the Brahmin woman said: "O Brahmin,
when you go to another village without a companion, you will have no one even to accompany you with your words."
"So let us take this cripple and go.
He replied, "I am not even able to carry myself by my own self;
how much less this cripple?"
She said, "I shall carry him inside this chest.
Then, his mind deluded by those fabricated words, he agreed.
When it was so carried out, on another day, the Brahmin, having rested near a well, was pushed by her while clinging to the lame man and fell into the well.

She too, taking hold of the cripple, entered a certain city. There, royal officers wandering here and there for the purpose of guarding against tolls and theft saw the basket on her head; they forcibly snatched it away and brought it before the king. And as soon as the king opened it, he beheld that cripple.
Then that Brahmin woman, lamenting, arrived there immediately after the king's men.
When asked by the king, "What is the news?
she replied, "This husband of mine was afflicted by disease and harassed by his kinsmen; with my mind overwhelmed by affection, I took him upon my head and brought him to your city."
Having heard that, the king said: "Brahmin lady, you are my sister.
Take two villages and live happily, enjoying pleasures together with your husband."
Then, by the power of fate, that Brahmin was rescued from the well by a certain virtuous person; while wandering about, he arrived at that very same city.
He was seen by his wicked wife and she informed the king:
"O King, this enemy of my husband has arrived!"
The king also ordered her execution; she said, "Your Majesty,
she has taken something belonging to me."
"If you are a lover of dharma, then cause it to be given.
The king said, "O blessed lady,
whatever has been taken by you from him that belongs to him, surrender that."
She said, "O King, I have not taken anything.
The Brahmin said, "Give me that which was offered by me three times as half of my own life."
Then, out of fear of the king, she died right there while still speaking: "Half of my life was given by him through these very three words.
Thereupon, the king asked in astonishment, "What is this?
And the brahmin related the entire previous account to him.

Therefore I say: "For whose sake one's own family was abandoned" (44). The monkey spoke again: "This story is indeed excellent; it is heard that a man entreated by women would give nothing and do nothing."
Where horses do not neigh and heads are shorn at every joint.
The crocodile asked, "How was that?
The monkey related—
Story 6.

There was a king named Nanda, whose strength and prowess were exceedingly renowned; whose footstool was matted together by the network of rays from the crowns of many lords of men; whose fame was as pure as the rays of the autumnal moon; and who was the sovereign of the earth bounded by the ocean. His minister was named Vararuci, who had mastered all the principles of every scripture.

And his wife became angry due to a lovers' quarrel; she was exceedingly dear to him, yet even though he sought to appease her in many ways, she would not be pacified. And the husband said, "My dear lady," [The remainder of the sentence follows: "...do not be angry with me. She replied, "I am not angry with you, nor have I ever been angry with you. But I am angry with this wicked crow who sits upon my head and defiles me with his excrement. He said, "My dear lady, I shall kill this crow right now. She said, "If you kill him, I shall die immediately. He said, "My dear lady, what can I do? This crow is very powerful and possesses great magical spells (*vidyā*). She said, "If that is so, then let him remain for a while; later, when he has become fat from eating the food of the king's cook, you may kill him. He said, "My dear lady, I shall do as you say. Then, having gone out, he remained outside the house. After some time, that crow, having grown fat from eating the food of the king's cook, fell into the hands of that man. Then, having seized him by the feet, he began to strike him with a stick. The crow said, "O man, do not strike me; I am your servant. He said, "Who is your master? The crow said, "That woman who lives in this house. He said, "If that is so, then come quickly; I shall go to her. The crow said, "Go yourself; I am unable to go. He said, "Why? The crow said, "Because of my fear of being struck with a stick. He said, "Do not fear; I shall protect you. The crow said, "If that is so, then take me there. Then, having taken the crow and entered the house, he said to his wife, "My dear lady, here is that crow whom you desired. She said, "If that is so, then release him. He released him. Then the crow, having bowed to the woman, sat upon her head. She said, "Wretch, why have you come here? The crow said, "Lady, I have come as your servant. She said, "If that is so, then perform service for me. The crow said, "Lady, what service shall I perform? She said, "Eat my excrement. The crow said, "Lady, how can I eat excrement? She said, "If you do not eat it, I shall die. The crow said, "Lady, if that is so, then I shall eat it. Then, having eaten her excrement, he flew up and perched upon the roof of the house. She said, "Wretch, why have you gone away? The crow said, "Lady, I am unable to stay. She said, "Why? The crow said, "Because of my fear of being struck with a stick. She said, "If that is so, then come back again. The crow said, "Lady, I shall come again. Then, having descended, he sat upon her head. She said, "Wretch, why have you come here? The crow said, "Lady, I have come as your servant. She said, "If that is so, then perform service for me. The crow said, "Lady, what service shall I perform? She said, "Eat my excrement. The crow said, "Lady, how can I eat excrement? She said, "If you do not eat it, I shall die. The crow said, "Lady, if that is so, then I shall eat it. Then, having eaten her excrement, he flew up and perched upon the roof of the house. She said, "Wretch, why have you gone away? The crow said, "Lady, I am unable to stay. She said, "Why? The crow said, "Because of my fear of being struck with a stick. She said, "If that is so, then come back again. The crow said, "Lady, I shall come again. Then, having descended, he sat upon her head. She said, "Wretch, why have you come here? The crow said, "Lady, I have come as your servant. She said, "If that is so, then perform service for me. The crow said, "Lady, what service shall I perform? She said, "Eat my excrement. The crow said, "Lady, how can I eat excrement? She said, "If you do not eat it, I shall die. The crow said, "Lady, if that is so, then I shall eat it. Then, having eaten her excrement, he flew up and perched
"Tell me in what manner you will be satisfied;
I shall certainly do it. Then, after some deliberation, she said: "If you shave your head and prostrate yourself at my feet,"
Then I became inclined toward grace;
when he had acted accordingly, she was pleased.
Now, Nanda’s wife likewise remained angry and was not appeased even though she was being conciliated.
He said, "O blessed lady,
I cannot live for even a moment without you;
falling at your feet, I entreat you for your favor."
She said, "If, having placed the bit in your mouth, I mount upon your back and make you run,
and if, once running, you neigh like a horse,
then I shall be pleased."
The king likewise carried out exactly that.
Then, at the time of dawn, as the king was seated in the assembly hall, Vararuci arrived in his presence.
Seeing him, the king asked: "O Vararuci!"
"Why have you shaved your head on a festival day?
He replied, "What would one not give? (45), and so forth.
"Therefore, O wicked crocodile!"
You too, like Nandavararuci, are a slave to women;
therefore, O good sir, having arrived, you began an effort toward a means of killing me,
but it was revealed solely through the fault of your own speech.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Parrots and mainas are caught because of the fault of their own mouths;
cranes are not caught therein; silence is the means for accomplishing all goals. (Pañcatantra 4.46)
And so it is said:
"Though well-concealed and guarded, and displaying a fierce form, the donkey was killed for his voice while disguised in a tiger skin. (Pañcatantra 4.47)
The crocodile asked, "How was that?
The monkey related—
Story 8.
The Story of the Washerman named Śuddhapata:
In a certain town there lived a washerman named Śuddhapata,
and he had a single donkey.
He too had become extremely weak due to the lack of fodder. Then, while wandering in the forest, that washerman saw a dead tiger and thought: "Aha!"
"An excellent opportunity has presented itself!
Covering the donkey with this tiger-skin, I shall let it loose in the barley fields at night;
thinking it to be a tiger, the nearby field-watchers will not drive it out."
When this was carried out, the donkey ate the barley as he pleased;
at dawn, the washerman would lead him back to his own dwelling again.
As time passed in this manner, the donkey became fat-bodied.
With great difficulty, he was even led to the place of confinement.
Then, on another day, being intoxicated with pride, he heard the sound of a female donkey from afar;
at the mere hearing of it, he himself began to bray.

Then those guardians of the field, realizing that this was a donkey disguised in a tiger skin, killed him with blows from clubs, arrows, and stones. Therefore I say: "Even when well-concealed... (47). So why will you depart by giving the *ardhacandra* [the threatening gesture] because of enduring excessive insult like Śyāmala?
The crocodile asked: "How was that?
The monkey said:
"Story 9."
The Story of the Merchant Mahādhaneśvara:
There is on this earth a city named Vikaṇṭaka;
there lived a merchant chief named Mahādhaneśvara.
Four sons-in-law of his arrived at Vikaṇṭakapura as guests from the seat of Avanti;
they were honored with great respect through food, clothing, and other necessities.
Thus, six months passed while they were residing there.
Then the Lord said to his wife, "Since these sons-in-law have been received with the utmost honor yet do not go to their own homes,
what can be said?
They will not leave without being insulted."
"Therefore, today at the time of the meal, water must not be given for washing the feet, so that they, perceiving this as an insult, will abandon us and depart.
When this was carried out, Garga [departed] because of the insult of not having his feet washed,
and Soma because of the offering of a low seat.
Datta departed because of his poor food;
thus all three of them left him.
While the fourth, Śyāmālaka, was still not leaving, he was expelled by being given the "half-moon" punishment.
Therefore I say:

"Garga indeed departed because of the washing of feet and the offering of a humble seat; Soma was given by Śyāmala-ka because of the gift of a wretched meal, and [he attained] the crescent moon. (Pañca 4.48)
