Those who are insignificant and destitute of wealth are not noticed even when dwelling right before one's eyes;
they are constantly born and destroyed like bubbles upon the water.

Leaving behind those of noble birth, virtue, and good character, multitudes of people always take delight even in one who is deficient in lineage, merit, and conduct, if he is wealthy—like [they flock to] a wish-fulfilling tree. (Pañca 5.8)
In this world, the merit of former good deeds becomes fruitless for those who, though learned and born of noble lineage,
must enter into servitude whenever another possesses power.
The world does not consider this man light, even though he is the lord of the waters, despite his roaring;
for in this world, whatever those who are full of themselves do, it all causes shame.
Having reflected thus, he thought once more: "Therefore, I shall give up my life by undertaking a fast;
what is the use of this miserable existence?
Having made this resolution, he fell asleep.
Then, in a dream, the Lotus-Treasure (Padmanidhi), appearing in the form of a mendicant (kṣapaṇaka), showed himself to him and said: "O merchant! Do not fall into despondency;
I am the Lotus-Treasure acquired by your ancestors."
Therefore, in this very form, I shall come to your house tomorrow morning;
you must strike me on the head with a blow from a club,
so that, having become made of gold, I may become imperishable.
Then, having awakened in the morning and remembering the dream, he remained mounted upon the wheel of anxiety, thinking: "Alas! Is this dream true, or will it prove false? It cannot be known.
Or rather, it must surely be false, since day and night I think of nothing but wealth alone. And it is said:
A dream seen by a person who is diseased, afflicted by grief, seized by anxiety, tormented by desire, or intoxicated is fruitless. (Pancavimshati 5.11)
In the meantime, his wife called for a barber to wash her feet; at that moment, the mendicant described appeared suddenly.
Upon seeing him, he was delighted in heart and struck him on the head with a wooden staff that was at hand.
He too, turning into gold, fell to the ground instantly.
Then that merchant, having taken him secretly into the middle of his own house, gratified the barber and said: "My good man, take this wealth and these garments which I have given you;
furthermore, this matter must not be told to anyone."
The barber also went to his own home and thought: "Surely all these naked ones, when struck on the head, become made of gold.
Therefore, tomorrow morning I too shall summon many people and strike them on the head with clubs, so that I may obtain abundant gold."
As he reflected thus, the night passed away with great difficulty.
Then, rising at dawn and preparing a large staff,
he went to the monastery of the Kṣapaṇakas and performed three circumambulations of the Lord of Jinas.
Falling to his knees upon the ground and placing the hem of his upper garment over the opening of his mouth, he recited this verse in a loud voice:
"Victorious are those Jinas, endowed with exclusive omniscience, for whom the mind has remained as barren as saline soil from birth until the arising of passion. (Pañcavimśati 5.12)
And furthermore:
That is a true tongue which praises the Jina; that is a true mind which delights in the Jina;
those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform worship to him. (Pañca 5.13)
And so it is said:

"Under the pretext of meditation, you contemplate [something else]; open your eyes for a moment and look at these people afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god! Though you are our protector, you do not protect us."
"You are falsely compassionate; what other man could be more merciless than you?"—may the Buddha, the Victor, who was thus addressed with envy by the wives of Māra, protect you. (5.14)

Having thus offered praise, he approached the chief mendicant; placing his knees and feet upon the ground, he uttered, "Homage! I bow to you! Having received the blessing of an increase in dharma and obtained the instruction for his vows through the favor of the *sukhamālikā* garland, he tied a knot in his upper garment.
With great humility, he said this: "Blessed One, today the act of dwelling should be performed in our home by you together with all the sages.
Having heard that, the barber said: "Blessed One, I know your Dharma."
Furthermore, many disciples of yours are calling out;

now, moreover, high-priced cloths suitable for covering books have been prepared, and likewise, funds have been accumulated for the scribes for the purpose of copying the books. Therefore, this is by all means a task appropriate for the occasion.
Then the barber also went to his own home.

Having gone there, he prepared a club made of acacia wood, fastened a pair of door-panels at the entrance, and at about the first watch of the night, he returned once more to the monastery gate; there, setting aside all the familiar lay disciples even though they were full of devotion, [he waited].
With joyful minds, they followed behind him.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Solitary, having renounced his home, with bowl in hand and clad only in the directions as his garment,"
Even he is oppressed by craving in this world; behold the wonder! (5.15)
The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth of one who grows old decay;
the eyes and ears also decay; yet craving alone remains ever youthful.
After that, having led them into the middle of the house and firmly closed the door,
he struck them on the head with blows from a club;
being thus beaten, some of them died.
Others, with their heads split open, began to shriek.
In the meantime, hearing that outcry, the guardian of the hollow cried out: "Ho there! What is this clamor in the middle of the city?
Let us go!"
All of them, obeying his command, went with him in haste to that house; when they arrived, they saw naked men fleeing with their bodies drenched in blood, and they asked, "O sirs, what is this?
They related the barber's story exactly as it had happened.
Those who remained after the slaughter also bound that barber and led him to the court of justice.
There, they questioned the barber:
"O man! Why have you committed such an evil deed?"
He said, "What shall I do?
I have witnessed such an occurrence in the house of the merchant Maṇibhadra.
He, too, related the entire account of Maṇiprabha exactly as it had been seen.
Then, having summoned the merchant, they said to him: "O merchant, have you killed any *kṣapaṇaka*?
Thereupon, he also reported the entire account of the *kṣapaṇaka* to them.
Then they said, "Aha! Let this wicked barber, who acted without due examination, be impaled on a stake!
When this had been carried out, they said:
"A cock that is poorly understood, poorly heard, and poorly examined [leads to ruin]."
Therefore, that which was done here by the barber should not be done by a man.
Or rather, it is well said:
"One should not act without examination; one should act only after thorough examination.
For later remorse arises, as in the case of the brahmin woman and the mongoose. (Pañcatantra 5.17)
Maṇibhadra asked, "How was that?
Those officials of justice replied:
"The Story (1)."
The Story of the Brahmin Woman and the Mongoose:
In a certain settlement there lived a brahmin named Devaśarman.
His wife gave birth and brought forth a son.
On that very day, the female mongoose gave birth to a male mongoose and passed away.

Then, out of maternal affection for her offspring, she nurtured that male mongoose just like her own children by providing milk, anointing him with oil, massaging him, and so forth; yet, she did not place full trust in him.

Because parental affection exceeds all other forms of affection, one constantly harbors this apprehension: "Perhaps, under the influence of the defects inherent to his own kind, he might act contrary to the interests of this child.
"Even a bad son brings joy to the hearts of men—even if he is ill-behaved, ugly, foolish, addicted to vice, or wicked. (Pañca 5.18)
And thus the world says: "Sandalwood is indeed cool;
yet the touch of a son’s body exceeds that of sandalwood. (5.19)
People do not desire the imprisonment of one who is friendly, beneficial, and a protector of the world, just as they would not desire the imprisonment of their own son.
Then, on one occasion, having laid her son upon the bed and taking a water-jar, she said to her husband: "O Brahmin, I shall go to the pond for water;
this boy must be protected by you from the mongoose."
Then, after she had gone, the Brahmin also left the empty house and went out somewhere for alms.
His mother, seeing his face drenched in blood, became apprehensive; thinking with certainty that "this wicked soul has surely devoured the boy," she in her anger [flung] that water-jar upon him.
She threw it;
thus, having killed the mongoose, as she was returning home while lamenting,
her son remained sleeping just as before.
Seeing a black snake nearby that had been cut into pieces, she began to strike her own head and chest out of grief for the death of her son.
In the meantime, the Brahmin arrived carrying the sacrificial offerings; as soon as he looked, he saw the Brahmin woman, tormented by grief for her son, lamenting: "O, O you greedy soul!
Overcome by greed, you did not follow my words."
Therefore, experience now the fruit of the tree of sorrow caused by the death of your son. Or rather, it is well said: "Excessive greed should not be practiced; one should act with moderation."
Through the fault born of excessive greed, the jackal met his death.
The Brahmin asked, "What is this?
She replied,
"A story."
The Story of the Wheel-Bearer Possessed by Greed.
In a certain town, four sons of brahmins lived together, having formed a bond of friendship with one another.
Afflicted by poverty, they consulted among themselves: "Alas, fie upon this state of destitution! And it is said:
Better is the forest inhabited by tigers, elephants, and the like, devoid of people and covered with many thorns,
where one’s bed is of grass and one’s garment is bark.
Life devoid of wealth is not valued even among one's kinsmen.
And so it is:
even when well-served, a master becomes hostile; even good kinsmen suddenly abandon one;
virtues no longer shine; sons desert; and calamities multiply.

Even a virtuous wife born of a noble lineage does not attend to those men who lack wealth; nor do friends remain with them, even if their prowess has been established through justice. (Pancatantra 5.23)
May he be a hero, handsome, fortunate, and eloquent; may he master both weapons and scriptures.
Without wealth, there is neither fame nor honor.
A mortal attains this here in the world of men.
Those very same senses remain unimpaired, that very name remains, that same intellect is unobstructed, and those very words remain;
yet it is that same person who is now bereft of the warmth of wealth.
That it becomes external in an instant—this is marvelous!
"Let us go somewhere for the sake of our purpose," they deliberated, and having abandoned their own country, their city, and their home along with their friends, they set out.
Or rather, it is well said:
"He abandons the truth and forsakes his circle of kinsmen."

In this world, a man whose mind is agitated by anxiety quickly abandons even his mother and his native land; renouncing them all, he goes to a foreign country, a place desired by the people. (Pancatantaka 5.26)
Proceeding in this manner by stages, they reached Avanti.

Having bathed there in the waters of the Siprā and paid homage to Mahākāla, as they were departing, a yogin named Bhairavānanda appeared before them. Then, having honored him according to the rites appropriate for Brahmins, they went with him to his monastery.
Then he asked them: "From where have you come, sirs? Where will you go? What is your purpose?"
Then they said, "We are seekers of spiritual success (*siddhi*).
We shall go to that place where there will be either the attainment of wealth or death; this is our resolve. And it is said:
"Desirable riches, though difficult to obtain, are acquired in great abundance."
Enough with these frail bodies, which are weighed down by the opportunities of reckless men.
And so it is said:
"Sometimes one falls from the sky, and water comes even from the netherworld (pātāla);
destiny is inconceivable and powerful, yet human effort is indeed powerful as well. (Pañca 5.28)
For the complete accomplishment of all desired goals for a person occurs through human effort;
even that which you call "fate" is merely a quality of the person known by the name of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Virtuous men of daring courage weigh the incomparable fear of the world of the ancestors as lightly as a blade of grass;
that they sacrifice their very lives is truly marvelous—such indeed is the conduct of the noble.
Without providing a portion of their afflictions, no pleasures whatsoever can be obtained here; by churning with effort, the honey-gatherer embraces Fortune with his arms.
How could the wife of that Viṣṇu, even though he is Nṛsiṃhaka, not be unshakable—
he who, remaining in the water, constantly indulges in sleep for four months?
The supreme state is difficult to attain as long as a person does not exercise courage;
here, the radiant sun, having ascended the scale, triumphs over the masses of clouds.

Therefore, tell us some means of acquiring wealth—whether it be entering a chasm, propitiating a *śākinī*, frequenting a cremation ground, selling human flesh, or serving a practitioner (*sādhaka*)—for you are heard to possess one of these marvelous powers.
We too are exceedingly daring; and as it is said:
Only the great are capable of accomplishing the purpose of the great;
who other than the ocean can sustain the submarine fire?
Bhairavānanda, for their sake and for the purpose of their accomplishment, prepared four wicks of perfected substances using many methods and handed them over.
He said: "Go toward the direction of the Himalayas.
When you have arrived there, wherever one of these wicks falls,"
"There, you will undoubtedly find a treasure.
Having dug up that spot and taken the treasure, you may return.
When they had acted accordingly and were on their way, a ring fell from the hand of one of them.
Then, as soon as he dug down to that entrance, he found the ground was made of copper.
Thereupon, he said: "Aha!
Take as much copper as you desire!"
Others said, "O fool!
What is the use of this, which does not even destroy abundant poverty?
Therefore, rise up; let us go on ahead."
He said, "Go, sirs;
I will not go first. Having spoken thus, he took as much copper as he desired and returned ahead of the others.
All three of them set out together at the front.
Then, when the leader had gone only a short distance, his wick fell out.
As soon as he began to dig it up, he found that the ground was made of silver.
Then, filled with great joy, he said: "O,
O, take as much silver as you desire!"
"One must not go forward.
They both said, "O sir, behind us is the copper-colored ground; in front is the silver-colored ground."
Therefore, it will surely be made of gold at first;
moreover, poverty is not destroyed even by such a vast amount.
Thus, let us two go there first.
Having spoken thus, both set out together;
he too, taking silver according to his own means, turned back.
Then, as they were traveling, a wick fell before one of them.
He too, being overjoyed, continued digging until he saw golden ground; then he said to his companion, "O friend,
take as much gold as you desire!"
"Nothing other than gold will be superior.
He replied, "Fool! You know nothing at all."
First copper, then silver, then gold.
Therefore, from this point forward, there will surely be jewels,
by even one of which the destruction of poverty occurs;
so, arise!
"Let us go on ahead.
What is the use of this great burden?
He replied, "May you proceed."
"I shall remain here and wait for you.
When he had done so, he too, traveling alone,
his body scorched by the heat of the summer sun and distressed by thirst, wandered here and there, having strayed from the path to success.
Then, while wandering, he saw a man upon the ground whose limbs were drenched in blood and whose head was being whirled by a spinning wheel.
Thereupon, going more quickly, he said to him: "O sir!"
"Who are you? Why do you stand upon my head with this discus?
Tell me that, if there is water anywhere!
As he was speaking thus, at that very moment, the discus moved from his head and settled upon the head of the Brahmin.
He said, "My good man, what is this? He replied, "Has this also fallen upon my head? He said, "Then tell me."
"When will this end? A great pain is afflicting me.
He replied, "When someone like you, having likewise come here while still holding the wick of unaccomplished practice,"
"When he speaks to you, then his head will shatter.
He asked, "How long have you remained in this state?
He replied, "Who is the king upon the earth at present?"
He said, "Prince Vatsarāja is skilled in playing the lute.
He replied, "I do not know the duration of that time;
however, when Rāma was king, I, afflicted by poverty, came along this path taking a magical wick."
Then I saw another man whose head was encircled by a wheel of sharp blades, and I questioned him;
from that, this [thought] arose.
He said: "O noble sir!"
"How did he obtain food and water while remaining in such a state?
He replied, "My good man,
out of fear that the Nidhi-haras would seize his treasure, Dhanada manifested this danger to the Siddhas in the form of the falling discus."
Therefore, no one at all comes there;
if anyone were to come,
they would be free from hunger, thirst, and sleep, devoid of old age and death, and would experience only such sensation as this.
"Therefore, give me leave to go to my own home," he said, and departed.
While he was delayed, Suvarṇasiddhi, intent on searching for him, followed his trail of footprints for some distance.
As he was entering another forest, he saw him sitting there, his body drenched in blood, in great pain from a sharp wheel spinning upon his head, moaning aloud;
then, approaching him, he asked for the sake of all: "Good sir, what is this?"
He said: "It is the application of a rule.
He asked: "How so? Tell me the reason for this."
He too, when questioned by him, related the entire account of the wheel.
Having heard this, the other, censuring him, said: "O sir!"
"You have been forbidden by me many times, yet you do not listen to my words. What can be done?
Though you possess learning and are of noble birth, you are in reality devoid of intelligence."
Or rather, it is well said: "Better is wisdom than that knowledge; wisdom is superior to knowledge.
Those devoid of wisdom perish, just like those who made the lion. (Pañca 5.35)
Cakradhara said: "How was that?
Suvarṇasiddhi said: "The third story."
The Story of the Foolish Brahmin Who Made a Lion:
In a certain town, four sons of Brahmins lived together, having entered into a state of great friendship.
Of them, three were masters of the scriptures, yet they were devoid of intelligence.

But there was one intelligent man who was entirely averse to the scriptures. Then, those friends once deliberated among themselves: "What is the use of learning, since by it one must go to another country?"
"We cannot acquire wealth by merely pleasing kings;
therefore, let us go to the eastern country.
When they had set out accordingly and traveled some distance on the road, the eldest among them said: "Aha!"
Among us, one is a fool—the fourth;
he is merely intelligent.
And royal favor is not obtained through mere intelligence.
"Without knowledge,
we shall not give him what he has earned himself;
let it go back to his home."
Then the second one said: "O Subuddhi,
go to your own home,
for you do not possess the knowledge."
Then the third said: "Oh, it is not at all proper to act in this way;
for we have played together in one place since our childhood."
"Therefore, let the one of great majesty come; he shall become a sharer in the wealth acquired by us. And it is said:
"What is the use of that fortune which is like a bride, belonging to only one?
It is not like a courtesan, who is enjoyed in common by travelers. (Pañca 5.36)
And so it is said:
"The calculation of 'this one is my own' or 'that one is a stranger' belongs to those of narrow minds; for those of noble conduct, however, the entire earth is but a single family. (Pañcatantra 5.37)
"Therefore, let him also come.
When they had acted accordingly, those who were traveling along the road saw the bones of a dead lion in the forest. Then one of them said: "Aha!"
Today, the efficacy of the vidyā is being tested.
This certain being lies here dead;
by the power of the vidyā, we shall restore him to life.
"I shall construct a heap of bones.
Thereupon, out of eagerness, he constructed the heap of bones;
by the second, the skin, flesh, and blood were joined together.
The third one also continued to move about for as long as he lived, until he was stopped by Subuddhi: "Sir, stop!
This lion is being prepared."
"If you restore him to life, then he will kill all of us as well.
Being addressed thus by him, he replied, "Fie on you, fool!
I shall not allow my magic science to be rendered fruitless."
Then he said, "In that case, wait a moment while I climb the tree.
When this was done,
as soon as they had been restored to life, the lion rose up and killed all three of them.
Furthermore, he descended from the tree and went home;
therefore I say: "Wisdom is better than that learning. Following this, it was said by Suvarṇasiddhi:
Even those who are skilled in the treatises, if they are devoid of worldly conduct,
all become objects of ridicule, just like those foolish scholars.
Cakradhara said: "How was that?
He replied:
"The Fourth Story."
The Story of the Foolish Scholar:

In a certain town, four Brahmins lived together, having formed a bond of friendship with one another. In their youth, the thought occurred to them: "O friends, let us go to another country and acquire knowledge."
Then, on another day, those brahmins, having reached a mutual agreement, went to Kānyakubja for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.
Having gone there to a school of learning (*vidyā-maṭha*), they studied;
and thus, having studied with single-minded devotion for twelve years, they [continued].
They all became proficient in the sciences.
Then those four, having gathered together, said: "We have reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge;
therefore, having taken leave of our preceptor, we shall go to our own country."
Having said, "Let it be carried out exactly so," the brahmins assisted their preceptor, and having obtained his permission and taken the books, they set out.
As they were traveling along a certain road,
two paths converged, and they all sat down.
There, one of them asked, "By which road shall we go?
At that time, in that city, a certain merchant's son had died;
the great multitude had gone there for his cremation.
Then, from among the four, one examined a book and said: "The path is that which the great multitude has taken. "Therefore, let us go by the way of the great multitude.
Then those wise men proceeded along with Elāpaka until they reached the great multitude.
Just then, a certain donkey was seen there in the cremation ground.
Then, the second [man] opened the book and looked at it:
"In times of festival, in times of calamity, when famine arrives, or in the crisis of an enemy's siege..."
He who stands by you at the king's gate and at the cremation ground is a true kinsman.
"Oh, this is our kinsman!
Then someone touched him on the neck,
while another washed his feet.
Then, while those wise men were surveying the directions, they saw a certain wicked person. They asked, "What is this?
Thereupon, the third one opened the book and said: "The course of Dharma is swift."
"Therefore, this must surely be the law.
Then the fourth said: "One should join the desired [reward] with the law.
Thereupon, the donkey was tied by them to the neck of the camel.
Someone reported this matter to the washerman, their master.
Just as the washerman arrived to administer blows to those foolish scholars, they had already vanished. Then, as they proceeded a short distance further along the path, they came upon a river.

Seeing a *palāśa* leaf come floating in the middle of the water, one wise man said: "Whatever leaf comes here will carry us across. Having said this, he fell upon that leaf and was carried away by the river; then, seeing him being swept along, another wise man seized him by the hair and said:
"When total ruin has occurred, the wise man abandons half."
One accomplishes one's purpose with half [of one's resources], for the destruction of everything is indeed unbearable.
Then, having traveled on, they reached a certain village.
They were invited by the villagers and led into separate houses.
Thereupon, a spoonful of rice mixed with the scum of clarified butter was given to one of them for his meal.
Then, having reflected, the wise man said, "One who procrastinates perishes.
Having spoken thus, he abandoned the food and departed.
In the same way, goods were given to the second man.
Therefore, it was said: "That which is excessively large and vast will not lead to long life.
He left, having abandoned that food.
Then, the third garden was given as food.
Even there, that wise man said, "In times of vulnerability, misfortunes multiply.

Thus, all three of those wise men, their throats parched with hunger and becoming objects of ridicule among the people, departed from that place for their own country. Then Suvarṇasiddhi said, "Since you did not understand worldly conduct, you did not heed my warnings and did not stop; therefore, you have come to such a state."
"Therefore, I say: 'Even those skilled in the treatises [may perish].
Having heard that, Cakradhara said: 'Oh, this is causeless! For indeed:
The wise perish, destroyed by malignant fate.'"
But even one of very little intelligence rejoices constantly in that family. (5.41)
And it is said:
"What is unprotected remains by the protection of fate; what is well-protected perishes when struck by fate.
Even one abandoned in the forest without a protector lives, while one who exerts every effort at home does not live. (Pañca 5.42)
And so it was said:
"This one with a hundredfold intellect is upon my head, and he with a thousandfold intellect hangs down;
but I, O blessed lady, possessing but a single intellect, sport in the pure water. (Pañca 5.43)
Suvarṇasiddhi asked, "How was that?
He replied:
"The Fifth Story."
The Story of the Fish and the Frog:
In a certain body of water there lived two fish named Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit. Now, a frog named Single-Wit became their friend.
Thus, all three of them, having enjoyed the pleasure of a discourse on wise sayings on the shore at the water's edge,
entered the water once again.
Then, one day, while they were engaged in their discourse, [certain beings] arrived at that body of water.
Then, seeing the body of water, they said to one another: "Aha! This lake appears to have many fish and very little water.
Therefore, we shall come here at dawn."
Having spoken thus, they went to their own homes;
and the fish, with dejected faces, consulted one another.
Then the frog said, "O Śatabuddhi!"
Have you heard what the fisherman said?
What, then, is appropriate to do in this situation— flight or defiance?
"Let that which is appropriate to be done today be commanded.
Having heard this, Sahasrabuddhi laughed and said, "O friend, do not fear!"
Upon merely hearing their words, one should feel no fear;
one must not be afraid. And it has been said:
"Of serpents and of wicked men—of all those with evil intent..."
Intentions do not succeed; therefore, this world continues to revolve.
For that long, even their arrival will not come to pass.
However, I shall protect you along with yourself by the power of my intellect;
for I am well-acquainted with many modes of moving through water.
Having heard that, Śatabuddhi said: "O sir, you have spoken rightly;
you are indeed Sahasrabuddhi.
Or rather, it is well said:"
Indeed, there is nothing in this world inaccessible to the intellect of those possessed of intelligence;
for by means of his intellect, Cāṇakya destroyed Nanda, even as they held swords in their hands.
Likewise:
"Wherever there is no passage for the wind or for the rays of the sun, even there the intellect of the wise always enters swiftly. (Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 5.46)
Therefore, even from merely hearing those words, it is impossible to abandon the place of birth inherited through one’s paternal lineage. And it has been said:
“O beautiful one, there is no happiness even in heaven that could equal the divine touch [of one's mother], where the birth of men occurs, even if it be in a wretched place. (Pañca 5.47)
"Therefore, you must never go there at any time;
I shall protect you through the power of my intellect.
The frog said, "Noble sirs!"
"As for me, my mind is set on flight alone;
therefore, I shall go this very day to another body of water along with my wife.
Having said this, the frog departed for another pond that very night.
At dawn, fishermen also arrived and caught various aquatic creatures—low, middling, and superior—such as fish, turtles, frogs, crabs, and the like.

Meanwhile, Śatabuddhi and Sahasrabuddhi, together with their wives, were fleeing; though they had long protected themselves through their specialized knowledge of movements and their skillful, evasive maneuvers, they eventually fell into the net.
And they were killed.
Then, at the time of the afternoon, those fishermen set out for their own homes, greatly delighted.
Because of his great weight, Śatabuddhi was carried on the shoulder by one man, while Sahasrabuddhi was led along, dangling down.
Then, a frog standing on the edge of the pond, seeing the two of them being led away in that manner, said to his wife:
"My dear, look, look!
Here is Śatabuddhi perched upon the head, and Sahasrabuddhi is hanging down."
"I am a single-minded being, O blessed lady, sporting in the pure water. (5.48)
"And therefore, intelligence is better than that mere learning. Regarding what you have said there, this is my opinion: that even intelligence is not an absolute authority.
Suvarṇasiddhi said: "Even if this is so, nevertheless, the word of a friend must not be transgressed."
But what can be done? Although you were restrained by me, you did not stop,
due to excessive greed and pride in your learning.
Or rather, it is well said:
"Well done, uncle! Though I spoke to you with song, you did not stop;
this unprecedented jewel has been secured, and the reward for my singing has been obtained."
Cakradhara asked: "How was that?
He replied:
Story 6.
The Story of the Donkey and the Jackal:
In a certain town there lived a donkey named Uddhata. He always performed the task of carrying loads at the washerman’s house, and at night he would roam about according to his own will.
Then, at dawn, out of fear of being bound, he would come to the washerman’s house of his own accord;
the washerman, for his part, would then fasten him with a tether.

Now, as he was wandering through the fields at night, friendship once arose between him and a jackal; and because of his stoutness, having caused the interruption of the [jackal's] livelihood, he [the dog] stayed together with the jackal in a field of *karkaṭikā* gourds.
He enters.
Thus, having eaten cucumber slices at their whim, the two of them return to their own places every day at dawn.
Then, on one occasion, while standing in the middle of the field, that donkey, arrogant with pride, said to the jackal: "O son of my sister!
Look, look!
The night is exceedingly clear."
"Therefore, I shall sing;
tell me, with which melody (*rāga*) shall I perform it?
He said, "My dear, why this vain pursuit of useless things?"
Since we two have engaged in the act of theft, thieves and paramours must remain here in concealment. And it has been said:
"A man who is prone to sleepiness should avoid a thief; if he is sleepy, he should avoid a wanton woman."
And he who, overcome by disease, still craves life here, possesses a greed for the tongue.
Furthermore, your song is not sweet-toned;
it resembles the sound of a conch shell and can be heard even from afar.
Therefore, the guards in this field are fast asleep.
They will rise up and carry out your execution or imprisonment;
therefore, eat these nectar-like morsels for now,
and do not be intent on the practice of singing here.
Having heard that, Rābhasa said: "O friend, because you dwell in the forest, you do not understand the essence of song;
therefore you speak thus. And it is said:
"When the darkness has been driven far away by the autumnal moonlight, and one is in the presence of a beloved..."
The nectar born from the humming of songs enters the ears of the fortunate.
The jackal said: "Uncle, that is true;
however, you do not understand song;
you merely howl."
"So what is the use of that which causes the loss of one's own interest?
The donkey said, "Fie, fie upon you, fool! Do you not know how to sing?"
Listen now to its divisions:
there are seven notes, three scales (grāmas), thirty-one melodic modulations (mūrcchanās), forty-nine tānas, three measures (mātrās), and three tempos (layas). (5.52)
There are three stages for ascetics, six notes, nine musical sentiments,
thirty-six passions, and forty-four emotional states (bhāvas) are thus recorded.
Indeed, this hundred and eighty-five auxiliary elements of song were proclaimed by Bharata himself of old as being beyond the scope of the Vedas.
Nothing else in the world is seen to be as dear to the gods as song;
Rāvaṇa seized the Three-Eyed One (Śiva) through the delight of his voice, which was like the sound of dry tendons.
"So how can you, my sister's son, forbid me while speaking as if you were ignorant of the situation?
The jackal said, "Uncle,
if that is so, then let me remain at the entrance of the field for as long as it takes to provide sustenance, while I keep watch over the field-guardian."
"You, however, should sing according to your own will.
When this was done, the guardian of the field, hearing the braying of the donkey, rushed forward in a rage, baring his teeth;
as soon as he saw the donkey, he struck it with blows from a club.
Just as he had been struck, he fell upon the surface of the ground;
then, having tied a mortar with a hole in it around his neck, the guardian of the field fell fast asleep.
The donkey, too, due to the innate nature of his own species, forgot his pain and rose up in an instant. And it is said:
For a dog, a horse, and especially for a donkey,
the pain produced by a blow would not persist beyond a moment.
Then, taking that very mortar and crushing his livelihood [the grain], he began to flee.
In the meantime, the jackal, having seen him from afar, said with a smile:
"Well done, uncle! Even though I spoke to you with a song, you did not stop."
Even though the jewel was previously unbound, it has now attained the characteristics of song.
"Therefore, you too did not desist even though you were being restrained by me.
Hearing this, Cakradhara said: "O friend, this is true."
Or rather, it is well said:
"He who possesses no wisdom of his own and does not act upon the advice of friends goes to his destruction, just like the weaver Manthara."
Suvarṇasiddhi asked, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 7.
The Story of Manthara the Weaver:
In a certain town there lived a weaver named Manthara.
Once, while he was engaged in his weaving work, all the wooden shuttles for his looms broke.
Then, taking his axe, he went into the forest for the sake of wood.
As he wandered along the shore of the ocean, he saw a *śiṃśapā* tree there.
He then thought, "This appears to be a great tree."
"By cutting this very tree, there will be many tools for weaving cloth.
Having resolved this, he raised his axe above it.
Now, a certain *vyantara* spirit was dwelling within that tree.
Then he said:
"O sir, this tree which is my refuge must be protected by all means,
for it is here that I dwell in great happiness."
Refreshed by the cool breeze from the touch of the ocean waves,
the Kaulika said: "O sir,
what shall I do?"
"Without a collection of wood, my family is tormented by hunger;
therefore, go elsewhere quickly.
I shall have this [wood] cut."
The Vyantara said:
"O sir, I am pleased with you;
therefore, let some desired boon be requested."
"Protect this tree," he said.
The weaver replied, "If that is so, then I shall go to my own home, consult with my friend and my wife, and then return;
after that, you may give it."
Then, when the spirit had agreed, saying "So be it," the weaver was overjoyed and returned toward his own home;
as he went along, he saw his friend the barber at the entrance of the village. He then informed him of the spirit's words.
"O friend, today a certain *vyantara* has been accomplished by me; therefore,
speak."
"What do you seek? I have come to ask you.
The barber said, "Good sir!"

"If that is so, then seek the kingdom, so that you may become king and I shall be your minister; thus, having experienced happiness in this world, we both shall experience the happiness of the next world. And it is said:
A king who is constantly devoted to giving attains fame in this world,
and by the power of that merit, he dwells again in heaven, vying with the gods.
The Kaulika said: "This is so; nevertheless, I shall ask my wife. He replied: "My good man, it is contrary to the scriptures that one should hold counsel with a woman."
For they are of limited intelligence. And it has been said:

"A wise man should provide women with food and clothing, and grant them union at the proper time; he should also give them ornaments and such, but he should not deliberate on secret matters with them. (Pañca 5.60)
"Where there is a woman, where there is a gambler, and where a child is the ruler, that household goes to ruin; for thus spoke Bhārgava."
A man remains with a serene countenance and devoted to his elders only so long as he does not hear the secret words of women in private.
These women are intent on their own interests and devoted solely to their own pleasure;
to them, no one is dear—not even a son—apart from their own happiness. (Pancatanttra 5.63)
The Kaulika said: "Nevertheless, she must be questioned by me;
for she is devoted to her husband, and furthermore, I shall do nothing without first asking her."
Having spoken thus, he went quickly and said to her: "My dear, today a certain *vyantara* spirit has been propitiated by us;
he grants whatever is desired."
Therefore, I have come to ask you this:
tell me, what should I request?
First, let my friend the barber request for himself a kingdom such as this.
She said, "Noble son, what is the opinion of barbers?
That speech should not be acted upon. And it has been said:"
One should not perform mantras with performers, panegyrists, low-caste men, barbers, even children, nor indeed with monks. (5.64)
Furthermore, this state of kingship is a great succession of afflictions; through peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and duplicity, it does not at any time bestow happiness upon a man.
For:
"At the very moment one is consecrated in the kingdom, at that very moment the mind turns toward vices."
At the time of the consecration of kings, the jars, along with the water itself, vomit forth calamity.
And so it is said:
"The departure of Rāma to the forest, the dwelling of the sons of Pāṇḍu in the woods,
the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, and the fall of King Nala from his kingdom;"
Having considered the state of Saudāsa upon the slaughter of Arjuna, and seeing the Lord of Laṅkā reduced to such mockery for the sake of a kingdom, one should not desire that [kingdom].
One should renounce from afar that kingdom for the sake of which even brothers and even one's own sons desire the death of kings who have established their rule.
The Kaulika said: "What you have said is true.
So tell me, what do you request? She replied:
"You currently produce one cloth every single day."
By that, all expenditure will be purified.
Now, however, ask for a second pair of arms and a second head for yourself,
by which you may produce two cloths— one for the front and one for the back.
With the price of one, you will maintain the household expenses as before;
with the price of the second, you will perform special duties.
In this way, time will pass for you while being praised among your own kin in happiness.
"And there will be the acquisition of both worlds.
Having heard this, he too was delighted and said: "Excellent, O devoted wife!
Excellent!"
What you have said is appropriate;
I shall do exactly that.
This is my firm resolve.
Then, having gone there, he entreated the *vyantara*:
"O, if you grant me my desire, then give me a second pair of arms and a head.
When this was said, at that very moment he became two-headed and four-armed.
Then, with a joyful mind, as he was returning home, he was struck by blows from clubs and stones by people who thought, "This is a *rākṣasa*," and he died.
Therefore I say: "He who has no wisdom of his own...
Cakradhara said, "O sir!"
This is true:
every person, having encountered the untrustworthy demoness of hope, becomes an object of ridicule.
Or rather, as it has been well said by someone:
He who entertains impossible thoughts concerning the future lies there pale, just like the father of Somaśarman.
Suvarṇasiddhi asked, "How was that?
He replied—
Story 8.
The Story of Somaśarman’s Father: In a certain city there lived a Brahmin named Svabhāvakṛpaṇa (Naturally Miserly).
He had filled a jar with the remnants of barley meal obtained through begging.
Having hung that jar on a wall-peg and placed his bed beneath it, he gazed at it constantly with an unblinking eye.
Then, once while asleep at night, he thought: "This jar is currently full of barley-meal;
what if a famine should occur?"
Thus, by this means, one hundred silver coins will arise;
from that, we shall be seized by me through the sacrifice.
Then, due to the six-month period until their birth, a herd will come into being from those two.
From those goats, I shall obtain many cows;
from the cows, female buffaloes;
and from the female buffaloes, mares.
From the breeding of mares, many horses will arise;
from their sale, there will be abundant gold;
and with that gold, a four-winged house will be completed.
Then a certain brahmin will come to my house and give me a daughter of marriageable age who is rich in beauty;
from her a son shall be born to me,
and I shall give him the name Somaśarman.
Then, when that [spot] has become suitable for moving about on my knees, I shall take the book and sit behind the horse-stable to study it.
In the meantime, Somaśarman, seeing me, will leave his mother’s lap and, intent on crawling on his knees, come toward me while staying near the horses’ hooves.
Then, overcome with anger, I shall say to the Brahmin woman: "Take the boy first!"
"She too, being preoccupied with household chores, will not hear my words;
therefore, I shall rise up and strike her with a kick.
While he was thus absorbed in meditation, he delivered a kick in exactly such a manner that the jar was shattered.
And he himself has become pale from the barley meal;
therefore I say: "Do not harbor thoughts concerning the future.
Suvarṇasiddhi said: "It is even so."
What fault is yours, since everyone, being deceived by greed, is afflicted? And it has been said:
"He who acts out of fickleness does not consider the future consequence."
He undergoes mockery, just as King Candra did.
Cakradhara asked: "How was that?
He replied:
"The Ninth Story."
The Story of King Candra:
In a certain city there lived a king named Candra.
His sons were devoted to playing with monkeys and constantly nourished a troop of monkeys with various kinds of food, edibles, and other provisions.
Now, the lord of monkeys was a knower of the doctrines of Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, and Cāṇakya, as well as their practical application, and he taught all of them.

Now, in that city of Rājagṛha, there was a flock of rams suitable for the young princes to ride. From among them, one ram, out of greed for his tongue, would enter the kitchen day and night without hesitation and eat everything he saw.
And whenever those cooks saw any wood, an earthen vessel, a bronze bowl, or a copper pot, they would immediately strike at it with it.
Seeing this, the leader of the monkey troop reflected: "Alas! This quarrel between the ram and the cooks will lead to the destruction of the monkeys;
for this ram is greedy for the taste of the flavors of the food."
And when the cooks, in their great anger, strike with whatever object is at hand—
if they should ever strike with a firebrand due to the absence of other objects—
then this sheep, being full of wool, will burst into flames even with a small fire.
Being burned by that, he will enter again the horse-stable situated nearby;
that too, due to its abundance of straw, will burst into flames,
and then the horses will suffer from the fire's heat.
Śālihotra, moreover, has stated this: that the defect caused by fire-burns in horses is pacified by the fat of monkeys.
Therefore, this must certainly be so;
having reached this conclusion, he summoned all the monkeys and spoke to them in private: "That—"
Where a quarrel arises between the cooks over a sheep,
that will undoubtedly bring about the destruction of the monkeys.
Therefore, one who desires life should avoid from afar that house where there is constant, causeless quarreling. (5.71)
Palaces end in quarrels, friendship ends in harsh words,
kingdoms end with bad kings, and the fame of men ends in evil deeds.
"Therefore, before all of them have perished, let us abandon this Rājagṛha and go to the forest.
Then, hearing those words of his, which were not to be believed, the monkeys, arrogant with pride, laughed and said: "O sir, due to your old age, a deficiency of intellect has arisen in you."
It is for this reason that you say so; and it has been said:
"The face, bereft of teeth, constantly drips with saliva;
the intellect does not function anywhere, especially in the child and the old. (Pañca 5.73)

"We will not abandon these various kinds of excellent foods, which are like nectar and provide enjoyments equal to those of heaven, given by the princes themselves, to instead eat fruits that are astringent, bitter, pungent, alkaline, and coarse in that forest.
Hearing this, he cast a gaze clouded with tears and said: "O you fools!"
"You do not know the consequence of this pleasure.
Is it not the case that this pleasure, which consists primarily of the tasting of the flavor of ripening, will become like poison in its result?
Therefore, I shall not myself witness the destruction of my lineage."
Now I shall go to the forest. And it is said:
"Blessed are those who do not witness the ruin of their country or the destruction of their family—a friend fallen into calamity, one's own home being tormented by others. (Pañcatantra 5.74)
Having spoken thus and abandoned them all, that leader of the herd went into the forest.

Then, on another day after he had departed, the ram entered the kitchen; when the cook could find nothing else, he struck him with a half-burnt log, whereupon his body burst into flames and, bleating loudly, he rushed toward the nearby stable for the horses.
He entered there;
as he rolled upon the ground covered with an abundance of grass, flames of fire rose up everywhere such that some horses, their eyes burst open, met their death.

Some, having snapped their bonds, with bodies half-burnt, ran hither and thither neighing loudly and threw the entire multitude of people into a state of agitation. In the meantime, the king, filled with despondency, summoned physicians learned in the science of horses and said: "O sirs! Let some remedy be declared for the allaying of these horses' burns."
They too, having consulted the treatises, said: "O King,
regarding this matter, it has been stated by the venerable Śālihotra that the defect arising from fire-burns [is cured] by the fat of monkeys."
It goes to its destruction like darkness at the rising of the sun.
"Therefore, let this remedy be applied immediately,
before these are destroyed by the calamity of fire.
Having heard this, he ordered the slaughter of all the monkeys.
In short, all those monkeys were slain with various weapons, clubs, stones, and the like.
Then that leader of the monkey troop, having learned of that destruction of his sons, grandsons, brothers, nephews, and others, fell into despair.
Abandoning the practice of eating, he wandered from forest to forest.
And he thought: "How shall I perform the service of repaying my debt to that base king? For it is said:
'He who, out of fear or even out of desire, tolerates here an insult inflicted by another—whether born of his own lineage or not—is to be known as the lowest of men. (Pañca 5.76)

Then, while wandering somewhere tormented by thirst, that old monkey reached a lake adorned with clusters of lotuses. As he observed it closely, he saw a trail of footprints belonging to forest-dwelling humans leading toward it, but no way out. He thought: "Surely this must have been entered by a wicked crocodile."
Taking that lotus-stalk and standing at a distance, I drank the water. When I had done so, a Rākṣasa emerged from within it, his neck adorned with a necklace of jewels, and said to him:
"O sir, whoever enters the water here becomes my food."
"There is no one more cunning than you, who drinks water by this method;
therefore, I am pleased— ask for whatever your heart desires."
The monkey said, "O sir,
what is my capacity for eating? He replied, "I can eat even hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of thousands [of fish], provided they have entered the water."
"Even a jackal is assailing me from the outside.
The monkey said, "I have an extreme enmity with a certain king;
if you give this jewel necklace to me,"
Having enticed that king and his retinue with a flow of persuasive speech, I shall cause them to enter this lake.
Having heard those credible words of his, he too gave him a necklace of jewels and said, "O friend,
whatever is appropriate must be done."
The monkey, too, was seen by the people wandering among the tree-palaces with his neck adorned with a jewel-garland;
and they asked him: "O leader of the herd, where have you been staying for all this time?"
"Where did you obtain such a jewel-necklace?
Its brilliance even outshines the sun.
The monkey replied, "In a certain forest, there is a very secluded and great lake created by Kubera, the Giver of Wealth."
In that place, whoever bathes when the sun has half-risen on a Sunday emerges with his neck adorned with such a necklace of jewels through the grace of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Then, having heard this from the king, [the minister said:]
That monkey was summoned and asked: "O leader of the troop,
is this true?"
"Is there a lake anywhere adorned with a jewel necklace?
The monkey said, "Master,
here is proof for you, by means of this jewel necklace currently upon my neck."
"Therefore, if there is need for a necklace of jewels, send someone with me so that I may show it to you.
Having heard this, the king said, "If that is the case, then I myself will come with my retinue."
"By which an abundance of jewel-garlands may be produced.
The monkey said, "Let it be done so.
When this was carried out by the king, all his wives and servants set out together with him, driven by greed for the jewel-garlands.
The monkey, too, was placed upon the king’s lap as he sat in a swing and was carried along comfortably and with affection.
Or rather, it is well said:
"O Goddess Tṛṣṇā, salutations to you, by whom even those possessed of wealth [are driven]."
They are incited to perform improper acts and are led astray even into difficult paths.
And so it is said:
"One who possesses a hundred desires a thousand; one who possesses a thousand strives for a hundred thousand;
likewise, the lord of a hundred thousand strives for a kingdom, and one established in a kingdom strives for heaven. (Pañca 5.78)
The hair of one who ages grows old; the teeth of one who ages decay;
the eyes and ears of one who ages fail; yet craving alone remains ever youthful.
Then, having reached that lake at the time of dawn, the monkey said to the king:
"O King, success belongs to those who enter while the sun has half-risen; therefore, let all the people enter at once.
You, however, must enter together with me."
"By which [path], having reached the place seen before,
I shall show you those many garlands of jewels. Then all those people entered and were devoured by the rākṣasa.
Then, while they were waiting for a long time, the king said to the monkey: "O leader of the troop, why is my retinue delayed?
Hearing this, the monkey quickly climbed a tree and said to the king: "O wicked monarch!
Your retinue has been devoured by a *rākṣasa* staying within the water."
I have fulfilled the enmity born of the destruction of my kin;
therefore, you may depart.
You were not admitted here because I considered you my master. And it is said:
One should return a favor for a favor done, and inflict injury in return for an injury received;
I see no fault in this, that one should act with wickedness toward the wicked.
"In that way, you have brought about the destruction of my lineage, and I, in turn, have done the same for yours.

Upon hearing this, the king, overcome with anger, departed on foot alone by the path by which he had come. When the monarch had gone, the one touched by the Rākṣasa emerged from the water and said joyfully:
The enemy is slain, a friend has been made, and the jewel-necklace was not lost; O monkey, you have done well in drinking the water through the stalk! (Pancatantra 5.81)
Therefore I say: "He who performs an action out of greed...
Having spoken thus, he said again to Cakradhara: "O friend, send me!"
"By which way shall I go to my own home?
Cakradhara said, "My good man,
wealth and friends are gathered for the sake of times of misfortune."
Therefore, having abandoned me in such a state, where will you go? And it is said:
"He who, displaying cruelty, abandons a friend in distress and departs—being ungrateful for that sin, he goes undoubtedly to hell. (Pañcatantra 5.82)
Suvarṇasiddhi said: "O sir, this would indeed be true if there were power in a place that can be reached;
however, this is a place that humans cannot reach."

No one has the power to release you; moreover, the more I observe the contortions of your face from the pain of the whirling wheel, the more I realize that I must depart immediately, lest some misfortune befall me as well. For it is said:
"O monkey, from the appearance of your face as it is seen, you have been seized by Death; he who passes [his time heedlessly] lives. (Pancatantra 5.83)
Cakradhara said: "How was that?
He replied:
Story 10.
The Story of the Evening Monkey:
In a certain city there lived a king named Bhadrasena.
He had a daughter named Ratnavatī, who was endowed with every auspicious mark.
A certain rākṣasa desires to carry her off;
he comes at night and enjoys her,
yet he is unable to seize her because she is protected by a magical safeguard.

At that time, she too experienced a state born from the presence of the *rākṣasa*, manifested through trembling and other such signs. After some time had passed, once during the middle of the night, that *rākṣasa* stood in a corner of the house.
Then the princess said to her friend: "Friend!"
"Look, this Vikāla constantly torments me at this very hour.
Is there any means to ward off that evil-souled one?
Upon hearing this, the Rākṣasa also reflected: "Surely, just as I do, some other person named Vikāla must also come here constantly for the sake of abducting her."
But even he is unable to carry her off.
Therefore, for the time being, having assumed the form of a horse and gone into the midst of the horses, I shall observe:
what is his appearance like, and what is his power?
Thus, having assumed the form of a horse, the rākṣasa stood in the midst of the horses.
When this was done, at the hour of midnight, a certain horse-thief entered Rājagṛha;
and having observed all the horses and recognizing that rākṣasa as the best among them, he mounted him.
In the meantime, the Rākṣasa thought to himself: "Surely this man named Vikāla, thinking me to be a thief, has come in anger to kill me.
So, what shall I do?
While he was reflecting thus, he too was struck with a whip-blow after the man had placed a bit in his mouth.
Then, his mind terrified by fear, he began to run;
the thief also, having gone some distance, began to try to steady him by pulling on the bridle,
but he went faster and faster with increasing speed.

Then, perceiving that the horse was ignoring the pull of the bit, the thief thought: "Aha! Horses of such a kind do not disregard the bit. Therefore, this must surely be a *rākṣasa* in the form of a horse.
Even though I see a certain patch of dusty ground, I shall throw myself there."
"I have no other way to live.
As he was thinking this and recollecting his chosen deity, the horse emerged from beneath the *baṭa* tree;
the thief, too, having reached a sprout of the *baṭa* tree, became entangled right there.
Then both of them, having become separate, partaking of supreme bliss and having regained hope for their lives, were restored.
Now, at that banyan tree, there was a certain monkey who was a friend of the rākṣasa;
seeing the rākṣasa terrified, he said: "O friend!"
"Why do you shrink away out of fear of the untruth?
This man is to be eaten; let him be eaten!
Hearing these words of the monkey, he too—
Assuming his true form, the thief turned back with a suspicious mind and faltering gait;
yet, recognizing that he had been summoned by the monkey, he seized the monkey's hanging tail with his mouth in anger and began to chew it.
The monkey, regarding him as even more formidable than a *rākṣasa*, said nothing out of fear.
Afflicted by pain alone, he remained with his eyes closed;
and the rākṣasa, beholding him in such a state, recited this verse:
"O monkey, from the appearance of your speech that is seen,"
"You have been seized at the wrong time; he who passes away lives."
Having said this, he vanished.
"Therefore, send me so that I may go home;
you, however, remain right here and enjoy the fruit of the tree of greed."
Cakradhara said: "O sir, this is without cause;
the auspicious and inauspicious for men come about through the power of destiny. And it has been said:
'Mount Trikūṭa is the fortress, and the ocean is the moat.'"
Rākṣasas were his warriors, wealth was obtained from the Giver of Riches (Kubera),
and the treatise composed by Uśanas was his scripture;
yet that Rāvaṇa perished through the power of fate.
And so it is said:
"The blind man, the hunchback, and the three-breasted princess—all three attained success through improper means, even though their karma was present before them. (Pañca 5.86)
Suvarṇasiddhi said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 11.
The Story of the Blind Man, the Hunchback, and the Three-Breasted Woman:
Here on this earth, in the northern region, there was a city named Madhupura;
there, a king named Madhusena reigned.

Once, while he was experiencing the pleasures of the senses, a daughter with three breasts was born to him. Then, having heard that a three-breasted girl had been born, the king said to his chamberlains: "Ho! Take this three-breasted girl and cast her far away into the forest, so that no one may know of her."
Having heard that, the chamberlains said: "O Great King, it is known that a girl with three breasts brings about misfortune;
nevertheless, Brahmins should be summoned and questioned so that neither of the two worlds is contradicted, for— [Verse follows]"
The intelligence of one who constantly inquires, listens, and retains [the teachings] without ceasing increases like a lotus by the rays of the sun.
And so it is said:
A wise man should always be one who asks questions;
in former times, a twice-born man was released from his bonds even though he had been seized by the Lord of Rākṣasas, through the power of his inquiries.
The king asked, "How was that?
They replied—
Story 12.
The Story of the Rākṣasa named Caṇḍakarman, O King.
In a certain region of the forest, there lived a rākṣasa named Caṇḍakarman.
Once, while wandering through the wilderness, he encountered a certain Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having mounted his shoulder, he said, "O leader, let us go.
The Brahmin, his mind terrified by fear, set out taking him with him.
Then, seeing his feet, which were as soft as the interior of a lotus, the Brahmin asked the Rākṣasa: "O sir!"
"Why are your feet so exceedingly tender?
The Rākṣasa replied, "Sir,
I have a vow."
"I do not touch the ground with my feet while they are still wet.
Having heard that, he reached the lake while reflecting on a means for his own liberation;
then the rākṣasa said: "O sir!"
"Until I have finished bathing and performed the ritual of worship to the deities and return, you must not go from this place to anywhere else.
When he had done so, the Brahmin thought: "Surely, after the ritual of worship to the deities is completed, he will devour me.
Therefore, I shall depart as quickly as possible."
"By this means, he shall not come upon my back with his feet still wet.
When this was carried out, the Rākṣasa, fearing a violation of his vow, did not go upon his back.
Therefore I say: "One should always be inquisitive."
Then, having heard that from them, the king summoned the twice-born and said: "O Brahmins, a daughter with three breasts has been born to me;
what remedy is there for her, or is there none?"
Any maiden among men who has missing limbs or extra limbs will lead to the destruction of her husband and the ruin of her own virtuous character.
Furthermore, any girl with three nipples who comes within the range of one's sight surely destroys her father quickly; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, let Your Majesty avoid seeing her;
likewise, if anyone should marry her, then having given her to him, [let this matter be concluded].
"He should be assigned to the abandonment of his country.
When this was done, there was no contradiction with the two worlds [of dharma and worldly custom].
Then, having heard those words of theirs, the king ordered a proclamation to be made everywhere by the sound of a drum: "O!"
"Whoever marries the princess Tristanī shall receive one hundred thousand gold pieces and undergo exile from the country.
While this proclamation was being made, a great deal of time passed,
yet no one accepted her hand in marriage.
She too, having reached the bloom of youth, remained in a well-concealed place, staying there while being guarded with great effort.
In that very city, there lived a certain blind man;
he had a hunchbacked servant named Mantharaka as his attendant, who carried a staff.
Having heard that sound of the drum from those two, they consulted with one another: "Let this drum be touched;
if by some chance, through fate, a maiden is obtained."
And there is the acquisition of gold;
thus, time passes in happiness through that acquisition of gold.
However, if death occurs due to some fault of his, [the result is different].
Then there comes an end to this suffering brought about by poverty. And it has been said:
"Modesty, affection, sweetness of voice, intellects, the splendor of youth, union with a beloved, attachment to one's kin, the removal of suffering, and elegance—[all these are lost]."
Dharma, the scriptures, the wisdom of the preceptor of the gods, purity, and concern for right conduct—all these exist within the full stomach-pot of living beings. (Pañcatantra 5.91)
Having spoken thus, the blind man went and touched that drum, and said: "O sir!"
"I shall marry that maiden, if the king grants her to me.
Then those royal officers went and reported to the king: "Your Majesty!"
"A certain blind man touched a drum;
in this matter, Your Majesty is the authority.
The king said:
Whether he be blind, deaf, afflicted with leprosy, or even of the lowest caste, let him take that maiden; he shall possess a hundred thousand [gold pieces] while living abroad.

Then, by the king’s command, those royal officers led him to the riverbank, gave the three-breasted woman to him according to the marriage rites along with a hundred thousand gold pieces, and having placed them on a boat, they said to the fishermen: "O men,
take this blind man together with his wife to some town in another country."
He was to be released along with the hunchback.
When this had been carried out, they reached a foreign land and, at a certain city pointed out by a fisherman, all three obtained houses for a price and spent their time in comfort;
however, the blind man remained lying on his couch.
Mantharaka performed the household duties;
as time passed in this manner, an illicit intimacy developed between Tristanī and Kubjaka.
Or rather, it is well said:
If the Śrītala tree were fire, if the moon were of the nature of burning, and if the ocean were sweet to women, then you would truly be a virtuous wife.
Then, on another day, Mantharaka was addressed by Tristanī: "O handsome one!
If this blind fellow could somehow be killed, then our time would pass in happiness."
"Therefore, let some poison be sought somewhere,
by giving which to him I may become happy.
One day, while wandering about, the hunchback found a dead black cobra.
Taking it, with a joyful mind, he went home and said to her: "O blessed lady, this black snake has been found.
Therefore, cut it into pieces, season it well with plenty of ginger and other spices, and give it to that blind man under the pretext that it is fish-meat, so that he may perish instantly."
"Since fish-meat is always dear to him," having said this, Mantharaka went outside.

She, too, having cut a black snake into pieces while the fire was blazing and placed it in a pot of buttermilk, became preoccupied with household chores and spoke to that one-eyed man with humility: "Noble husband!"
The fish meat you desire has been brought;
for you always inquire after it,
and those fish are now standing in the fire for purification.
"Therefore, while I attend to my household duties,
you take the ladle and stir them for a moment.
Having heard this, he too, with a joyful heart and licking the corners of his mouth, quickly rose, took the ladle, and began to stir.
Then, as he was crushing the fish, his eyes were touched by the vapor containing poison, and a blue film flowed down from them.
Though he had become blind, considering it to be of great benefit, he specifically began to catch the vapor with his eyes.
Thereupon, having regained his sight, he looked out as far as he could see.
For a while, he saw only pieces of black snakes in the midst of the buttermilk;
then he thought: "Aha! What is this?
She told me that my meal would be fish."
But these are indeed pieces of a black cobra;
therefore, I understand correctly the conduct of Triśaṅku.
Is this a sequence of means for my own destruction, or for that of the hunchback?
"Or is it someone else?
Thinking thus and concealing her true form, she performed her duties as before like one who was blind.
In the meantime, a hunchback arrived and, being fearless, began to serve the woman with three breasts by embracing, kissing, and other such acts.
Although he was blind, even as he looked about and saw no weapon whatsoever,
his mind agitated by anger, he went to the bed as before, seized the hunchback by both feet, whirled him over his own head with all his might, and struck Tristanī in the heart.
Then, by the blow from the hunchback, her third breast entered into her chest.
Likewise, by being whirled above the head by Bala, Kubja attained straightness.
Therefore I say: "The blind man and the hunchback" (84).
Suvarṇasiddhi said, "O sir, this is true."
Through the favor of destiny, everything becomes auspicious;
nevertheless, a person must act according to the words of the virtuous and should continue to conduct himself in this very manner.
Now, he who conducts himself in this very same way perishes just like you. And so it is said:
"Those with one belly but different necks, who consume various fruits,"
Those who do not remain united perish, like the Bharuṇḍa birds.
Cakradhara asked: "How was that?
He replied:
Story 13.
The Story of the Bhāruṇḍa Birds:

In a certain lake there lived a bird named Bhāruṇḍa, who had a single belly and two separate necks. While wandering along the shore of the ocean, he came upon a certain fruit, like nectar, which had been cast up by the waves.
While eating it, he said this: "Aha!
I have eaten many fruits brought by the waves of the ocean that were like nectar;
yet this has an unprecedented flavor."
"Is this produced from the Pārijāta or Haricandana trees? Or rather, has some fruit consisting of nectar been dropped by an unseen fate?
As he was speaking thus, it was said through his second mouth: "O sir!"
"If that is so, then give me a small portion as well, so that I too may experience the pleasure of the tongue.
Thereupon, laughing, the first speaker said: "For us two, there is but one stomach."
There is but one satisfaction; what, then, is the use of eating separately?
It would be better to satisfy one's beloved with this remainder.
Having spoken thus, he gave the remainder to Bhāruṇḍī;

she too, having tasted it, became exceedingly delighted and devoted to many endearments such as embracing, kissing, and showing honor. From that day forward, however, his second mouth remained anxious and despondent.
Then, on another day, a poisonous fruit was obtained through the second mouth.
Seeing it, he said to the other: "O pitiless one! O lowest of men!"
"O indifferent one!
I have obtained this poisonous fruit;
because of your insult, I shall eat it."
Another said: "Fool!
Do not do this! If you do so, there will be ruin for both of us."
Thus, by speaking in that manner, he consumed the fruit of his own contempt;
what more need be said? Both were ruined.
Therefore I say: "Those with one belly but separate necks" (92).
Cakradhara said: "This is true.
Therefore, go home; however, you must not go alone. And it has been said:"
One should not eat delicious food alone; one should not contemplate matters of profit alone;
one should not travel the road alone; and one should not remain awake alone among those who are asleep.
Moreover:
Even a base man can be a second companion on the road who brings security;
by having a crab as his second, [the merchant] preserved his life. (5.96)
Suvarṇasiddhi said, "How was that?
He replied:
Story 14.
The Story of the Brahmin Crab:
In a certain town there lived a Brahmin named Brahmadatta. Once, as he was setting out for a village on some business, he was addressed by his mother: "My dear child..."
"Why do you go alone?
Let some companion be sought.
He said, "Mother, do not be afraid."
"This path is free from danger;
I shall go alone for the sake of my task.
Then, having learned of his resolve, his mother took a crab from a nearby pond and said, "My child,"
"If you must certainly go,
then let this crab also be your companion;
take him with you and depart."
Following his mother’s words, he did not grasp it with both hands, but placed it inside a casket of camphor,
set it within his bowl, and set out quickly.
Then, as he was traveling, scorched by the heat of summer, he reached a certain tree standing by the road.
He was fast asleep right there. In the meantime, a snake emerged from a hollow in a tree and approached him;
out of extreme greed, it ate a small packet of camphor that had gone inside [his mouth].
That crab, remaining right there, took away the life of the serpent. When the Brahmin awoke and looked,
he saw a dead black snake lying near him upon a small casket of camphor.
Seeing him, he thought, "He has been killed by the crab," and becoming pleased, he said, "O friend!
What my mother said is true: that a man must have some companion."
"One should not travel alone;
for since I carried out his word with a heart filled with faith, I was protected from being killed by that crab.
Or rather, it is well said:"
The waning moon resorts to the sun, and when full, it causes the lord of waters to swell;
some are companions in times of misfortune, while others enjoy the prosperity of the wealthy.
In respect to a mantra, a sacred ford, a brahmin, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a teacher—
whatever one's conception is, such will be the accomplishment.
Having heard this, Suvarṇasiddhi took leave of him and returned to his own home.
Thus ends the fifth book, titled "The Unexamined Doer," in the *Pañcatantra* composed by Śrī Viṣṇuśarman. //5//
Even if this is so, nevertheless, show me that lion among thieves so that I may slay him;
for he who sees [him], he truly sees—
[let him be seized] by the king’s men.
